This distinction looks trivial and is anything but — it's the hinge the entire discipline turns on, and getting the notation right is the difference between "what I measured" and "what's actually true."
Statistics splits into two branches. Almost everything you'll ever do falls into one or the other, and confusing them is the single most common beginner mistake.

Statistics is the field that deals with the collection, organization, analysis, interpretation, and presentation of data. Every one of those steps points at a single destination: decision making. You gather data, make sense of it, and act — that's the whole arc, and if a step doesn't ultimately help someone decide something, it isn't doing its job.

Five percentiles capture the entire skeleton of a distribution — its center, its spread, and its extremes — in one compact summary. It's the basis of the box plot and of a beautifully simple, distribution-free way to flag outliers.

Central tendency and dispersion each compress a dataset to a single number. A histogram shows you the whole shape at once — it's the fastest way to see whether data is symmetric, skewed, or hiding fat tails.

Central tendency and dispersion summarize a distribution; percentiles locate a specific value within it. They're how you say "this observation is high" or "this is a bad day" precisely, without assuming any particular distribution shape.
A measure of central tendency answers the first question you ask of any dataset: where is it centered? There are three answers, and the gaps between them are as informative as the numbers themselves.

Center isn't enough. Two datasets can share the exact same mean and be completely different — one tightly clustered, one wildly spread. Dispersion measures that spread, and for a quant it's where risk lives.

Variance measures spread but leaves it in awkward squared units. Standard deviation is simply its square root — which puts the measure of spread back into the original units of the data, and that's why it's the number people actually quote.

documents.t: A random variable is a function that assigns a number to each outcome of a random process or experiment. The randomness lives in the process (a coin flip, a dice roll, tomorrow's market); the random variable is just the rule that turns each possible outcome into a value you can do math on.

A variable is any measurable property that can take different values from one observation to the next. Age, height, gender, price, return — each is a variable because it varies across the things you measure.

documents.t: The p-value defined precisely — how likely your observations are if the null were true — the significance level α, the 95% confidence region with its 0.025 tails, the coin-fairness example, and the decision rule p < α ⇒ reject.

The four outcomes of any test laid out as reality vs decision — the two correct ones and the two mistakes. Type I (false positive, rate α), Type II (false negative, rate β), statistical power, and the trade-off you can never fully escape.
documents.s: Type I and Type II Errors

documents.t: The estimation face of the same z/t machinery — a point estimate reached out by a margin of error to give a range for the unknown population mean. The formula point estimate ± z(α/2)·σ/√n, worked on the CAT-exam example to the 95% interval [480.8, 559.2].

What to do when the population σ is unknown — estimate it with the sample s and switch from the z to the t-statistic. Degrees of freedom (n − 1) explained, the fatter tails of the t, and why it converges to the normal as the sample grows.
Putting the t-distribution to work — a fully worked one-sample t-test. Does a medication change IQ? From hypotheses and degrees of freedom to the critical value ±2.045 and a t-statistic of 10.96.

The test for a mean when the population σ is known and n ≥ 30. The family of tests (z, t, chi-square, ANOVA), the z-statistic, and two fully worked examples — a two-tailed height test and a one-tailed bulb-warranty test — from hypotheses to p-value to verdict.
documents.s: Hypothesis Testing and Statistical Analysis: The Z-Test

documents.t: A single decision tree for choosing between the z-test and the t-test — driven by whether you know the population σ and whether the sample exceeds 30 — plus a side-by-side comparison.
documents.s: When to Use a t-test vs a z-test

documents.t: What statistics means for a quant, the topics in this section, and where to start.

Simple, multiple, and logistic regression seen through the unifying lens of generalized linear models (GLMs) — with runnable examples and a Bayesian ROPE-based view of when an effect actually matters.
Handling outliers, non-normal data, and distribution-free methods. Notes in progress.
AR, MA, ARMA, ARIMA, and GARCH models for financial data. Notes in progress.
Why derivatives exist — hedging, speculation, arbitrage and leverage — with worked FX and commodity examples, then options: premium, exercise style, calls, puts and the four positions.
A running log of the market blow-ups, manias and incidents worth understanding in full — what happened, the numbers, the charts, and the lesson.

A post-mortem of how Jane Street — the most profitable trading firm on Wall Street — took a ~$15B loss in July 2026, its first down month in a decade, from its 'hedge-fund side': AI-infrastructure bets, Asian equities, and a stake in the Situational Awareness fund. Why the same July storm wiped out one fund and barely dented the other.

A post-mortem of South Korea’s summer-2026 stock-market crash: how government-blessed single-stock leveraged ETFs, stacked on record margin loans and concentrated in Samsung and SK Hynix, turned a 116% boom into a 38.6% collapse — 360,000 retail accounts force-liquidated, and an emergency rewrite of the rules.

A Big Event: a coalition of state attorneys general, led by California's Rob Bonta, put Meta on trial in Oakland federal court in August 2026 — arguing Facebook and Instagram were deliberately designed to addict children, and that Meta knew and hid the harm. The 'Big Tobacco moment' for social media — the allegations, the internal documents, why Section 230 didn't save Meta this time, and how it ended in a $17 billion settlement.
documents.s: Meta on trial: the social-media reckoning

documents.t: A deep post-mortem of how Leopold Aschenbrenner's ~4x-levered, hyper-concentrated AI-infrastructure fund went from +439% to a 67% wipe-out in six trading days — the trigger, the positions, the failed hedges, the margin calls, and the block trade to Citadel.

A Big Event: on August 19, 2026, President Trump shared a White House podium with the CEOs of Coinbase, Ripple and Robinhood, flanked by the SEC and CFTC chairs — pushing the CLARITY Act and a regulate-by-agency pivot. Stacked with a Treasury buyback surprise, it sparked a sharp crypto rally: Bitcoin past $68,000, over $1B of shorts liquidated, Coinbase and Strategy up double digits. What a policy tailwind looks like — and why summits can also mark tops.
A Jupyter-style Python notebook that runs entirely in your browser — numpy, pandas and matplotlib included. No installs, no server.
A live, read-only view of my Alpaca paper-trading account — a scrubable equity curve, allocation, a performance read, open positions, closed round-trips, and the full order log.
My quantitative finance projects — models, backtests, tools, and experiments.
Read a book from the Library, right here in your browser.
Research papers in quantitative finance I'm reading, working through, and collecting — with a note on why each one matters.
Courses, lectures, and channels for learning quantitative finance.
An interactive, trackable roadmap for becoming a quant — five pillars across three levels, scored against the Trader, Developer, and Researcher tracks.
Quant firms and companies that hire from quantitative finance.
A market terminal — live stock charts and news.
Software and tools I use for quantitative finance work.
Study notes by field — Finance, Mathematics, Statistics, Probability, Economics, Programming, and Machine Learning.

About Who I am​ I'm Joyeb Kashyeb — a computer science student at Jacksonville State University with a concentration in data science, deliberately building toward a career in quantitative finance. This site is my public workbench for that climb. I'm currently open to internships and roles in quantitative finance, quantitative research, and data science. If you're hiring or just want to connect, the links below reach me directly. Why I built this​ I learn by building. Reading a formula tells me almost nothing; implementing it, breaking it, and watching it respond to a slider is when it becomes mine. The rule I hold myself to across every page here: if I can't simulate or test an idea, I don't trust that I've understood it. That's why the Python runs in your browser, the pricing models have draggable inputs, and every finished topic ends with a quiz. What I'm studying right now​ Stochastic calculus — Brownian motion, Itô's lemma, and the machinery under every pricing model. Derivatives pricing — payoffs, binomial trees, Black–Scholes and the Greeks. Bayesian inference — priors, posteriors, and MCMC, headed toward probabilistic models of returns. What I've built​ Beyond the notes themselves: a browser-based Python notebook with numpy, pandas and matplotlib, a set of interactive pricing and probability labs, a live market terminal, and finance-focused coding projects like a FIFO stock ledger. The full list lives on the Projects page. Where to find me​ The full source of this site lives on GitHub. If you spot an error in any note, the "Edit this page" link at the bottom of every doc opens the GitHub editor — corrections are welcome. How rates are set, the yield curve, and their effect on markets. Einstein (allegedly) called compound interest the eighth wonder of the world. Whether he said it or not, the math earns the title — a small rate difference, given enough time, becomes an enormous outcome difference: FV=P(1+rm)mtFV = P\left(1 + \frac{r}{m}\right)^{mt}FV=P(1+mr​)mt

LabCompound interest — the eighth wonder Starting amount $1,000 Monthly deposit $100 Annual rate 8.0% Years 20 CompoundingAnnuallyQuarterlyMonthlyDaily Final balance $64,222 You contributed $25,000 Interest earned $39,222 Growth multiple 2.57× 020,00040,00060,0000y5y10y15y20ybalancecontributionsYears The gap between the two curves is money your money made. Notice it barely exists for the first few years, then dominates — that is why quants say time in the market beats timing the market. Experiments to run: The time lever. Set 8% for 10 years, note the interest earned — now drag to 40 years. Quadrupling the time multiplies the interest by far more than 4×. Compounding is nonlinear. The rate lever. At 30 years, compare 4% vs 8%. Doubling the rate roughly quadruples the final interest. This is why the level of interest rates moves entire markets. Compounding frequency. Switch annual → daily. The gain is real but modest — frequency matters much less than rate and time. (The limit is continuous compounding, FV = Pe^rt.) Zero deposit test. Set the monthly deposit to $0 — pure compounding on the initial amount. That curve is discounting in reverse: it is exactly how bond prices relate to yields.

Discounting: every future cash flow is worth less today by exactly this math run backwards — present value = FV / (1 + r)ᵗ. All of fixed income sits on this. The yield curve plots the rate r for each maturity t. Its slope (steep, flat, inverted) is one of the most watched recession signals in macro. Policy rates (Fed, ECB, NRB) anchor the short end of the curve; expectations and term premia shape the rest.

Micro and macroeconomics, monetary vs. fiscal policy, and the economic context behind markets.

Markets don't move in a vacuum — they price expectations about growth, inflation, and policy. A quant doesn't need to be a macroeconomist, but the models don't hold without the context: interest rates set the discount factor in every valuation, central-bank policy moves the whole yield curve, and regime shifts break correlations that a backtest assumed were stable. Economics is the layer that explains why the inputs to your models change.

A forward and a future are an obligation. An option is a right, but not the obligation. Everything in this note follows from that one difference.
documents.s: Introduction to Derivative (Call & Put Option) – Part A

documents.t: You hold an option contract to buy XYZ stock at $100, three months from now. At t=3t = 3t=3 the market can be anywhere. Two cases: Case 1 — the stock rises to $110. Your contract lets you buy at $100 while the market charges $110. You exercise: buy at 100, and you are $10 better off. Case 2 — the stock falls to $90. Your contract says $100, the market says $90. Exercising would mean paying $100 for something worth $90 — a $10 loss. So you do not execute the deal. You walk away. With a forward or a future, Case 2 is not a choice: you are obligated, and you take the $10 loss. The option gives you the flexibility to buy or not.

Buyer (holder) of the option Seller (writer / underwriter) Has The right to buy or sell — Obliged? Not obligated Always obligated to buy or sell the underlying The buyer picks whichever outcome suits them; the seller has to live with that choice. Which raises the obvious question.
documents.s: Buyer and seller are not symmetric

documents.t: Because the seller is at a structural disadvantage. They carry the obligation and have no say in whether the contract is exercised. The premium is what compensates them for taking on that obligation. It flows once, at the start, from buyer to seller: Buyer (long) ──── premium ────→ Seller (short) holds the right carries the obligation
documents.s: Why does the buyer pay a premium?

documents.t: A call option gives the holder the right to buy the underlying asset at the strike price KKK, on a predetermined date. You would only want a fixed price to buy at if you think the price is going up. Position What you did Expectation Long call Bought the right to buy Price will rise → bullish Short call Sold the right to buy Price will decline → bearish

A put option gives the holder the right to sell the underlying asset at KKK, on a predetermined date. Position What you did Expectation Long put Bought the right to sell Price will fall → bearish Short put Sold the right to sell Price will rise → bullish A memory aid: a bull attacks by throwing its horns up; a bear swipes down. Note the pairing is not "call = bullish". It is the combination: long call and short put are bullish; short call and long put are bearish.

Underlying asset — stocks, commodities, currencies, bonds. Strike price KKK — the price the holder can buy or sell at. Expiration date — after which the option expires worthless. Exercise style — American (exercisable at any point) or European (exercisable only at maturity). These names are conventions, not geographical locations — a European-style option is not a European product. Premium — the price paid by the holder to the seller.
documents.s: The five characteristics of an option

documents.t: This distinction matters and is easy to blur: Payoff is the value of the option at expiry, ignoring the premium. Profit is the payoff minus the premium you paid (or plus the premium you received). Payoff — premium removed: Long call = max⁡(ST−K, 0)Short call = −max⁡(ST−K, 0)Long put = max⁡(K−ST, 0)Short put = −max⁡(K−ST, 0)\begin{aligned} \text{Long call} \;&=\; \max(S_T - K,\, 0) &\qquad \text{Short call} \;&=\; -\max(S_T - K,\, 0)\\[2pt] \text{Long put} \;&=\; \max(K - S_T,\, 0) &\qquad \text{Short put} \;&=\; -\max(K - S_T,\, 0) \end{aligned}Long callLong put​=max(ST​−K,0)=max(K−ST​,0)​Short callShort put​=−max(ST​−K,0)=−max(K−ST​,0)​ Profit — what you actually walk away with: Long call = max⁡(ST−K, 0)−premiumShort call = premium−max⁡(ST−K, 0)Long put = max⁡(K−ST, 0)−premiumShort put = premium−max⁡(K−ST, 0)\begin{aligned} \text{Long call} \;&=\; \max(S_T - K,\, 0) - \text{premium}\\[2pt] \text{Short call} \;&=\; \text{premium} - \max(S_T - K,\, 0)\\[2pt] \text{Long put} \;&=\; \max(K - S_T,\, 0) - \text{premium}\\[2pt] \text{Short put} \;&=\; \text{premium} - \max(K - S_T,\, 0) \end{aligned}Long callShort callLong putShort put​=max(ST​−K,0)−premium=premium−max(ST​−K,0)=max(K−ST​,0)−premium=premium−max(K−ST​,0)​ The max(·, 0) is the option's whole character: you never exercise into a loss, so the payoff can never go below zero. Only the profit can. Everything below is profit — the version with the premium in it, since that is what determines whether the trade made money. The short is always the negative of the long — the seller's payoff is −(long payoff)-(\text{long payoff})−(long payoff). Derivatives are a zero-sum game: what one side gains, the other loses, exactly. Note also who pays and who receives: Long call and long put → pay the premium. Short call and short put → receive the premium. The short put can also be written premium+min⁡(ST−K, 0)\text{premium} + \min(S_T - K,\, 0)premium+min(ST​−K,0), which is the same thing.

Above the strike each dollar of stock is a dollar of payoff. Breakeven is at ST=K+premium=95+1=96S_T = K + \text{premium} = 95 + 1 = 96ST​=K+premium=95+1=96
The mirror image, same K=95K = 95K=95, premium 111: STS_TST​ Payoff =1−max⁡(ST−95,0)= 1 - \max(S_T-95,0)=1−max(ST​−95,0) 90–95 +1 (keeps the whole premium) 96 0 97 −1 98 −2 99 −3 100 −4

Same K=95K = 95K=95, premium 111 — now the payoff runs the other way: STS_TST​ max⁡(K−ST,0)\max(K-S_T,0)max(K−ST​,0) − premium Payoff 90 5 −1 +4 91 4 −1 +3 92 3 −1 +2 93 2 −1 +1 94 1 −1 0 ← breakeven 95 0 −1 −1 96 0 −1 −1 97+ 0 −1 −1 Breakeven for a put is K−premium=94K - \text{premium} = 94K−premium=94. Worked from the contract's side: you bought the right to sell XYZ at $100. If the market goes to $110 you do not execute — why sell at 100 what fetches 110? If it drops to $90 you do execute, gaining K - S_T = 100 - 90 = \10$.

Long calllimited loss · unlimited profitShort calllimited profit · unlimited lossLong putlimited loss · limited profitShort putlimited profit · limited lossKKKK The asymmetry is the point: Position Loss Profit Long call Limited (the premium) Unlimited — the price can keep rising Short call Unlimited Limited (the premium) Long put Limited (the premium) Limited — the price can only fall to zero Short put Limited Limited (the premium) Selling a naked call is the one position here with genuinely unbounded loss.

An option is a right, not an obligation — the holder chooses, the writer must comply. The premium exists to compensate the writer for carrying that obligation. Call = right to buy, put = right to sell; long = holds the right, short = carries the obligation and receives the premium. Bullish: long call, short put. Bearish: short call, long put. All four payoffs are built from max(·, 0), and long and short are exact negatives — a zero-sum game. Breakeven is K+premiumK + \text{premium}K+premium for a call and K−premiumK - \text{premium}K−premium for a put. Next: moneyness, and what corporate actions do to an option.

Part A covered what calls and puts are and what they pay. This note covers the two things that decide whether you would exercise at all — moneyness — and the corporate actions that quietly rewrite the contract underneath you.
documents.s: Introduction to Derivative (Call & Put Option) – Part B

documents.t: The moneyness of an option refers to the relationship between the strike price of the option and the current price of the underlying asset. So it is a statement about the pair (ST, K)(S_T,\, K)(ST​,K), and there are only three possible relationships: ST>KST=KST<KS_T > K \qquad S_T = K \qquad S_T < KST​>KST​=KST​<K Three names follow: Term Meaning In the money (ITM) Money coming in — exercising is profitable At the money (ATM) No profit, no loss Out of the money (OTM) Money going out — exercising would lose

For a call (right to buy), you want the market above your strike: Call ITM ST>KS_T > KST​>K → profit ATM ST=KS_T = KST​=K → zero OTM ST<KS_T < KST​<K → loss For a put (right to sell), it is exactly reversed — you want the market below your strike: Put ITM ST<KS_T < KST​<K ATM ST=KS_T = KST​=K OTM ST>KS_T > KST​>K Side by side: Call Put ITM ST>KS_T > KST​>K ST<KS_T < KST​<K ATM ST=KS_T = KST​=K ST=KS_T = KST​=K OTM ST<KS_T < KST​<K ST>KS_T > KST​>K
documents.s: Which is which depends on the option

documents.t: Moneyness does not consider the premium. It is purely the intrinsic relationship between STS_TST​ and KKK. That matters, because an option can be in the money and still lose you money overall. From Part A: a long call with K=95K = 95K=95 and a premium of 1, at ST=95.5S_T = 95.5ST​=95.5, is ITM — but the payoff is 0.5−1=−0.50.5 - 1 = -0.50.5−1=−0.5. Moneyness tells you whether you would exercise; it does not tell you whether the trade was profitable. So moneyness decides one thing at expiry: whether the option is exercised or left to expire.
documents.s: One thing to be careful about

documents.t: The other half of "when can I act" is the exercise style: American — exercisable at any point during the life of the contract. Its moneyness can be checked, and acted on, all the way along. European — exercisable only at maturity. Moneyness only matters on the final date. American — exercisable at any pointEuropean — exercisable only at maturityt = 0maturity

An option contract is written on a number of shares at a strike price. A corporate action can change what a "share" even means — so the contract has to be adjusted, or the holder would be arbitrarily enriched or wiped out.

In a 3-for-1 stock split, three new shares are issued for each existing share. One XYZ share becomes three XYZ shares. The company is not worth more afterwards; the same value is just divided into more, cheaper pieces. So the option contract is adjusted to keep the holder exactly where they were. The rule: Quantity Adjustment for an nnn-for-1 split Strike price Divided by nnn → K/nK/nK/n Number of shares Multiplied by nnn

Suppose you hold a call option: Pre-split Post-split (3-for-1) Strike KKK $90 90/3=90/3 =90/3= $30 Shares per contract 100 100×3=100 \times 3 =100×3= 300 Total strike value 90×100=90 \times 100 = 90×100= $9,000 30×300=30 \times 300 = 30×300= $9,000 Identical. The split changed the units, not your position.

The same rule with n=4n = 4n=4: strike becomes K/4K/4K/4, share count becomes ×4\times 4×4. Pre-split Post-split Strike $100 $25 Shares 100 400 Total $10,000 $10,000 Again unchanged — which is the entire point of the adjustment.

A stock dividend involves a company issuing more shares to its existing stakeholders. A stock dividend is quoted as a percentage, and the trick is to convert that percentage into an equivalent split: 100%dividend % = shares you must already hold to receive one new share\frac{100\%}{\text{dividend }\%} \;=\; \text{shares you must already hold to receive one new share}dividend %100%​=shares you must already hold to receive one new share Stock dividend 100/%100/\%100/% Meaning Equivalent split 10% 10 1 new share for every 10 held 11-for-10 20% 5 1 new share for every 5 held 6-for-5 25% 4 1 new share for every 4 held 5-for-4 Once you have the equivalent split, the adjustment is the same rule as before. For a 25% stock dividend (a 5-for-4 split): shares → ×54K → ×45\text{shares} \;\to\; \times \tfrac{5}{4} \qquad\qquad K \;\to\; \times \tfrac{4}{5}shares→×45​K→×54​

Consider a put option contract to sell 100 shares of the company at $15 per share. The company then announces a 25% stock dividend. 100%/25%=4100\% / 25\% = 4100%/25%=4, so one new share for every four held — a 5-for-4 split. Pre-dividend Post-dividend Number of shares 100 100×54=100 \times \tfrac{5}{4} =100×45​= 125 Strike KKK $15 15×45=15 \times \tfrac{4}{5} =15×54​= $12 Total value 100×15=100 \times 15 =100×15= $1,500 125×12=125 \times 12 =125×12= $1,500 Unchanged, exactly as with a split.
documents.s: Worked example — a put, and a 25% stock dividend

documents.t: This one catches people out: A cash dividend does NOT adjust the option contract. If XYZ pays $3 per share in cash, the option contract is left alone. Only stock dividends and stock splits change the strike and the share count. (Cash dividends do still matter for pricing — they are an input to the Black-Scholes-Merton model — but they do not rewrite the contract terms.)

Moneyness is the relationship between STS_TST​ and KKK — ITM, ATM or OTM. For a call ITM means ST>KS_T > KST​>K; for a put it is reversed, ST<KS_T < KST​<K. Moneyness ignores the premium. It decides whether you exercise, not whether you profited. American options can be exercised any time, European only at maturity. A stock split divides the strike and multiplies the share count, leaving the contract's total value untouched. A stock dividend does the same thing, once you convert the percentage into an equivalent split via 100%/dividend %100\%/\text{dividend }\%100%/dividend % — a 25% dividend is a 5-for-4 split. A cash dividend does not adjust the contract at all.

A futures contract is marked to market daily: gains and losses are settled every single day rather than accumulating quietly until expiry. That is what stops a losing party from walking away at maturity owing more than they can pay — but it only works if there is money in the account to settle against. That money is the margin.
documents.s: Introduction to Derivative (Operation of Margin Account)

documents.t: a) Margin account — a type of account that traders must maintain with their broker in order to engage in trading. b) Initial margin (IM) — the minimum amount of capital a trader must deposit in the margin account to open a futures position. It is usually a small percentage of the contract's total value, typically ranging from about 2% to 12%. Where in that range depends on the volatility of the asset — a more volatile underlying demands more margin. It acts as collateral, ensuring the trader can cover potential losses. c) Maintenance margin (MM) — a threshold level the margin account must maintain after the trade has been initiated. It sits below the initial margin. d) Margin call — if the account balance falls below the maintenance margin, the broker issues a margin call, and the trader must deposit additional funds to bring the account back up to the initial margin level. Variation margin is the name for that top-up: the amount of money required to restore the account to the initial margin level. Note the asymmetry that trips people up: the call is triggered by falling below MM, but the amount you must pay restores you all the way to IM — not merely back to MM.

Initial margin $12,000, maintenance margin $9,000: Balance Below MM? Margin call Day 1 $11,000 No — Day 2 $10,000 No — Day 3 $8,000 Yes Deposit $4,000 to restore $12,000 That $4,000 is the variation margin.

This is the full mechanic, day by day. A trader contacts their broker to buy two December gold futures contracts. The current futures price is $1,250 per ounce, and the contract size is 100 ounces, so the trader has contracted to buy 200 ounces at that price. Parameter Value Position Long 2 contracts = 200 oz Trade price $1,250 / oz Initial margin $6,000 per contract = $12,000 Maintenance margin $9,000 Each day the position is marked to market. Because the trader is long 200 ounces, the daily gain is daily gain=(today’s settlement−yesterday’s settlement)×200\text{daily gain} = (\text{today's settlement} - \text{yesterday's settlement}) \times 200daily gain=(today’s settlement−yesterday’s settlement)×200 Day Settlement ($/oz) Daily gain ($) Cumulative ($) Balance ($) Margin call — 1,250.00 — — 12,000 1 1,241.00 −1,800 −1,800 10,200 2 1,238.30 −540 −2,340 9,660 3 1,244.60 +1,260 −1,080 10,920 4 1,241.30 −660 −1,740 10,260 5 1,240.10 −240 −1,980 10,020 6 1,236.20 −780 −2,760 9,240 7 1,229.90 −1,260 −4,020 7,980 ← below $9,000: call for $4,020 8 1,230.80 +180 −3,840 12,180 9 1,225.40 −1,080 −4,920 11,100 10 1,228.10 +540 −4,380 11,640 11 1,211.00 −3,420 −7,800 8,220 ← below $9,000: call for $3,780 12 1,211.00 0 −7,800 12,000 13 1,214.30 +660 −7,140 12,660 14 1,216.10 +360 −6,780 13,020 15 1,223.00 +1,380 −5,400 14,400 16 1,226.90 +780 −4,620 15,180 Reading it: Day 6 ends at $9,240. Uncomfortable, but still above the $9,000 maintenance margin — no call. Day 7 the price drops to 1,229.90, a $1,260 loss, taking the balance to $7,980. That is below the maintenance margin, so the broker calls for $4,020 — the amount that restores the account to the $12,000 initial margin, not to the $9,000 threshold. Day 11 is the big one: gold falls 17.10 in a day, which on 200 ounces is a $3,420 loss. Balance $8,220 → a second call for $3,780. The position then recovers. By day 16 the balance is $15,180. Sanity check on the whole thing: the trader deposited $12,000 + $4,020 + $3,780 = $19,800 and finished with $15,180 — a net loss of $4,620, which is exactly the cumulative column, and exactly (1,226.90 − 1,250.00) × 200. The margin account never changes the economics; it only guarantees the money is there to settle them.
documents.s: Worked example — two gold futures contracts

documents.t: Two related restrictions, both established by regulatory bodies (and so differing by country).

The maximum number of option contracts an investor or entity can hold on the same side of the market. "Same side" means positions expressing the same directional view: Side Positions Bullish long call and short put Bearish short call and long put So a long call and a short put count together against the limit — you cannot evade it by splitting a bullish bet across two instruments. With a limit of, say, 250,000 contracts, you cannot hold more than 250,000 option contracts on one side. Since one option contract is 100 shares, that is 250,000×100=25,000,000 shares250{,}000 \times 100 = 25{,}000{,}000 \text{ shares}250,000×100=25,000,000 shares Why the limit exists: to stop large entities from controlling too much of the market in a particular stock's options, and so to prevent market manipulation or liquidity problems.

Restricts the number of option contracts an investor or entity can exercise over a specific period — typically five consecutive business days. The position limit caps what you can hold; the exercise limit caps what you can act on in a window. Both close off the same abuse from different sides.

Futures are marked to market daily, and the margin account is what makes that settlement possible. Initial margin opens the position (~2–12% of contract value, driven by volatility). Maintenance margin is the lower threshold you must stay above. Fall below the MM and you get a margin call — and the variation margin you must post restores the account to the initial margin, not the threshold. On the gold example, two calls ($4,020 and $3,780) kept a position alive whose total loss was $4,620. Position limits cap contracts held on the same side of the market; exercise limits cap contracts exercised over ~5 business days. Both exist to prevent manipulation and liquidity problems.
Two worked examples, both with the numbers carried all the way through. The first uses options to reduce risk; the second uses them to magnify it. Same instrument, opposite purposes.
documents.s: Introduction to Derivative (Practical Example on Options)

documents.t: The situation. An investor owns 1,000 shares of Company A, currently trading at $28. They are concerned about a possible share price decline over the next two months and want protection. The choice. Buy ten July put option contracts on the company's stock with a strike price of $27.50. Parameter Value Shares held 1,000 @ $28 Strike KKK $27.50 Premium $1 per share Contract size 100 shares Contracts bought 10 → covers 1,000 shares Total cost 1×100×10=1 \times 100 \times 10 =1×100×10= $1,000 The strategy costs $1,000, but guarantees the shares can be sold for at least $27.50 per share during the life of the option. That sentence is the whole idea of a hedge: you have bought a floor.

Two separate P/Ls, then the combination: Option P/L = max⁡(27.5−S, 0)×1000 − 1000Stock P/L = (S−28)×1000\begin{aligned} \text{Option P/L} \;&=\; \max(27.5 - S,\, 0) \times 1000 \;-\; 1000\\[2pt] \text{Stock P/L} \;&=\; (S - 28) \times 1000 \end{aligned}Option P/LStock P/L​=max(27.5−S,0)×1000−1000=(S−28)×1000​ Stock price SSS Option P/L ($) Stock P/L ($) Combined ($) 20 +6,500 −8,000 −1,500 21 +5,500 −7,000 −1,500 22 +4,500 −6,000 −1,500 23 +3,500 −5,000 −1,500 24 +2,500 −4,000 −1,500 25 +1,500 −3,000 −1,500 26 +500 −2,000 −1,500 27 −500 −1,000 −1,500 28 −1,000 0 −1,000 29 −1,000 +1,000 0 30 −1,000 +2,000 +1,000 32 −1,000 +4,000 +3,000 34 −1,000 +6,000 +5,000 Read the last column. Below $27.50 the combined result is frozen at −$1,500, no matter how far the stock falls. At $20 the unhedged shareholder has lost $8,000; the hedged one has lost $1,500. Above the strike the put expires worthless and the investor keeps the upside, minus the $1,000 premium. Where does −$1,500 come from? The floor is $27.50 per share, so the shares are worth at least 27.50 × 1000 = $27,500; subtract the $1,000 premium and the position is worth $26,500 against the $28,000 it started at. maximum loss = 28,000−(27.50×1000)+1,000 = $1,500\text{maximum loss} \;=\; 28{,}000 - (27.50 \times 1000) + 1{,}000 \;=\; \$1{,}500maximum loss=28,000−(27.50×1000)+1,000=$1,500 The trade-off: the investor gave up $1,000 of certain money to convert an open-ended downside into a known, capped one. On the option leg alone, breakeven is at S=26.50S = 26.50S=26.50 (where the $1 premium is exactly recovered).
documents.s: What it does, price by price

documents.t: The situation. A speculator believes a stock will increase in value over the next two months. The stock currently trades at $20. A two-month call option with a $22.50 strike is selling for $1. The speculator is willing to invest $2,000. Two ways to spend the same $2,000: Alternative What it buys A 100 shares at $20 = $2,000 B 2,000 call options (20 contracts) at $1 = $2,000

December stock price A: 100 shares B: 20 call contracts $15 (down) −$500 −$2,000 $27 (up) +$700 +$7,000 The same $2,000, the same view, and wildly different consequences. On the way up the option returns ten times what the shares do. On the way down it loses everything, while the shareholder is down only a quarter of their stake.

Option P/L = max⁡(S−22.5, 0)×2000 − 2000Stock P/L = (S−20)×100\begin{aligned} \text{Option P/L} \;&=\; \max(S - 22.5,\, 0) \times 2000 \;-\; 2000\\[2pt] \text{Stock P/L} \;&=\; (S - 20) \times 100 \end{aligned}Option P/LStock P/L​=max(S−22.5,0)×2000−2000=(S−20)×100​ SSS Option P/L ($) Stock P/L ($) 15.5 −2,000 −450 16.5 −2,000 −350 17.5 −2,000 −250 18.5 −2,000 −150 19.5 −2,000 −50 20.5 −2,000 +50 21.5 −2,000 +150 22.5 −2,000 +250 23.5 0 +350 24.5 +2,000 +450 25.5 +4,000 +550 26.5 +6,000 +650 27.5 +8,000 +750 Note the shape. The option line is flat at −$2,000 for every price below the $22.50 strike — the speculator is wiped out identically whether the stock ends at 15.5 or 22.5. Then it turns and climbs at 2,000 per dollar, twenty times the slope of the share position. Breakeven is at S=K+premium=22.50+1=$23.50S = K + \text{premium} = 22.50 + 1 = \$23.50S=K+premium=22.50+1=$23.50 which is where the option column crosses zero.

Leverage the position with options. The option gives exposure to 2,000 shares for the price of 100. That is the leverage: a large exposure for a small outlay. It amplifies the return — and amplifies the loss in exactly the same proportion. The shareholder needs the stock to fall to zero to lose everything; the option holder only needs it to finish a cent below $22.50.

The same instrument hedges or speculates depending on how it is used against the position you already hold. A protective put buys a floor: the 1,000-share holder converted an $8,000 loss at $20 into a capped $1,500, at a cost of $1,000, while keeping the upside. A long call used for speculation gives leverage: $2,000 controlled 2,000 shares instead of 100, turning a $700 gain into $7,000 — and a $500 loss into a total $2,000 loss. Breakeven in both cases is the strike adjusted by the premium: K−PK - PK−P for the put leg, K+PK + PK+P for the call.

Good models and rigorous validation are not enough on their own. Someone has to own the framework, staff it, and be accountable when it fails. That is governance. Model risk governance is provided at the highest level by the Board of Directors (BOD) and Senior Management (SM), when they establish a bank-wide approach to model risk management. It fits into the broader risk management of the organisation.
# Component 1 Board of Directors and Senior Management 2 Policies and Procedures 3 Roles and Responsibilities 4 Internal Audit 5 External Resources 6 Model Inventory 7 Documentation

The BOD delegates to Senior Management, whose duties are: Establishing policies and procedures Establishing compliance Assigning competent staff Overseeing model development Overseeing model implementation Evaluating results Overseeing model validation And the board's own responsibility is stated in risk terms: Board members must ensure that model risk is within the tolerance limit. That phrasing matters — it treats model risk the same way a board treats credit or market risk: something with a stated appetite that must be kept inside it, not a technical matter delegated away entirely.
documents.s: 1 — Board of Directors and Senior Management

documents.t: All aspects of model risk management should be covered by suitable policies. Those policies must cover: Model and model risk definitions Acceptable practices for model development Assessment of model risk Appropriate model validation Model governance Policies should identify the roles and responsibilities within the MRM framework, with clear detail on: staff expertise authority reporting lines Note the recurrence of authority and reporting lines — the same requirement that made validation independence meaningful. A policy that names a validator without granting them standing achieves nothing.

The roles in MRM can be divided into ownership, control and compliance. Business units are responsible for the model risk associated with their business strategies. That is the important allocation: model risk belongs to the business that uses the model, not to the quantitative team that built it.

The model owner holds accountability for the model — its performance development implementation use validation One named person is answerable for the whole lifecycle. Without that, a model with problems has no natural home and drifts.

A bank's internal audit should assess the overall effectiveness of the MRM framework. Audit checks the framework, not the models The guidance is careful here, and the distinction is easy to miss: Internal audit should not replicate MRM activities, but instead evaluate whether the MRM is comprehensive, rigorous and effective. Validation asks is this model right? Internal audit asks is the validation function itself working? Duplicating the validators' work would waste the audit's independence on a question already being answered. Staff that look at the effectiveness of MRM should be expert in their field of work. What internal audit checks: Procedures for updating models are clearly documented Check model owners are meeting standards or not Data is reliable or not Review validation activities

Although MRM is an internal process, a bank can also decide to engage external resources for the MRM framework — for developing, implementing, validating, or model governance. But engaging outside help does not transfer responsibility: Whenever external resources are used: the scope of work should be clearly written and agreed there must be a designated internal team which should look upon the work conducted by the external resources

Banks should maintain a comprehensive set of information for: models implemented models under development models retired — the ones not being used now A team maintains a firm-wide inventory of all the models, in order to evaluate the model risk in aggregate. That last phrase is the reason the inventory exists. The overview note established that aggregate model risk is affected by interaction and dependencies among models — one model's output feeding another's input. You cannot see that exposure model-by-model. Only a firm-wide inventory makes the dependency graph visible.
Purpose of the model Product for which the model is designed and used Any limitations List of input variables and output variables Function of the model When the model was last updated

Documentation runs through everything above, and the guidance's position is consistent: if it is not written down, it did not happen. Model choice, assumptions, data, limitations, validation findings, deficiencies, and the reasons validation could not be performed all have to be recorded.

A financial institution buying in vendor data or a vendor model / software takes on model risk with it. Banks should ensure that there are appropriate processes for selecting vendor models. Banks require the vendor to provide development evidence — the model's design (input, processing, output) and intended use — so the bank can judge whether the model is appropriate for the bank or not. Limitations and assumptions must be documented clearly by the vendor. When the vendor will not share the mathematical formula, implementation code, back end, or adjustments — which is common, since these are trade secrets — the bank must compensate with its own testing: Sensitivity analysisBenchmarkingStress testing\text{Sensitivity analysis} \qquad \text{Benchmarking} \qquad \text{Stress testing}Sensitivity analysisBenchmarkingStress testing The notes name real systems in this category: QRM, Polypath and Calypso in banking, Aladdin (BlackRock), and ADCO for mortgage. The bank must still conduct ongoing monitoring and outcome analysis on a vendor model. A black box does not exempt you from validation — it changes the technique. If you cannot inspect the internals, you test the behaviour.

Banks should comply with a strong MRM framework, covering: Model development Model implementation Validation Model governance Which is the whole document in four lines, and the four notes of this module.

Model risk governance sits with the Board and Senior Management, who set a bank-wide approach that fits into the organisation's broader risk management. The board must keep model risk within its tolerance limit. Seven components: board/senior management, policies and procedures, roles and responsibilities, internal audit, external resources, model inventory, documentation. Policies must cover definitions, development practices, risk assessment, validation and governance — with explicit staff expertise, authority and reporting lines. Roles divide into ownership, control and compliance; business units own the model risk of their strategies, and a named model owner is accountable for performance, development, implementation, use and validation. Internal audit assesses whether the MRM framework works — it does not replicate validation. External resources can be engaged, but need an agreed scope and a designated internal team overseeing them. A firm-wide model inventory — implemented, under development and retired — exists to evaluate model risk in aggregate, which is the only way to see risk that arises between models. Vendor models still require validation. Demand development evidence; where the vendor withholds internals, substitute sensitivity analysis, benchmarking and stress testing, and keep doing ongoing monitoring and outcome analysis.

Model risk management begins with robust model development, implementation and use. Another essential element is sound model validation. Note the order. Validation comes second. You cannot validate your way out of a badly built model — which is why this section comes before Section 5. The third leg is model governance, which sets an effective framework with defined roles and responsibilities for clear communication of model assumptions and limitations.

a) A clear objective — a statement of purpose. b) Design, theory and logic underlying the model, which should be well documented and generally supported by published research and sound industry practice. That documentation has to cover four things: Mathematical specification the equations themselves Numerical technique how they are solved Approximation what shortcuts were taken Strengths / weaknesses → the model's limitations The developer should ensure that the components of the model are appropriate for the intended business use case.
documents.s: What an effective development process starts with

documents.t: Comparison with alternate theories and approaches is a fundamental component of a sound modelling process. This is a requirement people routinely skip. It is not enough to build M1M_1M1​ and show it works — you have to be able to say why M1M_1M1​ and not M2M_2M2​, M3M_3M3​ or M4M_4M4​: M1 ✓⟶implementedM2, M3, M4⏟considered and rejected⟶justifyM_1 \;\checkmark \longrightarrow \text{implemented} \qquad \underbrace{M_2,\; M_3,\; M_4}_{\text{considered and rejected}} \longrightarrow \textbf{justify}M1​✓⟶implementedconsidered and rejectedM2​,M3​,M4​​​⟶justify This module has already done exactly that several times — the three VaR methods disagreeing by 12.6% at 95%, or Vasicek versus CIR fitting the same data with mean-reversion speeds 100× apart. In both cases the choice between models mattered and could not be settled by fit alone. Writing down why you chose one is the documentation SR 11-7 is asking for.

Rigorous assessment of data quality and relevance is required. The developer should be able to demonstrate that the data and information are suitable for the model and that they are consistent with the use case. The lecturer's shorthand is the old one, and it is exactly right: “Garbage In, Garbage Out”\textbf{“Garbage In, Garbage Out”}“Garbage In, Garbage Out”

If data isn't available, data proxies are used — something with the same behaviour. But a proxy is a substitution, and substitutions are where risk hides: Proxies must be carefully identified, justified and documented. Otherwise the proxy itself becomes a source of model risk — the model looks fine, and the thing it is actually measuring is not the thing you think.
documents.s: When the data does not exist

documents.t: Testing various components of the model, and its overall functioning, is evaluated to determine whether the model is performing as intended or not. And which tests apply depends entirely on what the model assumes: Statistical tests depend on specific distribution assumptions. For a linear regression model: # Test 1 Linearity — QQ plot 2 Homoskedasticity 3 Autocorrelation between residuals 4 Multicollinearity — VIF 5 Normality of residuals For a time series model: # Test 1 Augmented Dickey-Fuller (ADF) test 2 KPSS For a Value at Risk model: # Test 1 Kupiec test 2 Traffic Light Approach 3 Christoffersen test 4 Binomial test

Different tests have different strengths and weaknesses under different conditions. Do not rely on a single test. Use a variety of tests to develop a sound model. This is the exact gap Module 6 identified The Kupiec note ended on a limitation: Kupiec counts breaches but cannot see whether they clustered. Three breaches spread across a year and three on consecutive days score identically — and the second is far more alarming. Christoffersen's test is the one that closes that gap, by testing independence of breaches rather than just their number. Which is precisely why SR 11-7 lists all four together and says not to rely on any single one. The guidance is not being vague; it is describing a real blind spot that a second test covers.

Models should be used only for the purpose for which they were designed and validated. Black-Scholes⟶European option ✓\text{Black-Scholes} \longrightarrow \text{European option} \;\checkmarkBlack-Scholes⟶European option✓ Misusing a model beyond its intended scope leads to incorrect decisions and heightened risk → model risk.

Users must understand the assumptions, limitations and weaknesses of the model. Users must interpret the model output correctly and critically. This includes understanding the sensitivity of the result to input changes and assumptions. Why the guidance cares about the reader, not just the model The deck makes this concrete with a small scenario. A model reports VaR = $5M. Two people read that number: Reads it as User A (technical background) a potential loss at a stated confidence level User B a profit figure Same output, opposite conclusions. The model was correct in both cases. This is why "model risk" is defined as arising from incorrect or misused outputs. A validated model handed to someone who misreads it produces exactly the same adverse decision as a broken one — and no amount of validation prevents it. Only documentation, training and clear reporting do.

MRM begins with development, implementation and use — validation is the second line of defence, not the first. A sound build starts with a clear objective and documented design, theory and logic, supported by published research and industry practice, covering specification, numerical technique, approximations and limitations. Comparison with alternative approaches is required — justify why this model and not another. Data must be assessed for quality and relevance ("garbage in, garbage out"), and proxies must be identified, justified and documented. Test against the model's own assumptions — regression diagnostics, ADF and KPSS for time series, four different backtests for VaR. Never rely on a single test; different tests fail in different ways. Kupiec counts breaches, Christoffersen catches clustering. Use the model only as designed, and users must understand its assumptions and interpret output critically — a correct model misread produces the same bad decision as a wrong one.

The longest section of the guidance, and the one a model validation job is built around. Model validation is the set of processes and activities intended to verify that models are performing as expected, in line with their design objectives and business uses.

All three model components — the ones defined in the overview — should be subjected to validation: InputProcessingReporting\text{Input} \qquad \text{Processing} \qquad \text{Reporting}InputProcessingReporting And it applies regardless of who built it: Source Validation required? Internal team model Yes Vendor model Yes Buying a model does not outsource responsibility for it.

The rigour and sophistication of validation should be commensurate with: the bank's overall use of the model the complexity and materiality of the model the size and complexity of the bank's operations So validation effort is scaled to risk, not applied uniformly. A model driving a material book gets more scrutiny than one driving a small one. The lecturer's illustration: compare the Vasicek interest rate model with a Hull-White two-factor model. The validation practices are the same — but Hull-White is more complex, the relationships between variables are more complex, and so it demands more and more validation. Same framework, more of it.

Staff doing validation should have the required knowledge, skill and expertise. In practice that means quantitative credentials — MS in Quantitative Finance or Financial Engineering, FRM, CFA, or a machine learning / statistics background. You cannot validate Black-Scholes without understanding stochastic calculus; you would have no way to tell whether the derivation is right. Staff conducting validation work should have explicit authority to challenge the developer or unit, and to elevate their findings, including issues and deficiencies. Independence is the point, not a formality Model development and model validation must be independent. The process runs as a loop, not a rubber stamp: Developer builds⟶Validator reviews→ issues & deficiencies Developer refines⟶⋯\text{Developer builds} \longrightarrow \text{Validator reviews} \xrightarrow{\;\text{issues \& deficiencies}\;} \text{Developer refines} \longrightarrow \cdotsDeveloper builds⟶Validator reviewsissues & deficiencies​Developer refines⟶⋯ The reason the guidance is explicit about authority is that a validator who reports to the model's developer cannot do the job. Finding a deficiency has to be a career-neutral act, or deficiencies stop being found. This is the same structural idea as an audit function — competence alone is not enough without the standing to say no.
documents.s: Who does it — and with what authority

documents.t: The range and rigour of validation conducted prior to first use of a model should be in line with the potential risk presented by the model. And validation has teeth: If significant deficiencies are noted, use of the model should not be allowed. If the deficiencies are too severe to be addressed, the model should be rejected. If it is not feasible to conduct the necessary validation prior to the model because of data or other limitations, that fact should be documented and communicated to the user, senior management and relevant parties. That last clause matters: "we could not validate this" is an acceptable outcome, but only if it is said out loud. Silence is not.
# Element Includes 1 Evaluation of conceptual soundness development evidence 2 Ongoing monitoring process verification and benchmarking 3 Outcome analysis backtesting
documents.s: The three elements of comprehensive validation

documents.t: This element involves the quality of model design and construction. It entails review of documentation and empirical evidence supporting the method used and the variables selected for the model. Development evidence should be reviewed before the model goes into use. The questions a validator asks of a regression predicting, say, a bank's balances: What method did you follow? What variables did you select? Are those variables significant? Sound development means documenting all evidence in support of the model choice: Theory Assumptions Data Mathematical framework Limitations and a complete validation adds: Sensitivity analysis Stress testing Backtesting Accuracy of the model Comparison with alternative theories

Change one input and check the result on the output. For a model y=β0+β1x1+β2x2+β3x3y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2 + \beta_3 x_3y=β0​+β1​x1​+β2​x2​+β3​x3​, vary x1x_1x1​ by ±1%, ±5%, ±10% while holding x2x_2x2​ and x3x_3x3​ constant, and observe the impact on yyy. Then repeat for each input in turn. The worked failure is the best thing in this section Doing exactly that on the balance-prediction model, a +10% shock to x2x_2x2​ produced a negative yyy. Balances cannot be negative. They are only positive. The model is not broken arithmetically — the regression is doing precisely what a linear model does, extrapolating a straight line past the region where it makes sense. But a balance model that can output a negative balance is conceptually unsound, and no amount of goodness-of-fit hides that. The fixes offered: either impose a cap or floor on x2x_2x2​, or remove x2x_2x2​ from the model. This is what "conceptual soundness" means in practice — not does it fit? but can it produce an answer that could never happen?

Three scenarios, run through the same model: Scenario The notes' example Base current values — interest rate, inflation, HPI Adverse the COVID period, 2020 Severely adverse the 2007-08 financial crisis Feed each scenario's inputs in and compare the outputs. If the model behaves weirdly under the severely adverse case, then the model is not able to stress test the SA condition — and changes in the model are required. Note this is the same idea as Stressed VaR from Module 6: run the machinery over a deliberately catastrophic window and see whether it still makes sense.

The second element of the validation process. Ongoing monitoring confirms that the model is appropriately implemented and is performing as intended. It means monitoring the models to evaluate whether changes in product, exposure, activities or market necessitate development (changes) or redevelopment. Why it is needed: a model calibrated on 2020 market conditions, still running in 2025, is being asked about a world that has changed. When it isn't performing the way it has to, that is model risk — and the response is to adjust the model or redevelop it. Model limitations should be assessed regularly when ongoing monitoring is performed — every time, not once at inception.

a) Process verification. Check all model components are functioning as designed. Verify internal and external data. Computer code implementation should be subject to rigorous quality and change control procedures. That last point is the one this course has repeatedly demonstrated the need for. The Monte Carlo VaR sheet whose live formulas no longer reproduced its own reported numbers is exactly a process-verification failure — the theory was fine, the implementation had drifted, and nothing caught it. b) Benchmarking. Comparing your model with an alternative model. Pricing a derivative, for instance: Method Price Black-Scholes $110 Binomial tree … Monte Carlo $100 A gap that large between methods is a signal to investigate. Module 4 did this without naming it: three methods priced the same SPY call at 1.7131, 1.7054 and 1.7065 — agreement within a cent, which is a passing benchmark test. Module 6's three VaR methods disagreeing by 12.6% at 95% is a benchmark test that raises a question worth answering.

The third element of the validation process. Analysing the outcome of the model by comparing model output with actual outcome. Predicted balance against actual balance, plotted together — the visual form of the whole exercise. Outcome analysis depends on quantitative measures or statistical tests. Model type Measures Linear regression RMSE, MSE, MAE, MAPE Logistic regression Accuracy, Precision, F1 score, Recall, AUC-ROC curve VaR Kupiec test Which closes a loop opened two modules ago: backtesting a VaR model is outcome analysis, the third element of validation under SR 11-7. Module 6 did the technique; this section is the governance framework that requires it and says who must sign it off.

Model validation verifies that models perform as expected, in line with design objectives and business uses — covering input, processing and reporting, for internal and vendor models alike. Rigour scales with the model's use, complexity, materiality, and the bank's size — same practices, more of them for harder models. Validators need genuine quantitative expertise and explicit authority to challenge developers and escalate findings; development and validation must be independent. Validation can block a model from use and reject it outright; if validation isn't feasible, that must be documented and communicated. Three elements: Conceptual soundness — design quality, documented evidence, sensitivity analysis and stress testing (base / adverse / severely adverse). A balance model that outputs a negative balance is unsound regardless of fit. Ongoing monitoring — process verification (components, data, code change control) and benchmarking against alternative models. Outcome analysis — compare predicted against actual, using measures appropriate to the model type; for VaR that is backtesting.
Every previous module in this course built a model. This one asks the question regulators started asking after 2008: how do you know the model is any good, and who is accountable when it is not?

SR 11-7 is the Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management, issued jointly by the Federal Reserve Board (FRB) and the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) in 2011. Dated 4 April 2011, it is the standard reference for model risk management in US banking, and it is what a model validation team is measured against.
Lessons learned from the 2008 financial crisis. Failures in model reliability during the financial crisis highlighted the need for robust model risk management practices.

Banks rely heavily on quantitative analysis and models for most of their decision making. The guidance lists the range: underwriting credits, valuing exposures, measuring risk, managing client assets, determining capital and reserve adequacy, and many other activities. The expanding use of models in all aspects of banking reflects the extent to which models can improve business decisions — but models also come with a cost. Cost What it is Direct cost the resources spent building all the models Indirect cost the consequences of relying on the outcomes of the model And the indirect cost is the one that matters here: Decision⟶model gives an incorrect result⟶banks have faced large financial losses\text{Decision} \longrightarrow \text{model gives an incorrect result} \longrightarrow \textbf{banks have faced large financial losses}Decision⟶model gives an incorrect result⟶banks have faced large financial losses which is why it is important to actively manage model risk.

The document's own structure, which the rest of this module follows: Section Contents 1 Introduction 2 Purpose and Scope of SR 11-7 3 Overview of Model Risk Management (MRM) 4 Robust model development, implementation and use 5 Components of effective validation 6 Salient features of sound governance, policies and controls 7 Conclusion

The purpose of this document is to provide comprehensive guidance for banks on model risk management. Rigorous model validation plays a critical role in MRM. However, sound development, implementation and use of the model are also vital elements. That balance is the guidance's central posture, and it is worth stating plainly: validation is not a substitute for building the model properly. The chain runs: Model development⏟build the model⟶Model validation⏟validate the same model⟶Approve the model⏟\underbrace{\text{Model development}}_{\text{build the model}} \longrightarrow \underbrace{\text{Model validation}}_{\text{validate the same model}} \longrightarrow \underbrace{\text{Approve the model}}_{}build the modelModel development​​⟶validate the same modelModel validation​​⟶Approve the model​​ with two further requirements on the far side: the user must know the model's usage, and the model must be implemented the right way.

The definition is precise, and it is broader than most people expect: The term model refers to a quantitative method, system, or approach that applies statistical, economic, financial, or mathematical theories, techniques and assumptions to process input data into quantitative estimates.
documents.s: Section 3 — What counts as a model

documents.t: A model consists of three components. # Component Role 1 Information input delivers assumptions and data to the model 2 Processing transforms inputs into estimates 3 Reporting translates the estimates into useful business information Input⟶Processing⟶Output / Reporting\text{Input} \longrightarrow \text{Processing} \longrightarrow \text{Output / Reporting}Input⟶Processing⟶Output / Reporting The definition is deliberately wide Two consequences worth noticing. A spreadsheet is a model. Nothing in the definition requires code, a database, or sophistication — the Black-Scholes sheet from Module 4 meets it in full. Expert judgement can be an input. The guidance explicitly covers "quantitative approaches whose inputs are partially or wholly qualitative or based on expert judgment, provided that the output is quantitative in nature." So a scorecard driven by analyst opinion is still a model if it produces a number.

Models are simplified representations of real-world relationships. Simplification is inevitable, due to the complexity of those relationships, but also intentional — to focus attention on the aspects considered most important for a given application. Model quality can be measured in many ways: precision, accuracy, discriminatory power, robustness, stability and reliability, to name a few. Which metric applies depends on the model's job: Model type Relevant metrics Regression model RMSE, MSE, MAE, MAPE VaR model Traffic Light Approach, Kupiec Test That second row is the direct link back to Module 6: backtesting a VaR model is model validation, done by the standards this document sets. Models are never perfect, and the appropriate metric of quality depends on the situation.

The use of models invariably presents model risk, which is the potential for adverse consequences from decisions based on incorrect or misused model outputs and reports. It can lead to financial loss, poor business and strategic decision making, or damage to a bank's reputation. Reason 1 — the model may have fundamental errors. The model may have fundamental errors and may produce inaccurate output when viewed against the design objective and intended use. Errors can enter anywhere along the chain: the mathematical calculation and quantification the choice of sample design the selection of inputs and estimation the implementation Errors can occur at any point from design through implementation. The lecturer's example is an implementation error you can see: the Vasicek model is drt=a(b−rt)dt+σ dWtdr_t = a(b - r_t)dt + \sigma\,dW_tdrt​=a(b−rt​)dt+σdWt​, but deployed as drt=a(b−rt)σ dt+σ dWtdr_t = a(b - r_t)\sigma\,dt + \sigma\,dW_tdrt​=a(b−rt​)σdt+σdWt​ — the theory is right and the code is not. Is the model deployed correctly? is a separate question from is the model correct? Reason 2 — the model may be used incorrectly or inappropriately. The example here is one this course has already built: Black-Scholes prices a European option. Point it at an American option and it will return a number — a wrong one, because the model assumes exercise only at maturity. Black-Scholes→European ✓Black-Scholes→American ✗→model risk\text{Black-Scholes} \rightarrow \text{European} \;\checkmark \qquad \text{Black-Scholes} \rightarrow \text{American} \;✗ \rightarrow \textbf{model risk}Black-Scholes→European✓Black-Scholes→American✗→model risk It is very important to understand the limitations of a model, to avoid using it in ways that are not consistent with the original intent. That is the sharpest practical lesson in the whole document: a model does not fail loudly when misused. It returns a plausible number.
documents.s: Model risk, and the two ways it arises

documents.t: Model risk should be managed like any other kind of risk — identified, measured, controlled. Banks should identify the source of risk and assess the magnitude. Model risk increases with greater model complexity. Aggregate model risk is affected by interaction and dependencies among models — where one model's output is another's input, errors propagate: M1→ output M2→ output decisionM_1 \xrightarrow{\;\text{output}\;} M_2 \xrightarrow{\;\text{output}\;} \text{decision}M1​output​M2​output​decision

Even with skilled modelling and robust validation, model risk cannot be eliminated. So the guidance turns to containment instead: establish limits on model use monitor model performance adjust or revise the model over time ad-hoc analysis — extra checks to make sure everything is correct Monitoring runs on a defined cycle — monthly, quarterly, semi-annual, annual, or two-yearly — and the outcome is either to adjust the model or build a new one. This is the same posture the hedging module took: you do not remove the risk, you decide how much of it to carry and check on it regularly.

SR 11-7 is the Fed/OCC Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management (2011), issued after the 2008 crisis exposed failures in model reliability. A model is any quantitative method processing input data into quantitative estimates, with three components: input, processing, reporting. The definition covers spreadsheets and expert-judgement inputs. Models are deliberate simplifications and never perfect; quality metrics depend on the job — RMSE for a regression, traffic light and Kupiec for a VaR model. Model risk is the potential for adverse consequences from decisions based on incorrect or misused model outputs. It arises two ways: fundamental errors (anywhere from design through implementation) and incorrect or inappropriate use (Black-Scholes on an American option). It increases with complexity and compounds across linked models. It cannot be eliminated — so it is contained with limits on use, monitoring, revision and ad-hoc analysis.
