The previous note measured a portfolio on its own terms. These three measure it against a benchmark — and all three come out of a single regression of portfolio returns on market returns.

Alpha measures the excess return of an investment relative to a benchmark index. It indicates whether the investment outperformed or underperformed the market, after accounting for risk. Alpha Meaning Positive The investment outperformed the market Negative The investment underperformed the market Zero The investment performed in line with the market Alpha is the part of the return the benchmark does not account for. If the S&P 500 returned 15% and your portfolio returned 15%, you produced no alpha — whatever skill you applied, the market would have given you the same result.

Beta measures the sensitivity of the investment return to the market's movement. Beta Meaning β>1\beta > 1β>1 The investment is more volatile than the market β<1\beta < 1β<1 The investment is less volatile than the market β=1\beta = 1β=1 The investment moves in line with the market Worked: a stock with β=1.2\beta = 1.2β=1.2 — when the market rises by 10%, the stock is expected to rise by 12% when the market falls by 10%, the stock is expected to fall by 12% Beta cuts both ways. It is amplification, not advantage — a high-beta portfolio in a rising market looks like skill and is not. Beta is the systematic risk from Module 6 This is the same quantity that Treynor's ratio divides by in the next note, and conceptually the same split the variance-covariance VaR note relied on: risk that comes from the market as a whole cannot be diversified away, and risk specific to the holding can be. Beta measures only the first kind.

R-squared measures the percentage of an investment's movement that can be explained by the movement in the benchmark index. It comes from the same linear regression of portfolio returns against the benchmark. R2R^2R2 Meaning 100% (or 1) The portfolio's returns are fully explained by the benchmark 0 The portfolio's returns aren't explained by the benchmark at all 85% (or 0.85) 85% of the portfolio's returns are explained by the benchmark, while 15% are due to unique factors R2R^2R2 is the honesty check on the other two. A beta computed against a benchmark that explains almost nothing is not telling you much — the regression line exists, but the relationship it describes is weak.

The workbook regresses the 50/50 JPM + MS portfolio against SPY over 1,256 daily observations: Regression statistic Value Multiple R 0.768685 R Square 0.590877 Adjusted R Square 0.590551 Standard Error 0.013086 Observations 1,256 Coefficient Value Standard error t Stat Intercept 1.000176 0.00037 2705.66 X Variable 1 (beta) 1.188091 0.027918 42.56 Recomputed independently from the underlying return columns: β = 1.1881, R² = 0.5911, correlation = 0.7689 — matching the sheet to three decimals (the small difference is a two-row range discrepancy).

β = 1.1881. The portfolio is 19% more volatile than the market. When SPY moves 10%, this portfolio is expected to move about 11.9%. That is unsurprising for two investment banks — they are levered to the economic cycle in a way the broad index is not. R² = 0.5909. 59% of the portfolio's movement is explained by SPY, and 41% comes from factors specific to JPM and MS — bank-sector news, earnings, regulation. So the benchmark explains most of the story but nowhere near all of it. α = 0.0176% per day. Where the intercept of 1.0002 comes from The regression intercept is 1.000176, not the near-zero you would expect, and the sheet then computes alpha as =(Y51-1)*100. The reason: the regression was run with (1 + portfolio return) as the dependent variable against the market return as the independent one. So 1+rp=a+βrm⟹rp=(a−1)+βrm1 + r_p = a + \beta r_m \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad r_p = (a - 1) + \beta r_m1+rp​=a+βrm​⟹rp​=(a−1)+βrm​ which makes the true alpha a−1=0.000176a - 1 = 0.000176a−1=0.000176. Verified directly: regressing rpr_prp​ on rmr_mrm​ gives an intercept of 0.000167, and 1+0.000167=1.0001671 + 0.000167 = 1.0001671+0.000167=1.000167 against the sheet's 1.000176. It is a valid setup, just an unusual one — and it means the intercept must have 1 subtracted before it means anything. Reading 1.000176 as "alpha" would be wildly wrong. Alpha is daily; everything beside it is annualised The summary table reports α = 0.0176% alongside an annualised return of 23.03%, annualised volatility of 32.47% and a Sharpe ratio built from annual figures. But that alpha is a daily number. Annualised it is 0.00017612×252=0.0444=4.44%0.00017612 \times 252 = 0.0444 = \mathbf{4.44\%}0.00017612×252=0.0444=4.44% which is a materially different claim — 4.44% of annual outperformance, not 0.018%. The ratios in the next note are internally consistent (all annual); alpha is the one figure left in daily units while sitting in an annual table. Worth knowing which convention a reported alpha is in before comparing it to anything.

Measure Question it answers Alpha Did we beat the benchmark? Beta How much market risk did we take to do it? R² Is the benchmark even the right comparison? Read alone, each is misleading. A high alpha with a beta of 1.9 is mostly leverage. A confident beta with an R² of 0.1 is a number computed against an irrelevant index. The three are one answer, not three.

Alpha is excess return relative to a benchmark — positive means outperformance, negative underperformance, zero means in line. Beta is sensitivity to market movement: β>1\beta > 1β>1 more volatile, β<1\beta < 1β<1 less, β=1\beta = 1β=1 in line. A β of 1.2 moves 12% when the market moves 10% — in both directions. R² is the percentage of movement explained by the benchmark; the remainder is unique factors. On the real JPM/MS portfolio against SPY: β = 1.1881 (19% more volatile than the market), R² = 0.5909 (59% explained, 41% bank-specific), and α = 0.0176% daily, all independently verified. The intercept is 1.000176 because (1 + rₚ) was regressed on r_m — subtract 1 to get alpha. That alpha is daily while the rest of the table is annualised; annualised it is 4.44%.

Return alone says nothing. 23% earned by taking enormous risk is not the same achievement as 23% earned quietly, and these three ratios are how that difference is made visible. All three share the same numerator — excess return — and differ only in what they divide it by.

The Sharpe ratio measures the excess return earned per unit of total risk. Sharpe ratio=Rp−Rfσp \boxed{\;\text{Sharpe ratio} = \frac{R_p - R_f}{\sigma_p}\;}Sharpe ratio=σp​Rp​−Rf​​​ RpR_pRp​ Portfolio return RfR_fRf​ Risk-free rate σp\sigma_pσp​ Standard deviation of the portfolio The numerator Rp−RfR_p - R_fRp​−Rf​ is the excess return — what you earned above what you could have had risk-free. There is no credit for matching the Treasury rate. A higher Sharpe ratio indicates better risk-adjusted return. Sharpe Reading > 1 Good investment — generating decent return relative to the risk < 1 Bad investment — poor; the return you are generating does not justify the level of risk you are taking The notes' illustration: a portfolio returning 12% with 20% volatility has a Sharpe below 1 — you are being paid 12 for carrying 20.

The Sortino ratio refines the Sharpe ratio by considering only the downside risk — negative volatility. Sortino ratio=Rp−Rfσd \boxed{\;\text{Sortino ratio} = \frac{R_p - R_f}{\sigma_d}\;}Sortino ratio=σd​Rp​−Rf​​​ where σd\sigma_dσd​ is the downside volatility. This metric is more significant for risk-averse investors. A high Sortino ratio indicates better return relative to the downside risk. Reason: it penalises the investment only for negative deviation from the threshold. That is the whole argument for it. Sharpe's denominator punishes a portfolio for going up unexpectedly, which no investor actually minds. Sortino removes that penalty.

The Treynor ratio measures the excess return per unit of systematic risk (beta). Treynor ratio=Rp−Rfβp \boxed{\;\text{Treynor ratio} = \frac{R_p - R_f}{\beta_p}\;}Treynor ratio=βp​Rp​−Rf​​​ where βp\beta_pβp​ is the portfolio beta. Goal: the Treynor ratio focuses on how well the portfolio compensates the investor for market risk rather than total risk. The distinction matters for anyone holding more than one portfolio. Risk specific to a holding can be diversified away across a wider book; market risk cannot. So for a portfolio that is one sleeve of something larger, market risk is the only risk that genuinely survives — and Treynor is the ratio that prices it.

The deck closes with this comparison, and it is the cleanest summary of the module: Ratio Risk measured Formula Denominator is Sharpe Total risk (σ\sigmaσ) Rp−Rfσ\dfrac{R_p - R_f}{\sigma}σRp​−Rf​​ Standard deviation Sortino Downside risk (σd\sigma_dσd​) Rp−Rfσd\dfrac{R_p - R_f}{\sigma_d}σd​Rp​−Rf​​ Downside standard deviation Treynor Market risk (β\betaβ) Rp−Rfβ\dfrac{R_p - R_f}{\beta}βRp​−Rf​​ Beta Same numerator, three denominators. Choosing between them is choosing which risk you think the investor actually bears.

Computed on the 50/50 JPM + MS portfolio, with a risk-free rate of 4.323%: Input Value Annualised return RpR_pRp​ 23.031% Risk-free rate RfR_fRf​ 4.323% Excess return 18.708% Annualised volatility σ\sigmaσ 32.465% Annualised downside deviation σd\sigma_dσd​ 21.608% Beta β\betaβ 1.188091 Sharpe=0.23031−0.043230.324653=0.5762\text{Sharpe} = \frac{0.23031 - 0.04323}{0.324653} = \mathbf{0.5762}Sharpe=0.3246530.23031−0.04323​=0.5762Sortino=0.23031−0.043230.216081=0.8658\text{Sortino} = \frac{0.23031 - 0.04323}{0.216081} = \mathbf{0.8658}Sortino=0.2160810.23031−0.04323​=0.8658Treynor=0.23031−0.043231.188091=0.1575\text{Treynor} = \frac{0.23031 - 0.04323}{1.188091} = \mathbf{0.1575}Treynor=1.1880910.23031−0.04323​=0.1575 All three reproduce when recomputed independently from the return series.

Sharpe of 0.576 is below 1 — by the deck's own rule of thumb, the return does not justify the total risk taken. 23% sounds excellent until you notice it came with 32% volatility. Sortino of 0.866 is markedly higher than Sharpe — a 50% improvement. That gap is informative: it means a large share of this portfolio's volatility was upside, which Sharpe penalised and Sortino does not. Downside deviation (21.6%) is only two-thirds of total volatility (32.5%). Treynor of 0.158 is not comparable to the other two — its denominator is a beta, not a percentage, so the number lives on a different scale entirely. Treynor is only meaningful compared against another portfolio's Treynor, never against a Sharpe. One number to check before you compare anything These three ratios are internally consistent — all use annualised return, volatility and risk-free rate. But as the previous note flagged, alpha in the same summary table is left in daily units (0.0176%, or 4.44% annualised). Mixing conventions inside one table is the kind of quiet error that survives review, because every individual number looks reasonable. It is precisely what SR 11-7's process verification is meant to catch.

This module measured investments; the previous eight built the things being measured. The through-line across all nine is narrower than it looks: return is only meaningful once divided by the risk taken to get it\textbf{return is only meaningful once divided by the risk taken to get it}return is only meaningful once divided by the risk taken to get it Modules 1-3 priced derivatives and hedged the Greeks — managing risk one exposure at a time. Modules 4-5 modelled the processes underneath, and found that three pricing methods agree to within a cent when built correctly. Module 6 put a number on the tail, and showed what VaR refuses to tell you. Module 7 valued the swaps that convert one risk into another. Module 8 asked who is accountable when the model is wrong. Module 9 asks, finally, whether any of it was worth doing — and answers with a ratio.
documents.s: Module 9, and the bootcamp, in closing

documents.t: All three ratios share the numerator excess return Rp−RfR_p - R_fRp​−Rf​ and differ only in the denominator. Sharpe divides by total risk (σ\sigmaσ): above 1 is good, below 1 means the return does not justify the risk. Sortino divides by downside risk (σd\sigma_dσd​), penalising only negative deviation from the threshold — better suited to risk-averse investors. Treynor divides by beta, pricing market risk rather than total risk — the right measure when the portfolio sits inside a larger, diversified book. On the real portfolio: Sharpe 0.576, Sortino 0.866, Treynor 0.158, from a 23.03% return against a 4.323% risk-free rate. Sortino exceeding Sharpe by 50% shows much of the volatility was upside — which Sharpe wrongly penalised. Treynor is not comparable to Sharpe or Sortino — different denominator, different scale.
The final module of the bootcamp, and the one that measures whether an investment was actually any good. It starts with three quantities everything else is built from.

A return is the money made or lost on an investment over a period of time. Returns are expressed in percentage. A positive return represents a profit, a negative return represents a loss — $100 falling to $98 is a return of −2%. There are two ways to compute one.

Simple return=St−St−1St−1or equivalently StSt−1−1 \text{Simple return} = \frac{S_t - S_{t-1}}{S_{t-1}} \qquad\text{or equivalently}\qquad \boxed{\;\frac{S_t}{S_{t-1}} - 1\;}Simple return=St−1​St​−St−1​​or equivalentlySt−1​St​​−1​

Log return=ln⁡(StSt−1) \boxed{\;\text{Log return} = \ln\left(\frac{S_t}{S_{t-1}}\right)\;}Log return=ln(St−1​St​​)​ In Excel, LN is the one you want The notes flag a trap: Excel's LN is the natural logarithm — that is what "log return" means here. Excel's LOG is base 10 and is not what you want.

Performing short-term analysis → simple return. Simple returns are the default for short-term investment analysis, because they are what people actually understand. But they have three limitations. 1) Less accurate with large price fluctuations. The notes' example is Bitcoin — with moves that large, simple returns distort, and log returns are the right choice. 2) Not suitable for statistical modelling. This is the substantive one, and it connects back through the whole course: Model Assumes Black-Scholes the stock price follows log returns Time series volatility models — ARCH, GARCH log returns Linear regression normality of residuals Log returns are preferred because they are stable and often closer to a normal distribution. Which is exactly the point Black-Scholes rests on: returns are normal, the price is log-normal. Feed a model simple returns when it assumes log returns and you have created model risk of the "used incorrectly" kind. 3) Not suitable for high-frequency data. Second-by-second data — 15-second, 10-second, 1-second bars — should use log returns.

It is less interpretable for a non-technical audience. A 2% simple return means you have 2% more money. A 1.98% log return does not mean that, quite. When the audience is not quantitative, interpretability wins.
documents.s: So why not always use log returns?

documents.t: Volatility (or standard deviation) is a statistical measure that quantifies the amount of variation in a stock. In the context of finance it measures the volatility of an asset or portfolio. σi=∑i=1n(Ri−Rˉ)2n−1\sigma_i = \sqrt{\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(R_i - \bar{R}\right)^2}{n-1}}σi​=n−1∑i=1n​(Ri​−Rˉ)2​​ RiR_iRi​ individual return Rˉ\bar{R}Rˉ average return nnn number of periods What 20% volatility means: a $100 portfolio moves to 100 \times (1 + 20\%) = \120ontheupside,oron the upside, orontheupside,or100 \times (1 - 20%) = $80$ on the downside. Volatility Meaning High More risk — more deviation in the stock price Low Less risk In Excel it is simply STDEV.S(daily returns).

σannual=σdaily×252 \boxed{\;\sigma_{\text{annual}} = \sigma_{\text{daily}} \times \sqrt{252}\;}σannual​=σdaily​×252​​ And the notes derive it rather than asserting it, which is worth following: Variance is the square of standard deviation, V=σ2V = \sigma^2V=σ2, so σ=V\sigma = \sqrt{V}σ=V​. Variance increases linearly with time: Vannual=Vdaily×252V_{\text{annual}} = V_{\text{daily}} \times 252Vannual​=Vdaily​×252 Take the square root of both sides: Vannual=Vdaily×252⟹σannual=σdaily×252\sqrt{V_{\text{annual}}} = \sqrt{V_{\text{daily}}} \times \sqrt{252} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \sigma_{\text{annual}} = \sigma_{\text{daily}} \times \sqrt{252}Vannual​​=Vdaily​​×252​⟹σannual​=σdaily​×252​ 252 because a year has 365 days minus Saturdays, Sundays and holidays. This is the same T\sqrt{T}T​ rule that scaled VaR across horizons and the same Δt\sqrt{\Delta t}Δt​ that scaled the Brownian shock in GBM — it is variance that adds, so standard deviation grows with the square root.

Downside standard deviation is a measure of the downside risk of an investment. It focuses only on negative deviations. Unlike standard deviation, which captures both upside volatility and downside volatility. That distinction matters because ordinary volatility treats a $100 stock going to $120 as exactly as "risky" as it going to $80. An investor does not. Downside standard deviation considers only downside volatility. This is particularly useful for risk-averse investors. Downside std dev=∑min⁡(Ri−T, 0)2n \boxed{\;\text{Downside std dev} = \sqrt{\frac{\sum \min\left(R_i - T,\; 0\right)^2}{n}}\;}Downside std dev=n∑min(Ri​−T,0)2​​​ RiR_iRi​ return of the stock / portfolio TTT target return / threshold nnn number of periods

With a threshold of T=0%T = 0\%T=0%: RiR_iRi​ min⁡(Ri−T, 0)\min(R_i - T,\, 0)min(Ri​−T,0) Counted? +2% min⁡(2%, 0)=0\min(2\%,\, 0) = \mathbf{0}min(2%,0)=0 No −2% min⁡(−2%, 0)=−2%\min(-2\%,\, 0) = \mathbf{-2\%}min(−2%,0)=−2% Yes positive return→0negative return→counted\text{positive return} \rightarrow 0 \qquad\qquad \text{negative return} \rightarrow \text{counted}positive return→0negative return→counted The min is a filter. Good days contribute nothing to the risk measure; only shortfalls below the threshold do.
documents.s: How the min() does the work

documents.t: Correlation is a statistical measure that quantifies the relationship between 2 variables, showing how they move relative to each other. It is always between −1 and 1: Correlation Meaning +1 Perfect positive correlation — the stocks move in the same direction −1 Perfect negative correlation — the stocks move in opposite directions 0 No correlation — the stocks are independent of each other Why sector matters: AAPL and MSFT are both technology, so their correlation is higher — because they are influenced by similar industry trends. Correlations are not fixed NOTE: Correlations are not fixed. They can change over time. This is the assumption that breaks in a crisis, and it broke expensively in 2008. A portfolio diversified on historical correlations can find those correlations converging toward 1 exactly when diversification was supposed to help. It is also why the variance-covariance VaR note measured a 10.14% diversification benefit on a bank portfolio and then noted that all three banks correlated at ~0.66 because they were the same sector. The benefit is real, and it is not guaranteed to persist.

The workbook runs all of this on a 50/50 JPM + MS portfolio benchmarked against SPY, over 1,256 daily returns from 2020. JPM MS Portfolio Mean daily return 0.000745 0.001083 0.000914 Annualised return 18.78% 27.29% 23.03% Daily volatility 0.020498 0.022507 0.020451 Annualised volatility 32.54% 35.73% 32.47% Downside deviation (annualised) 21.61% Two things are visible immediately. A return is money made or lost over a period, expressed as a percentage. Simple return =St/St−1−1= S_t/S_{t-1} - 1=St​/St−1​−1; log return =ln⁡(St/St−1)= \ln(S_t/S_{t-1})=ln(St​/St−1​) — and in Excel that is LN, not LOG. On the real 50/50 JPM/MS portfolio: 23.03% annualised return, 32.47% volatility, 21.61% downside deviation, 142.67% cumulative — with portfolio volatility below both constituents thanks to a 0.8088 correlation.

The Black-Scholes model is a mathematical model for pricing European-style options. It was developed by Fischer Black and Myron Scholes in the early 1970s, and it provides a theoretical estimate of the price of a European-style option.

Three reasons, and only the first is the obvious one. a) Fair pricing. The model helps determine the fair market value of the option. This ensures neither the buyer nor the seller is at a disadvantage — there is a defensible number, rather than two parties guessing. b) Regulatory compliance. Financial institutions are required to mark their positions to market and ensure they are accurately valued. Doing that at scale means using a quantitative model — and Black-Scholes is the one. c) Hedging the portfolio. This is the link back to everything in the previous two modules: BS model⟶price of option⟶Greeks⟶hedging\text{BS model} \longrightarrow \text{price of option} \longrightarrow \text{Greeks} \longrightarrow \text{hedging}BS model⟶price of option⟶Greeks⟶hedging The model produces a price. Differentiate that price and you get the Greeks — delta, gamma, rho, theta, vega. Delta in particular: Δ=change in option pricechange in the underlying\Delta = \frac{\text{change in option price}}{\text{change in the underlying}}Δ=change in the underlyingchange in option price​ where Black-Scholes supplies the numerator. And delta is what delta hedging runs on. So the chain closes: BS → price → Greeks → hedging. Without a pricing model there are no Greeks, and without Greeks there is no hedge.

Six of them, and the lecturer flags this section hard — the assumptions are where the model's failures live. (a) No dividends are paid during the life of the option. (b) No transaction cost in buying the option. (c) The returns of the underlying asset are normally distributed. This is the one that breaks. The margin note names the counterexamples directly: 2007-2008 and the pandemic, where returns spiked far outside what a normal distribution allows. The response is either other models or tweak the existing model. It is also the assumption most often misstated, so the notes draw the distinction carefully: Returnsnormally distributed−ve+ve0Stock pricelog-normally distributed0strictly +vefloor Returns are normally distributed — symmetric, taking negative and positive values alike. The stock price is not. A stock cannot go negative; it is floored at 0. So the price is log-normally distributed while the returns are normally distributed. Those are two different statements, and the model only claims the second. (d) The model can be used only for European options — options exercised only at maturity. An American option can be exercised at any point in time, so Black-Scholes does not apply to it. The notes mark this with an explicit ✗. (e) The risk-free rate and the volatility of the underlying are known and constant. In the geometric Brownian motion that underlies the model, these are the two parameters: GBM term Symbol Set to Drift μ\muμ the risk-free rate Diffusion σ\sigmaσ the volatility (f) Markets are random, so market movements cannot be predicted. Which is why Black-Scholes is a stochastic model — it does not forecast the price, it describes the distribution the price is drawn from.

A single trading day is therefore T→1252T \rightarrow \frac{1}{252}T→2521​ rrr — the risk-free rate, and the notes are specific about how to pick it: match the maturity of the option. The notes leave the boxes for India and Germany blank, which is the point: the risk-free rate is jurisdiction-specific, and you use the government curve of the currency you are pricing in.

Volatility (σ\sigmaσ) is a measure of how much the price of the underlying asset is expected to fluctuate over a year. Higher volatility means the asset price can move more dramatically. It comes in two kinds: Looks Is Historical volatility backward How the price of the underlying has fluctuated in the past — computed from historical data Implied volatility forward Derived from the market price of the option; represents the market's expectation of future volatility

a) Historical analysis — when performing any analysis based on past price movements, and for backtesting a trading strategy or risk management. b) Comparative study — when you compare past volatility across different assets.

a) Forward-looking analysis — when the goal is to incorporate the market's expectation of future volatility, and for pricing options. b) Trading and hedging — for a trader it is very important to understand market sentiment and expectation. This is the branch that feeds Black-Scholes → hedging. The division is simple: you price with implied, you study the past with historical.
This is the part worth slowing down on, because the two look similar and are not.
documents.s: What N(d₁) and N(d₂) actually mean

documents.t: N(d1)N(d_1)N(d1​) is the probability that the stock price will be higher than the strike price at maturity — the probability the option expires ITM. For a call: ST>K ⟹ In the MoneyS_T > K \;\Longrightarrow\; \text{In the Money}ST​>K⟹In the Money And the reason a CDF appears at all: N(⋅)⟶CDF of the standard normal⟶probability⟶ITM⟶exercisedN(\cdot) \longrightarrow \text{CDF of the standard normal} \longrightarrow \text{probability} \longrightarrow \text{ITM} \longrightarrow \text{exercised}N(⋅)⟶CDF of the standard normal⟶probability⟶ITM⟶exercised Example. N(d1)=60%N(d_1) = 60\%N(d1​)=60%, or 0.6 — there is a 60% chance the option expires in the money, i.e. that ST>KS_T > KST​>K.
documents.s: N(d₁) — the probability of finishing in the money

documents.t: N(d2)N(d_2)N(d2​) is the probability that the stock price will end up above the strike price, but adjusted to account for the time value of money. It is also a CDF of the standard normal. The distinction is what it is the probability of: that you will actually make money from the option. Example. N(d2)=55%N(d_2) = 55\%N(d2​)=55%, or 0.55 — there is a 55% chance you will actually make money from the option.
documents.s: N(d₂) — the probability of making money

documents.t: Answers N(d1)N(d_1)N(d1​) Will it be in the money, or not? N(d2)N(d_2)N(d2​) Will you make money, or not? The gap between 60% and 55% is not noise — it is time and the risk-free rate. Finishing above the strike is not the same as profiting, because the strike you pay is paid later, and must be discounted: N(d2) e−rTN(d_2)\,e^{-rT}N(d2​)e−rT An option can expire in the money and still lose you money. N(d1)N(d_1)N(d1​) does not know that; N(d2)N(d_2)N(d2​) does.

With that, the call formula stops being opaque: C=S0 N(d1)⏟what you get − Ke−rTN(d2)⏟what you payC = \underbrace{S_0\,N(d_1)}_{\text{what you get}} \;-\; \underbrace{K e^{-rT} N(d_2)}_{\text{what you pay}}C=what you getS0​N(d1​)​​−what you payKe−rTN(d2​)​​ First term — S0N(d1)S_0 N(d_1)S0​N(d1​). The present value of the expected payoff if the option is exercised, weighted by the probability N(d1)N(d_1)N(d1​) that it finishes ITM. This is the asset you receive. Second term — Ke−rTN(d2)K e^{-rT} N(d_2)Ke−rTN(d2​). The present value of the strike price, weighted by N(d2)N(d_2)N(d2​). This is the cash you hand over, discounted back from expiry because you do not pay it today. So the price of a call is what you expect to receive minus what you expect to pay, each weighted by the probability that you receive or pay it at all. The put formula is the same idea with the two sides swapped and the probabilities mirrored, N(−d1)N(-d_1)N(−d1​) and N(−d2)N(-d_2)N(−d2​).
documents.s: Reading the formula term by term

documents.t: Black-Scholes prices European options only — Black and Scholes, early 1970s — and exists for fair pricing, regulatory mark-to-market, and hedging. It is the head of the chain BS → price → Greeks → hedging: the model supplies the option price that every Greek is a derivative of. Six assumptions: no dividends, no transaction costs, normally distributed returns, European exercise only, known and constant rrr and σ\sigmaσ, and random markets. Returns are normal; the stock price is log-normal — because a price cannot go below zero. C=S0N(d1)−Ke−rTN(d2)C = S_0 N(d_1) - K e^{-rT} N(d_2)C=S0​N(d1​)−Ke−rTN(d2​), with d2=d1−σtd_2 = d_1 - \sigma\sqrt{t}d2​=d1​−σt​ and N(⋅)N(\cdot)N(⋅) the standard normal CDF. N(d1)N(d_1)N(d1​) is the probability of expiring in the money; N(d2)N(d_2)N(d2​) is the probability of making money. The difference between them is the time value of money. Match rrr to the option's maturity, and use implied volatility to price, historical volatility to study the past.

Any variable whose value changes over time in an uncertain way is said to be a stochastic process. Stochastic process → “random” process. Stocks are random processes; they are stochastic in nature, random in nature. We are trying to model the randomness. The two stock sketches show irregular paths rising, falling and rising again. Their annotation reads: stocks follow stochastic process as it's random in nature.
A DT SP is a process in which the value of the variable can change over certain fixed points in time.
A CT SP is a process where the value of the variable can change at any point in time. Example: GBM (Geometric Brownian Motion).

Markov process: a Markov process is a type of stochastic process where the current value of the variable is relevant for predicting the future, but the past values of the variable are irrelevant. The timeline marks the past as irrelevant, highlights t₀ (the current value) as relevant, and points from it to t + 1 to predict the future. Markov property: the Markov property states that the future state of a process depends only on the present state, not on its past values. For a stochastic process: {Xt}t>0,\{X_t\}_{t>0},{Xt​}t>0​, it satisfies the Markov property when: P(Xt+1∣Xt,Xt−1,…,X0)=P(Xt+1∣Xt).P(X_{t+1}\mid X_t,X_{t-1},\ldots,X_0) =P(X_{t+1}\mid X_t).P(Xt+1​∣Xt​,Xt−1​,…,X0​)=P(Xt+1​∣Xt​). The diagram again shows t − 2, t − 1, t, and t + 1, with the current value at t highlighted: no need of historical data beyond the current state for this conditional prediction.

The sketch takes stock (XYZ) from $20, 5 years ago, to $100 today. Whatever price you see today captures everything that has happened in the past. Markov process is memoryless: the current state contains all the information needed to predict the future. Note: stock prices are also assumed to be a Markov process in the world of quantitative finance. This is the modeling assumption in these notes.
Black Scholes Model → price European option. The Black Scholes Model assumes that the stock price follows GBM (Geometric Brownian Motion), which is a Markov process.
Stochastic interest-rate models — Vasicek, CIR, Hull White Model, Ho Lee Model — consume Brownian motion. Brownian motion follows the Markov property.

A Wiener process is a continuous-time stochastic process that models random motion. It is widely used in physics and finance. The physical analogy is a mosquito / honey bee in a container, with a wandering path drawn inside it. The diagram labels Wiener process / Brownian motion → random process. Mathematically, a Wiener process is denoted by: {Wt}t≥0.\{W_t\}_{t\geq0}.{Wt​}t≥0​. This is a continuous-time stochastic process. The stock sketch is labelled GBM, and the adjacent relationship is BM → GBM.
To qualify as a Wiener process, it should satisfy 5 properties.
documents.s: Properties of Wiener process / Brownian motion

documents.t: The process should start at zero: W0=0.\boxed{W_0=0}.W0​=0​. The initial-point sketch places the process at t = 0.

The changes in the process are independent of each other. The notes connect this to the Markov property. The honey bee in a container example sketches several possible movements between t and t + s, with s = 1 second as an illustration. Wt+s−Wt.W_{t+s}-W_t.Wt+s​−Wt​. These increments are independent of each other over non-overlapping time intervals. The non-overlap qualification makes the handwritten statement precise.

For any s > 0, the change is normally distributed: Wt+s−Wt∼N(0,s).\boxed{W_{t+s}-W_t\sim N(0,s)}.Wt+s​−Wt​∼N(0,s)​.N(0,s)⟶mean=0,variance=s.N(0,s)\quad\longrightarrow\quad \text{mean}=0,\qquad\text{variance}=s.N(0,s)⟶mean=0,variance=s. Variance is proportional to the time increment. The timeline labels the endpoints Wₜ and Wₜ₊ₛ, with normal distribution written beside the increment: Δt=t+s−t=s.\Delta t=t+s-t=s.Δt=t+s−t=s.

The Wiener process should “evolve smoothly over time”, which means that there should be no jumps. The stock-path sketches contrast a connected path with broken paths, highlight no gap, and conclude it's a CTSP. Terminology clarification: “smoothly” here means continuously, as the no-jump explanation says; Brownian paths are not differentiable smooth curves.

Martingale process: a martingale is a process where the future expected value is always equal to the current value. For a Wiener process Wₜ, at any time t, the future value Wₜ₊ₛ (s > 0) depends only on where it is at t, not on how it got there. Mathematically: E[Wt+s∣Wt]=Wt.E[W_{t+s}\mid W_t]=W_t.E[Wt+s​∣Wt​]=Wt​. The best guess for the future value is just the current value.
documents.s: 5. Wiener process is also a martingale

documents.t: Expectation → average value or mean. E[Xt]=0.E[X_t]=0.E[Xt​]=0. The derivation switches to the symbol X for the same standard Brownian process. From the Brownian-motion definition: Xt=X0+sum of independent increments.X_t=X_0+\text{sum of independent increments}.Xt​=X0​+sum of independent increments. The handwritten expectation step is: E[Xt]=E[X0]+E[ΔX].E[X_t]=E[X_0]+E[\Delta X].E[Xt​]=E[X0​]+E[ΔX]. Here ΔX represents the sum of the increments over the interval. The initial value is: X0=0⟹E[X0]=0.X_0=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad E[X_0]=0.X0​=0⟹E[X0​]=0. ΔX → normal distribution → mean = 0. Therefore: E[Xt]=E[X0]+E[ΔX]=0+0,E[Xt]=0.\begin{aligned} E[X_t]&=E[X_0]+E[\Delta X] \\ &=0+0, \\ \boxed{E[X_t]}&=\boxed{0}. \end{aligned}E[Xt​]E[Xt​]​​=E[X0​]+E[ΔX]=0+0,=0​.​

The notes pose Var(Xₜ) = t = ??, then add the independent increment variances: Var⁡(Xt)=Var⁡(X0)+Var⁡(ΔX1)+Var⁡(ΔX2)+⋯+Var⁡(ΔXn).\operatorname{Var}(X_t)=\operatorname{Var}(X_0) +\operatorname{Var}(\Delta X_1)+\operatorname{Var}(\Delta X_2) +\cdots+\operatorname{Var}(\Delta X_n).Var(Xt​)=Var(X0​)+Var(ΔX1​)+Var(ΔX2​)+⋯+Var(ΔXn​). Each increment has variance equal to its time length: Var⁡(ΔXi)=Δt.\operatorname{Var}(\Delta X_i)=\Delta t.Var(ΔXi​)=Δt. Thus: Var⁡(Xt)=0+Δt+Δt+⋯+Δt.\operatorname{Var}(X_t)=0+\Delta t+\Delta t+\cdots+\Delta t.Var(Xt​)=0+Δt+Δt+⋯+Δt. The timeline divides the interval from 0 to t into n equal intervals, each labelled Δt: Var⁡(Xt)=nΔt=t.\operatorname{Var}(X_t)=n\Delta t=t.Var(Xt​)=nΔt=t.Var⁡(Xt)=t.\boxed{\operatorname{Var}(X_t)=t}.Var(Xt​)=t​. The final margin reminds us that at X₀, the mean is 0 and the variance is 0.
The closing diagram connects Brownian motion to both: GBM. Black Scholes Modeling.

GBM → model a single stock. Now consider two stocks: S₁ → ABC. S₂ → XYZ. The example labels both as financial companies and asks whether S₁ and S₂ will have correlation or not: yes. When we model our stocks using geometric Brownian motion, we need to make sure that the same correlation is also integrated within the GBM process. The diagram shows S₁ and S₂ linked by correlation before modeling, each passing through a GBM arrow, with correlation retained between the two resulting processes. To integrate the correlation between the processes, we use Cholesky decomposition.
The example's correlation between S₁ and S₂ is ρ = 0.6 or 60%. Σ=[1ρρ1].\Sigma=\begin{bmatrix}1&\rho\\\rho&1\end{bmatrix}.Σ=[1ρ​ρ1​]. Note: −1≤ρ≤1.-1\leq\rho\leq1.−1≤ρ≤1.

GBM is a stochastic process which is widely used to model the behaviour of assets (stock price). GBM ensures that the asset price remains positive and incorporates randomness proportional to the current price level, making it suitable for quantitative modeling. The stock-price margin contrasts “−ve ?? ” with “0 or +ve”. GBM with a positive starting price stays strictly positive at finite times. The notes say: we use GBM to model stock price; we don't use it to model interest rate. The interest-rate branch instead points to mean reversion process → stochastic interest-rate model. This describes the course's model choices.

Start with the generalized Wiener equation: dXt=μ dt+σ dWt.dX_t=\mu\,dt+\sigma\,dW_t.dXt​=μdt+σdWt​. For GBM, the change is proportional to the current value of Sₜ: dStSt=μ dt+σ dWt.\frac{dS_t}{S_t}=\mu\,dt+\sigma\,dW_t.St​dSt​​=μdt+σdWt​. Therefore the GBM equation, an SDE to solve for modeling stock prices, is: dSt=μSt dt+σSt dWt.\boxed{dS_t=\mu S_t\,dt+\sigma S_t\,dW_t}.dSt​=μSt​dt+σSt​dWt​​. μ: the margin lists both risk-free rate and stock's rate of return. These correspond to risk-neutral pricing and a real-world return model, respectively; the spreadsheet below uses its specified drift. σ: volatility of the stock price. Quant model → assumption; quant processes → assumption.

The reminder dWₜ = Z × sqrt(t) points to a standard normal process. The margin also names Poisson and Bernoulli as other distributions; they are not used for the standard-normal Z in this GBM construction. dXt=μ dt+σ dWt.dX_t=\mu\,dt+\sigma\,dW_t.dXt​=μdt+σdWt​. The comparison labels DE / regular calculus with the handwritten schematic dXₜ = μdt + σ, and SDE / random with dXₜ = μdt + σdWₜ. The dWₜ term is boxed as the Wiener process; an unfilled distribution reminder is drawn as [ ] N [ ].
dSt=μSt dt+σSt dWt.dS_t=\mu S_t\,dt+\sigma S_t\,dW_t.dSt​=μSt​dt+σSt​dWt​.

Instead of modeling Sₜ directly, let: Yt=ln⁡(St).Y_t=\ln(S_t).Yt​=ln(St​). The ln → +ve / −ve margin is the reminder to take a real logarithm of a positive price. The logarithm itself can be negative when the price is between 0 and 1.

documents.t: dSt=μSt dt+σSt dWt.dS_t=\mu S_t\,dt+\sigma S_t\,dW_t.dSt​=μSt​dt+σSt​dWt​. 1st component: 1St dSt=1St(μSt dt+σSt dWt)=μ dt+σ dWt.\begin{aligned} \frac{1}{S_t}\,dS_t &=\frac{1}{S_t}\left(\mu S_t\,dt+\sigma S_t\,dW_t\right) \\ &=\mu\,dt+\sigma\,dW_t. \end{aligned}St​1​dSt​​=St​1​(μSt​dt+σSt​dWt​)=μdt+σdWt​.​ 2nd component: 121St2(dSt)2=121St2(μSt dt+σSt dWt)2.\frac12\frac{1}{S_t^2}(dS_t)^2 =\frac12\frac{1}{S_t^2}\left(\mu S_t\,dt+\sigma S_t\,dW_t\right)^2.21​St2​1​(dSt​)2=21​St2​1​(μSt​dt+σSt​dWt​)2. The annotations say ignore the higher-order dt contributions: dt → small = 1/252, dt² → infinitely small = 1/(252)², with a zero-like oval beside the latter. In Itô differential algebra, the rules being used are (dt)² = 0, dt dWₜ = 0, and (dWₜ)² = dt; the finite number 1/(252)² is small, not literally zero. This is the contract Monte Carlo exists for. An Asian option has no closed-form solution, so the European note's check against Black-Scholes was the last time an independent answer was available. From here, simulation is the answer.
Type Contracts Standard contract European, American Exotic contract Asian, Barrier, Digital And Monte Carlo handles all of them — European, Asian, Barrier.

Asian options are exotic options where the payoff depends on the average price of the underlying asset over a specified period. The contrast is the whole idea: Unlike a European option, which considers the price of the stock at expiry / maturity, an Asian option reduces the risk and uncertainty by taking the average price of the stock. European — the terminal price only: C=max⁡(ST−K, 0)P=max⁡(K−ST, 0)C = \max(S_T - K,\, 0) \qquad\qquad P = \max(K - S_T,\, 0)C=max(ST​−K,0)P=max(K−ST​,0) where STS_TST​ is the stock price at maturity. Asian — the average instead: C=max⁡(Savg−K, 0) P=max⁡(K−Savg, 0) \boxed{\;C = \max(S_{avg} - K,\, 0)\;} \qquad\qquad \boxed{\;P = \max(K - S_{avg},\, 0)\;}C=max(Savg​−K,0)​P=max(K−Savg​,0)​ where SavgS_{avg}Savg​ is the average of the stock price over all the time steps: Savg=a+b+c+d+e+f6S_{avg} = \frac{a + b + c + d + e + f}{6}Savg​=6a+b+c+d+e+f​

A path generated by GBM visits these prices over six steps to maturity: ttt 1 2 3 4 5 6 Price 100 101 102 103 104 105 Savg=100+101+102+103+104+1056=102.5S_{avg} = \frac{100 + 101 + 102 + 103 + 104 + 105}{6} = \mathbf{102.5}Savg​=6100+101+102+103+104+105​=102.5 A European option on this path would settle on 105. The Asian settles on 102.5. Same path, different number — and the difference is the point of the contract.

The structure from the notes: every simulation is a column, every time step a row, all starting from the same price. Step Sim 1 Sim 2 Sim 3 … Sim 10,000 0 49 49 49 ⋮ 49 1 ▢ ▢ ⋮ ▢ 2 ▢ ▢ ⋮ ▢ ⋮ 6 ▢ ▢ ⋮ ▢ Each column steps forward recursively under GBM. Then each column collapses to a single number: Path 1→SavgPath 2→Savg⋯Path 10,000→Savg\text{Path 1} \rightarrow S_{avg} \qquad \text{Path 2} \rightarrow S_{avg} \qquad \cdots \qquad \text{Path 10,000} \rightarrow S_{avg}Path 1→Savg​Path 2→Savg​⋯Path 10,000→Savg​ Each SavgS_{avg}Savg​ becomes a payoff: C=max⁡(Savg−K, 0)C = \max(S_{avg} - K,\, 0)C=max(Savg​−K,0) and from there it is the standard Monte Carlo ending — average, then discount: Avg payoff=Payoff1+Payoff2+⋯+Payoff10,00010,000\text{Avg payoff} = \frac{\text{Payoff}_1 + \text{Payoff}_2 + \cdots + \text{Payoff}_{10{,}000}}{10{,}000}Avg payoff=10,000Payoff1​+Payoff2​+⋯+Payoff10,000​​Discounted payoff=e−rT[Avg payoff]\text{Discounted payoff} = e^{-rT}\left[\text{Avg payoff}\right]Discounted payoff=e−rT[Avg payoff] which is the price of the Asian call option. Note where the only change lives: one extra averaging step per path, inserted between the simulation and the payoff. Everything else — GBM, average across paths, discount — is identical to the European case. That is how cheaply Monte Carlo absorbs path dependence.

The notes are careful that "average" is ambiguous, and both forms are used. Arithmetic average: Savg=S1+S2+S3+⋯+S66S_{avg} = \frac{S_1 + S_2 + S_3 + \cdots + S_6}{6}Savg​=6S1​+S2​+S3​+⋯+S6​​ Geometric average: Savg=(S1×S2×S3×S4×S5×S6)1/6S_{avg} = \left(S_1 \times S_2 \times S_3 \times S_4 \times S_5 \times S_6\right)^{1/6}Savg​=(S1​×S2​×S3​×S4​×S5​×S6​)1/6 which generalises to the geometric mean: Geometric mean=(∏i=1nxi)1/n\text{Geometric mean} = \left(\prod_{i=1}^{n} x_i\right)^{1/n}Geometric mean=(i=1∏n​xi​)1/n where ∏\prod∏ means product — the multiplicative counterpart of ∑\sum∑. And for a one-year Asian option, n=252n = 252n=252 trading days: (S1×S2×S3×⋯×S252)1/252\left(S_1 \times S_2 \times S_3 \times \cdots \times S_{252}\right)^{1/252}(S1​×S2​×S3​×⋯×S252​)1/252

Same contract, same layout as the European sheet — 100 paths across columns O:DJ, 6 daily steps down rows 3-8 — with one row inserted: Cell Label Formula K5 Number of steps (days) 6 K6 No. of sims 100 O3:O8 The GBM path steps forward from O2 O9 Average stock price =AVERAGE(O3:O8) O10 Option payoff (call) =MAX(O9-$B$6,0) O11 Option payoff (put) =MAX($B$6-O9,0) O12 Average payoff (call) =AVERAGE(O10:DJ10) O13 Discounted price (call) =O12*EXP(-B8*B7) O14 / O15 The same two steps for the put Row 9 is the entire Asian modification. The European sheet reads O8, the terminal price; the Asian sheet reads AVERAGE(O3:O8). One cell. Note also that the average runs O3:O8 and excludes O2 — the starting price S0S_0S0​ is not part of the average, only the six simulated steps are. That is correct: S0S_0S0​ is known, not sampled. This sheet inherits the European sheet's drift error The per-step formula is the same one flagged in the European note: it multiplies the drift by SQRT(N3) instead of N3, and uses a daily mean return where the risk-free rate belongs. The averaging logic above is sound — the path generator underneath it is not.

The notes claim it does. It is checkable, and it is true — with the risk-neutral generator, 400,000 paths on the SPY contract: Std dev Terminal price STS_TST​ 9.41 Path average SavgS_{avg}Savg​ 6.10 The average is 35% less variable than the terminal price. Averaging six draws cancels some of the noise in each — the same reason a sample mean is steadier than a single observation. And because an option is priced on uncertainty, less uncertainty means a cheaper option: Call Put European 1.7063 6.9642 Asian 0.6060 6.1748 The Asian call costs about a third of the European. That is not a mispricing — it is the contract being genuinely less exposed. An Asian option cannot be made valuable by one lucky day at expiry, and it cannot be ruined by one unlucky one. Which is also why they exist commercially: a corporate hedging a year of fuel purchases cares about the average price it paid, not the price on one arbitrary December afternoon. The contract matches the exposure.

Asian options are exotic: the payoff depends on the average price of the underlying over a period, not the terminal price. C=max⁡(Savg−K, 0)C = \max(S_{avg} - K,\, 0)C=max(Savg​−K,0) and P=max⁡(K−Savg, 0)P = \max(K - S_{avg},\, 0)P=max(K−Savg​,0). Worked: a path visiting 100…105 averages to 102.5, where a European would settle on 105. The average can be arithmetic or geometric, the latter being (∏xi)1/n\left(\prod x_i\right)^{1/n}(∏xi​)1/n — 252 factors for a one-year contract. In the simulation, the only change is one averaging step per path, before the payoff. Average across paths and discount exactly as before. In Excel the whole modification is =AVERAGE(O3:O8) in place of reading the terminal cell — and S0S_0S0​ is correctly excluded. Averaging cuts variability by ~35%, which makes the Asian call worth about a third of the equivalent European. Less uncertainty, cheaper option.
The Asian option was path-dependent through an average. A barrier option is path-dependent through a threshold — and the whole contract can be switched on or off by a single moment along the way.

Barrier options are a type of exotic contract where the payoff depends on whether the underlying asset price reaches a predetermined barrier level or not — at any point during the life of the option contract. That last clause is what makes it path-dependent. Not the price at expiry; the price at every moment. Barrier BS₀crosses → ACTIVEnever touchesnever toucheshit

Type Variants 1. Knock-in Up & In, Down & In 2. Knock-out Up & Out, Down & Out 3. Double barrier Double knock-in, Double knock-out And the rule that governs all six: In⟶ActiveOut⟶Deactivate\textbf{In} \longrightarrow \text{Active} \qquad\qquad \textbf{Out} \longrightarrow \text{Deactivate}In⟶ActiveOut⟶Deactivate

These options become active (knock in) only if the underlying asset hits a certain barrier level during the life of the option contract. If the barrier is never reached, the option expires worthless. Path Result Payoff Hits the barrier Active max⁡(ST−K, 0)\max(S_T - K,\, 0)max(ST​−K,0) for a call, max⁡(K−ST, 0)\max(K - S_T,\, 0)max(K−ST​,0) for a put Never touches it Inactive 0 Up & In — the path crosses an up barrier from below → active. Down & In — the path crosses a down barrier from above → active. The contract becomes active when the barrier is crossed (up or down), otherwise the contract will expire worthless.

The mirror image: the option deactivates when the barrier is crossed. Crosses the barrier Never crosses Up & Out Inactive Active Down & Out Inactive Active So a knock-out holder is hoping the level never trades, and a knock-in holder is hoping it does.

There is both an up barrier and a down barrier. Rule Double knock-in If either barrier is crossed, the contract becomes active; otherwise inactive, payoff = 0 Double knock-out If either barrier is breached, the contract becomes inactive; if not breached, active For a double knock-in, a path that wanders quietly between the two barriers is worth nothing — it needed to break out in one direction or the other. For a double knock-out, that same quiet path is the only one that pays.

documents.t: In a simulation, "did it touch?" is just a question about the range of the path: Barrier Test Up barrier max⁡(range)≥B\max(\text{range}) \ge Bmax(range)≥B Down barrier min⁡(range)≤B\min(\text{range}) \le Bmin(range)≤B The notes work a down-barrier example: with B=100B = 100B=100, a path that drifts down to 90 gives min⁡(range)=90≤100\min(\text{range}) = 90 \le 100min(range)=90≤100 → barrier crossed. Two lines of logic, and they are the entire difference between a barrier option and a vanilla one.

Seven steps, of which only step 4 and 5 are new: # Step 1 Initialise the parameters 2 Generate random numbers using the standard normal distribution 3 Use those numbers in the GBM equation and simulate the stock price 4 Check if, during the life of the option, any barrier is crossed or not 5 Apply the knock-in / knock-out rule to get the payoff 6 Average the payoffs 7 Discount the average Step 5 branches: Crossed⇒Active⇒max⁡(ST−K, 0)Not crossed⇒Inactive⇒Payoff=0\text{Crossed} \Rightarrow \text{Active} \Rightarrow \max(S_T - K,\, 0) \qquad\qquad \text{Not crossed} \Rightarrow \text{Inactive} \Rightarrow \text{Payoff} = 0Crossed⇒Active⇒max(ST​−K,0)Not crossed⇒Inactive⇒Payoff=0 and then it is the familiar ending: Avg payoff=Payoff1+Payoff2+⋯+Payoff10,00010,000\text{Avg payoff} = \frac{\text{Payoff}_1 + \text{Payoff}_2 + \cdots + \text{Payoff}_{10{,}000}}{10{,}000}Avg payoff=10,000Payoff1​+Payoff2​+⋯+Payoff10,000​​Price of barrier option=e−rT[Avg payoff]\text{Price of barrier option} = e^{-rT}\left[\text{Avg payoff}\right]Price of barrier option=e−rT[Avg payoff]

Same 100-path, 6-step grid as before. The barrier logic is four rows: Cell Label Formula K7 Up barrier 557 O9 Max value =MAX(O3:O8) O10 Barrier crossed (?) =IF(O9>$K$7,"Yes","No") O11 Check barrier (call) =IF(MAX(O3:O8)>=$K$7, MAX(O8-$B$6,0), 0) O12 Check barrier (put) =IF(MAX(O3:O8)>=$K$7, MAX($B$6-O8,0), 0) O13 Average payoff (call) =AVERAGE(O11:DJ11) O14 Discounted price (call) =O13*EXP(-B8*B7) O11 is the whole contract in one cell: if the path's maximum reached the barrier, pay the ordinary call payoff; otherwise pay nothing. With an up barrier and payment on crossing, this sheet implements an up-and-in call. Two small inconsistencies in the sheet O10 — the human-readable "Yes/No" — tests O9 > K7 (strictly greater), while the payoff cells O11/O12 test >= K7. A path whose maximum lands exactly on 557 is reported as "No" but paid as though it crossed. Harmless in floating point, but the two should agree. The path generator also carries the same drift error flagged in the European note — drift multiplied by SQRT(N3) instead of N3, and a daily mean return in place of the risk-free rate. The barrier logic above is correct; the prices it produces are not.

There is no closed form here either — but barrier options come with an identity that makes them self-checking: Up-and-in+Up-and-out=Vanilla European\text{Up-and-in} + \text{Up-and-out} = \text{Vanilla European}Up-and-in+Up-and-out=Vanilla European Every path either touches the barrier or it doesn't. The knock-in collects the payoff in the first case, the knock-out collects it in the second, and between them they collect every payoff exactly once. Simulated over 400,000 paths on the SPY contract, barrier 557: Call Up-and-in 1.6658 Up-and-out 0.0357 Sum 1.7015 European 1.7015 Exact. That identity is the barrier equivalent of the European note's Black-Scholes check — a way to know the simulation is right when no formula is available to compare against. Two things it reveals about this contract: 31% of paths reach the barrier. With six trading days, an 11.1% volatility and the barrier only 8 points above spot, most paths never get there. The up-and-out call is nearly worthless — 0.0357 against the vanilla's 1.7015. To pay anything it must finish above 555 while never having touched 557: a two-dollar window it has to land in and stay in. Almost every path that finishes in the money got there by going through the barrier first, and knocked itself out on the way. Which is the general lesson about barriers. Moving a barrier a couple of points can take most of the value out of an option, because it is not the destination being priced — it is every step of the route.
documents.s: Checking it: in + out must equal the vanilla

documents.t: That completes the module's four pricing methods on the same SPY contract: Method Handles Call price How it works Binomial tree European, American 1.7131 Discrete up/down lattice, valued backwards Black-Scholes European only 1.7054 Closed-form formula Monte Carlo European, American, exotic 1.7065 Simulate, payoff, discount, average Monte Carlo, up-and-in Barrier 1.6658 The same, plus a path condition The three methods that price the vanilla call agree to within a cent — a lattice, a formula and 400,000 random walks converging on the same number from three unrelated directions. And the progression through the module is one of increasing generality bought with increasing computation. Black-Scholes is instant but only handles one contract type. The binomial tree adds early exercise. Monte Carlo is the slowest and handles everything, because it does not need a formula for the payoff — it only needs to be able to simulate the path and read the payoff off it. Averaging, thresholds, or anything else you can express as a rule on a price series.

Barrier options are exotic contracts whose payoff depends on whether the price reaches a predetermined level during the life of the contract. Knock-in options are inactive until the barrier is touched — if it is never reached, the option expires worthless. Knock-out options are active until the barrier is touched, then deactivate. Six variants: Up/Down × In/Out, plus double knock-in and double knock-out, which trigger on either of two barriers. The test is on the range of the path: max⁡(range)≥B\max(\text{range}) \ge Bmax(range)≥B for an up barrier, min⁡(range)≤B\min(\text{range}) \le Bmin(range)≤B for a down barrier. Valuation adds two steps to Monte Carlo — check the barrier, apply the in/out rule — then average and discount as always. The Excel sheet builds an up-and-in call in a single IF. In + out = vanilla is the identity that verifies the simulation; here 1.6658+0.0357=1.70151.6658 + 0.0357 = 1.70151.6658+0.0357=1.7015, matching the European exactly. A barrier a few points away can remove almost all of an option's value — the route is being priced, not just the destination.

A European option already has a closed form. So why simulate one? Because it is the test case. If Monte Carlo cannot reproduce Black-Scholes on a contract where the answer is known, there is no reason to trust it on an exotic one where it is not. That check is done at the end of this note — and it is the most useful thing in it.

1) Initialise all the parameters. The notes' worked values: μ=5%σ=5.5%Δt=1252\mu = 5\% \qquad \sigma = 5.5\% \qquad \Delta t = \frac{1}{252}μ=5%σ=5.5%Δt=2521​ feeding GBM → stock price. 2) Generate a random number. ZtZ_tZt​ is a random number drawn from the standard normal distribution. The margin note that matters Beside this step the notes write μ → r ↳ risk-free rate. That is the risk-neutral pricing rule, and it is not a detail. When pricing an option you do not drift the stock at its historical expected return μ\muμ — you drift it at the risk-free rate rrr. Otherwise you are pricing your own forecast rather than the contract. Keep this in mind; the workbook does not follow it. 3) Put ZtZ_tZt​ into the GBM equation. St+Δt=Stexp⁡[(μ−12σ2)Δt+σΔt Zt]S_{t+\Delta t} = S_t \exp\left[\left(\mu - \frac{1}{2}\sigma^2\right)\Delta t + \sigma\sqrt{\Delta t}\,Z_t\right]St+Δt​=St​exp[(μ−21​σ2)Δt+σΔt​Zt​] 4) Calculate the payoff at maturity: Payoffcall=max⁡(ST−K, 0)Payoffput=max⁡(K−ST, 0)\text{Payoff}_{\text{call}} = \max(S_T - K,\, 0) \qquad\qquad \text{Payoff}_{\text{put}} = \max(K - S_T,\, 0)Payoffcall​=max(ST​−K,0)Payoffput​=max(K−ST​,0) 5) Average the payoffs. Avg payoff=Payoff1+Payoff2+⋯+Payoff100100\text{Avg payoff} = \frac{\text{Payoff}_1 + \text{Payoff}_2 + \cdots + \text{Payoff}_{100}}{100}Avg payoff=100Payoff1​+Payoff2​+⋯+Payoff100​​ 6) Discount the average payoff. Option price=e−rT[Avg payoff] \boxed{\;\text{Option price} = e^{-rT}\left[\text{Avg payoff}\right]\;}Option price=e−rT[Avg payoff]​

For every path, you will generate the price of the stock every day. The chain is recursive — each day starts from the previous day's price: S1=S0exp⁡[(μ−12σ2)Δt+σΔt Z1]S_1 = S_0 \exp\left[\left(\mu - \tfrac12\sigma^2\right)\Delta t + \sigma\sqrt{\Delta t}\,Z_1\right]S1​=S0​exp[(μ−21​σ2)Δt+σΔt​Z1​]S2=S1exp⁡[(μ−12σ2)Δt+σΔt Z2]S_2 = S_1 \exp\left[\left(\mu - \tfrac12\sigma^2\right)\Delta t + \sigma\sqrt{\Delta t}\,Z_2\right]S2​=S1​exp[(μ−21​σ2)Δt+σΔt​Z2​]⋮\vdots⋮S7=S6exp⁡[(μ−12σ2)Δt+σΔt Z7]S_7 = S_6 \exp\left[\left(\mu - \tfrac12\sigma^2\right)\Delta t + \sigma\sqrt{\Delta t}\,Z_7\right]S7​=S6​exp[(μ−21​σ2)Δt+σΔt​Z7​] and S7S_7S7​ is the stock price at maturity for path 1. A fresh ZZZ is drawn at every step of every path. Then that single terminal price produces a single payoff, and the whole path is reduced to one number. Repeat 100 times, average, discount.

Built on SPY240709C00555000 — the same contract the binomial tree and Black-Scholes notes priced, so all three are directly comparable. Cell Input Value B5 Stock price SSS 549 B6 Strike KKK 555 B7 Maturity ttt =6/252 B8 Risk-free rate rrr 0.055 K1 Initial stock price =B5 K2 Drift rate μ\muμ =AVERAGE(F3:F253) → 0.00090561 K3 Volatility σ\sigmaσ =STDEV.S(F3:F253)*SQRT(252) → 0.11102 N3:N8 Time increment =1/252 The grid itself: Region Holds Row 2 S0=549S_0 = 549S0​=549, repeated across every path Rows 3-8 The 6 daily steps Columns O:DJ 100 simulated paths, one per column Row 9 Call payoff — =MAX(O8-$B$6,0) Row 10 Put payoff — =MAX($B$6-O8,0) O11 =AVERAGE(O9:DJ9) — the average call payoff O12 =O11*EXP(-B8*B7) — discounted → the call price O13 / O14 The same two steps for the put That is steps 4, 5 and 6 in three rows: payoff, average, discount. The per-step formula is: O3 = O2*EXP(($K$2-0.5*$K$3*$K$3)*SQRT(N3)+$K$3*SQRT(N3)*NORM.S.INV(RAND())) NORM.S.INV(RAND()) is how Excel draws a standard normal: take a uniform draw on (0,1), then invert the normal CDF. That is ZtZ_tZt​.

This is the point of pricing a European option by simulation. Running the procedure as the notes describe it — risk-neutral drift rrr, drift scaled by Δt\Delta tΔt — over 400,000 paths: Method Call Put Black-Scholes (closed form) 1.7054 6.9791 Monte Carlo, done correctly 1.7065 6.9760 Difference 0.0011 0.0031 Monte Carlo converges on Black-Scholes. Two completely different methods — one an analytic formula, one 400,000 random walks — agree to about a tenth of a cent. That agreement is the whole justification for using simulation on contracts where no formula exists. It is also the Law of Large Numbers made visible: the average of the simulated payoffs converged to the expected value, and the expected value is what Black-Scholes computes directly.
documents.s: Does it work? Check it against Black-Scholes

documents.t: The workbook does not reproduce that agreement, and it is worth understanding why rather than copying it. a) The drift is scaled by Δt\sqrt{\Delta t}Δt​ instead of Δt\Delta tΔt. In the formula above, SQRT(N3) multiplies both terms. But GBM scales the two terms differently — drift with time, diffusion with the square root of time: (μ−12σ2)Δt⏟not Δt+σΔt⏟correctZt\left(\mu - \tfrac12\sigma^2\right)\underbrace{\Delta t}_{\text{not } \sqrt{\Delta t}} + \sigma\underbrace{\sqrt{\Delta t}}_{\text{correct}}Z_t(μ−21​σ2)not Δt​Δt​​+σcorrectΔt​​​Zt​ With Δt=1/252\Delta t = 1/252Δt=1/252: Δt=0.06299\sqrt{\Delta t} = 0.06299Δt​=0.06299 against Δt=0.003968\Delta t = 0.003968Δt=0.003968 — the drift term is applied 15.9× too strongly. b) μ\muμ is a daily mean return, but σ\sigmaσ is annualised. K2 is AVERAGE(F3:F253), the mean daily return (0.0009). K3 is STDEV.S(...) *SQRT(252), an annualised volatility (0.111). The two sit in the same expression in different units. And per the notes' own margin annotation, the drift should have been rrr, the risk-free rate, not a historical average at all. What it costs: Call Put Black-Scholes 1.7054 6.9791 MC as the workbook builds it 1.2543 8.2804 Workbook's saved values (100 paths) 1.5993 7.9632 The method is biased 26% low on the call and 19% high on the put. The saved values sit between the two because 100 paths is a very small sample — the sampling noise on a single recalculation is larger than the bias itself, which is exactly why the error is easy to miss when you are looking at one draw. Fix the two scaling issues and the sheet lands on Black-Scholes. Left as-is, it demonstrates the mechanics correctly but does not price the option.
documents.s: Two defects in the source workbook

documents.t: The procedure: initialise parameters → draw ZtZ_tZt​ → step GBM → payoff → average → discount. Option price=e−rT[Avg payoff]\text{Option price} = e^{-rT}\left[\text{Avg payoff}\right]Option price=e−rT[Avg payoff], with a fresh ZZZ at every step of every path. The Excel sheet lays out 100 paths as columns, 6 daily steps as rows, then does payoff / average / discount in three rows. Done correctly, Monte Carlo reproduces Black-Scholes to ~0.001 — that agreement is the reason simulation can be trusted on exotics. Price with the risk-free rate rrr, not the historical drift μ\muμ — the notes say so in the margin. The source workbook scales drift by Δt\sqrt{\Delta t}Δt​ instead of Δt\Delta tΔt and mixes daily drift with annualised volatility, which biases the call 26% low. Understand the layout from it; do not copy the formula.

The Monte Carlo method is a computational technique used to model and solve financial problems that involve uncertainty or complex dynamics. In computational finance it is the fallback — and the notes are precise about when you reach for it.

It is particularly used in areas where the closed-form analytical solution is difficult to derive. The notes make the idea of a "closed form" concrete with a quadratic equation: ax2+bx+c=0⟹x=−b±b2−4ac2aax^2 + bx + c = 0 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad x = \frac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a}ax2+bx+c=0⟹x=2a−b±b2−4ac​​ That second expression provides a direct formula for xxx. Put the numbers in, get the answer out — no iteration, no simulation. That is a closed form. Options split the same way: Contract Closed form? Method European call / put ✅ Yes Black-Scholes Exotic contract (e.g. Asian option) ❌ Not possible Monte Carlo C=S0N(d1)−Ke−rTN(d2)C = S_0 N(d_1) - K e^{-rT} N(d_2)C=S0​N(d1​)−Ke−rTN(d2​) is the closed form for a European call. For an exotic contract whose closed form is not possible, you simulate instead.

a) Option pricing. Monte Carlo is used for pricing exotic options whose payoff depends on the path of the underlying asset — not just where it ends up. That word path is the whole distinction: Option Payoff Depends on European max⁡(ST−K, 0)\max(S_T - K,\, 0)max(ST​−K,0) The terminal price only Asian max⁡(SˉT−K, 0)\max(\bar{S}_T - K,\, 0)max(SˉT​−K,0) The average along the way where the average is built from prices sampled during the contract's life: SˉT=S1+S2+S3+S44\bar{S}_T = \frac{S_1 + S_2 + S_3 + S_4}{4}SˉT​=4S1​+S2​+S3​+S4​​ Black-Scholes cannot see the middle of the path. Monte Carlo generates the whole path, so it can. Which method covers which contract: Method Applies to Black-Scholes European Binomial American (and European) Monte Carlo European, American, and exotic contracts Monte Carlo is the most general of the three. That generality is what you buy with the computation. b) Risk management. Financial institutions use the method to assess the risk of their portfolio under various scenarios — they simulate the stock prices in the portfolio, which gives Value at Risk. VaR — how much potential loss you can have at a specific confidence interval in a given time frame. VaR itself has three approaches: Monte Carlo, the historical method, and the variance-covariance method. c) Portfolio optimization.

a) Define the problem statement — e.g. determine the price of an exotic option. b) Identify the inputs of the model — what has to be simulated: simulate the interest rate (the notes name the Vasicek model) simulate the stock price c) Generate random numbers. Use a random generator to produce input for the model. These inputs should represent the uncertainty. documents.t: The notes stop here to justify the method, and the justification is two theorems.

Three students score 100, 90, 80. The class average is 100+90+803\frac{100 + 90 + 80}{3}3100+90+80​ Nobody finds that controversial. Monte Carlo is doing the same thing with payoffs instead of marks — the only question is whether the average of a sample tells you about the truth. Which is exactly what the two theorems answer.

The CLT states that under certain conditions, the average of a large number of iid random variables with finite mean and variance will approximate a normal distribution. iid = independent, identically distributed random variables. This is why the method's machinery is legitimate: the increments of a Wiener process are iid and normally distributed, drawn as ZΔtZ\sqrt{\Delta t}ZΔt​ with the same distribution at every step. And: According to the CLT, as the number of random samples rises, the distribution of the sample mean will approximate the normal distribution. Monte Carlo methods are often used to estimate the expected value of a complex random process — and the CLT is what says the estimate is well-behaved.

The LLN states that as the number of trials (or runs) in the random process increases, the average of the results obtained from these trials is likely to converge to the expected value of the random process. And the line that matters: This convergence is the reliability of the Monte Carlo method. The CLT tells you the shape of the estimate's error. The LLN tells you the error goes away if you run enough paths. Together they are the reason a simulated average is a price and not a guess. This is also why the notes keep writing 10,000: more paths, so that you can get higher accuracy. The more simulations you run, the closer the average sits to the true expected value of the option.

Step 1 — define the input parameters. All of them feed GBM: Parameter Meaning Value in the notes S0S_0S0​ Initial price μ\muμ Drift (expected return) σ\sigmaσ Annualised volatility Δt\Delta tΔt Time step 1/2521/2521/252 TTT Maturity NNN Number of steps N=T/ΔtN = T/\Delta tN=T/Δt nnn Number of simulated paths 10,000 Step 2 — simulate random numbers. Zt∼N(0,1)Z_t \sim N(0,1)Zt​∼N(0,1) Generate a random number from the standard normal distribution for each time step and each path. Note each time step and each path — a 10,000-path run over 252 days needs 2.52 million draws. This is why the method is computational. Step 3 — calculate the stock price using the GBM equation. Step 4 — payoff, discount, average → the option price.

A worked illustration of why any of this is necessary. A path visits: Point 1 2 3 4 5 Price 100 102 104 106 108 A European option looks only at the last number: max⁡(108−K, 0)\max(108 - K,\, 0)max(108−K,0). An Asian option takes the average of the stock at certain points of the contract: SˉT=100+102+104+106+1085=104\bar{S}_T = \frac{100 + 102 + 104 + 106 + 108}{5} = 104SˉT​=5100+102+104+106+108​=104 The notes call this a path-dependent variable, and it is precisely what a closed-form formula cannot reach. Black-Scholes prices a destination; Monte Carlo prices a journey.
documents.s: Path dependence, which is the point

documents.t: Monte Carlo is a computational technique for problems involving uncertainty or complex dynamics — used where no closed-form solution exists. A closed form is a direct formula, like the quadratic root formula or Black-Scholes. Exotic contracts do not have one. Applications: option pricing, risk management (VaR), portfolio optimisation. VaR's three methods are Monte Carlo, historical, and variance-covariance. The method: define the problem → identify inputs → generate random numbers → run trials → aggregate → average the discounted payoffs. Option price=1N∑e−rT×payoff\text{Option price} = \frac{1}{N}\sum e^{-rT}\times\text{payoff}Option price=N1​∑e−rT×payoff — simulate, discount, average. It works because of the CLT (the sample mean is normally distributed) and the Law of Large Numbers (the sample mean converges to the expected value). That convergence is the reliability of the method. More paths means more accuracy — hence 10,000. It is the only one of the three methods that handles path dependence.

Binomial Tree is a mathematical model which is used to price derivatives (European Option, American Option). It basically assumes that stock prices can move in 2 directions, i.e. up direction or down direction. This is the assumption.

Stock price → $20. It is known that at T = 3 months, the stock price will be 22 or 18. Interest → value a call option: buy the stock at $21 at t = 3 months. K = $21. The stock-price and option-payoff tree is: Stock = $22; K = $21 / Option payoff = $1 Stock price = $20 \ Stock = $18; K = $21 Option payoff = $0 Today t = 3 months When the stock is $22, the option payoff is: Option payoff=max⁡(ST−K,0)=max⁡(22−21,0)=1.\begin{aligned} \text{Option payoff} &= \max(S_T-K,0) \\ &= \max(22-21,0) \\ &= 1. \end{aligned}Option payoff​=max(ST​−K,0)=max(22−21,0)=1.​ When the stock is $18, the option payoff is: Option payoff=max⁡(ST−K,0)=max⁡(18−21,0)=0.\begin{aligned} \text{Option payoff} &= \max(S_T-K,0) \\ &= \max(18-21,0) \\ &= 0. \end{aligned}Option payoff​=max(ST​−K,0)=max(18−21,0)=0.​

documents.t: The generalized Wiener process is an extension of the standard Wiener process that incorporates a drift and volatility term. dWt=Zdt⟶standard Wiener process.\boxed{dW_t=Z\sqrt{dt}}\quad\longrightarrow\quad \text{standard Wiener process}.dWt​=Zdt​​⟶standard Wiener process.

documents.t: A further type of stochastic process is “Itô's process”. It generalizes the Wiener process so the parameters μ and σ are functions of the underlying variable x and time t: dx=μ(x,t) dt+σ(x,t) dWt.\boxed{dx=\mu(x,t)\,dt+\sigma(x,t)\,dW_t}.dx=μ(x,t)dt+σ(x,t)dWt​​. x → underlying → stock; t → time. Unlike the constant-parameter case, μ and σ are not necessarily constant. The earlier constant form is recorded in the margin as μdt + σdWₜ.

Itô's lemma is a fundamental result in stochastic calculus which extends the classic chain rule of calculus to stochastic processes driven by Brownian motion. Let Xₜ be a stochastic process which follows Itô's process: dXt=μ(Xt,t) dt+σ(Xt,t) dWt.dX_t=\mu(X_t,t)\,dt+\sigma(X_t,t)\,dW_t.dXt​=μ(Xt​,t)dt+σ(Xt​,t)dWt​. Let f(Xₜ, t) be a twice differentiable function of Xₜ and t. Then: df(Xt,t)=∂f∂t dt+∂f∂x dXt+12∂2f∂x2σ2(Xt,t) dt.df(X_t,t)=\frac{\partial f}{\partial t}\,dt +\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\,dX_t +\frac12\frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x^2}\sigma^2(X_t,t)\,dt.df(Xt​,t)=∂t∂f​dt+∂x∂f​dXt​+21​∂x2∂2f​σ2(Xt​,t)dt. Delta hedging kills direction but leaves gamma. Gamma hedging stabilises delta but leaves direction. Delta-gamma hedging does both.

Delta-gamma neutral hedging is a risk-management strategy which aims to neutralise both delta and gamma. Δp=0andΓp=0\Delta_p = 0 \qquad\text{and}\qquad \Gamma_p = 0Δp​=0andΓp​=0 And each of the two conditions has a plain-English reading: Condition What it means Delta neutral (Δp=0\Delta_p = 0Δp​=0) The portfolio's total delta is zero — it is not sensitive to small price changes in the underlying asset Gamma neutral (Γp=0\Gamma_p = 0Γp​=0) The portfolio's total gamma is zero — delta does not change with a change in the underlying asset Put together, the portfolio is protected against small and large moves. Delta neutrality handles the small ones; gamma neutrality is what keeps that protection standing when the move is big.
Long 200 call options on XYZ stock, with: Delta = 0.4 Gamma = 0.05 Goal: make the portfolio delta-gamma neutral.

Delta is +80, so sell 80 shares (delta −80): Portfolio=long 200 calls + short 80 stock\text{Portfolio} = \text{long 200 calls} \;+\; \text{short 80 stock}Portfolio=long 200 calls+short 80 stockΔp=80−80=0⇒ delta neutral\Delta_p = 80 - 80 = \mathbf{0} \quad \Rightarrow\ \textbf{delta neutral}Δp​=80−80=0⇒ delta neutral

documents.t: The portfolio gamma is still +10, and stock contributes nothing to it. To cancel +10 we need −10, and negative gamma comes only from the short side: Gamma Position Positive Long call, long put Negative Short call, short put From the market we find a call option contract which, taken short, carries: Δ=−0.3Γ=−0.05\Delta = -0.3 \qquad\qquad \Gamma = -0.05Δ=−0.3Γ=−0.05 Short 200 of them: 200×(−0.05)=−10200 \times (-0.05) = \mathbf{-10}200×(−0.05)=−10 The portfolio's gamma, leg by leg: Γp=+10⏟long 200 calls + 0⏟short 80 stock + −10⏟short 200 calls = 0\Gamma_p = \underbrace{+10}_{\text{long 200 calls}} \;+\; \underbrace{0}_{\text{short 80 stock}} \;+\; \underbrace{-10}_{\text{short 200 calls}} \;=\; \mathbf{0}Γp​=long 200 calls+10​​+short 80 stock0​​+short 200 calls−10​​=0 Gamma neutrality achieved.
documents.s: Step 3 — make the portfolio gamma neutral

documents.t: This is the step people forget. Entering that call option contract changed the portfolio's delta, because the option we just shorted carries delta as well as gamma: Δp=200×(−0.3)⏟the new short calls + 0⏟already-neutral portfolio=−60\Delta_p = \underbrace{200 \times (-0.3)}_{\text{the new short calls}} \;+\; \underbrace{0}_{\text{already-neutral portfolio}} = \mathbf{-60}Δp​=the new short calls200×(−0.3)​​+already-neutral portfolio0​​=−60 We were at zero; we are now at −60. So buy 60 shares (+60 delta): Δp=−60+60=0\Delta_p = -60 + 60 = \mathbf{0}Δp​=−60+60=0 And buying stock does not disturb gamma, because stock has none. Final state: Δp=0andΓp=0\Delta_p = 0 \qquad\text{and}\qquad \Gamma_p = 0Δp​=0andΓp​=0 That is delta-gamma hedging.
documents.s: Step 4 — the option leg broke the delta, so fix it again

documents.t: The example teaches a sequence, and the sequence is not arbitrary: Hedge gamma first, with options. Only an option can change gamma. Hedge delta second, with stock. Stock changes delta and nothing else. The reason is that the two instruments are not symmetric: Instrument Affects delta Affects gamma Stock ✅ (±1 per share) ❌ (always 0) Option ✅ ✅ Because the option leg moves both Greeks, it must be sized first — from the gamma requirement, which stock cannot help with. The stock leg is then a pure correction: it mops up whatever delta the option leg left behind, without touching the gamma you just fixed. Do it the other way around — delta first, then gamma — and the gamma trade knocks your delta back out of neutral, which is exactly what happened between Step 2 and Step 4 above. Step 2 was not wasted (it is how the bookkeeping is kept legible), but the final delta number can only be computed once the option leg is set.

Delta-gamma hedging neutralises both Greeks at once: Δp=0\Delta_p = 0Δp​=0 and Γp=0\Gamma_p = 0Γp​=0, protecting against small and large moves in the underlying. Delta neutral = insensitive to small price changes. Gamma neutral = delta itself stops changing. Worked: long 200 calls at Δ\DeltaΔ 0.4 / Γ\GammaΓ 0.05 → Δp=80\Delta_p = 80Δp​=80, Γp=10\Gamma_p = 10Γp​=10; short 80 stock; short 200 calls at Δ\DeltaΔ −0.3 / Γ\GammaΓ −0.05 to zero the gamma; then buy 60 stock to re-zero the delta the option leg introduced. Gamma is hedged with options, delta with stock — and because options carry delta too, the option leg is sized first and the stock leg last.

Knowing the Greeks is one thing; doing something about them is another. That is hedging, and there are six Greek-based varieties: Hedge a) Delta hedging b) Gamma hedging c) Delta-Gamma hedging d) Vega hedging e) Theta hedging f) Rho hedging This note is the first — and the foundation for the rest.

Delta hedging is an option trading strategy that aims to make the portfolio "delta neutral" — so that a change in the underlying asset will not impact the option position's value. Recall the definition it is built on: Δ=change in option price$1 change in the underlying asset\Delta = \frac{\text{change in option price}}{\$1 \text{ change in the underlying asset}}Δ=$1 change in the underlying assetchange in option price​ An option derives its price from the stock, so the stock moving up or down drags the option with it. Delta hedging severs that link: the stock price can change and it will not affect our position. For reference: Δcall\Delta_{\text{call}}Δcall​ runs 0 to 1, and Δput\Delta_{\text{put}}Δput​ runs −1 to 0.

This is what makes the hedge possible. Position Delta Buy a stock +1 Sell (short) a stock −1 A share moves dollar-for-dollar with itself. So shares are the instrument you use to add or subtract delta from a portfolio at will.
documents.s: The key fact: a share has a delta of 1

documents.t: Assume: You own 100 call options The underlying asset is the stock Delta of the call option = 0.5

1 call=0.5⟹100 calls=0.5×100=501 \text{ call} = 0.5 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad 100 \text{ calls} = 0.5 \times 100 = \mathbf{50}1 call=0.5⟹100 calls=0.5×100=50 So Δp=50\Delta_p = 50Δp​=50, which reads: if the stock price changes by $1, the position's value changes by $50.

You need to add −50 of delta. Since a short share carries −1: +50⏟100 calls + (−50)⏟short 50 shares = 0\underbrace{+50}_{100 \text{ calls}} \;+\; \underbrace{(-50)}_{\text{short 50 shares}} \;=\; \mathbf{0}100 calls+50​​+short 50 shares(−50)​​=0 Short 50 shares and the portfolio is delta neutral.

Suppose the stock price rises by $1: Leg Effect 100 call options 0.5×100×1=0.5 \times 100 \times 1 =0.5×100×1= gain $50 Short 50 shares loss $50 Net +50−50=+50 - 50 =+50−50= 0 — no impact The position is immunised against the move. That is the whole idea.
documents.s: Checking it — impact of a price movement

documents.t: The hedge always takes the opposite sign of the position's delta: You hold Its delta Hedge with Call option positive Sell stock Put option negative (−1 to 0) Buy stock A put already carries negative delta, so you add positive delta by buying shares to bring the total to zero.
Delta hedging protects the option portfolio from price changes in the underlying asset. It removes directional risk — you stop caring which way the stock goes.

Four, and they are the reason delta hedging is a job rather than a one-off trade. a) Continuous rebalancing. Delta is not constant — it changes with every fluctuation in the underlying asset price. The moment the stock moves, your carefully constructed 50-share hedge is no longer the right size, so you must buy or sell stock again to restore neutrality. That is why the strategy needs frequent delta-hedging adjustments. b) Transaction cost. Regular rebalancing incurs cost, because it means frequently buying and selling the underlying asset. A hedge that must be adjusted constantly is a hedge that is constantly paying fees and spread. c) Market condition. Delta hedging is less effective in a highly volatile environment — precisely when the stock is jumping around, delta moves fastest and the hedge is stalest. d) Gamma risk. The deepest one: Delta hedging reduces directional risk but introduces gamma risk. Because gamma measures the rate of change of delta with respect to the underlying price, a delta-neutral portfolio is only neutral at this instant and at this stock price. Move the stock, and gamma tells you how fast your neutrality decays. You have not eliminated risk — you have traded delta risk for gamma risk. Which is exactly why the next hedge exists.

In a financial institution the frequency depends on several factors: market condition volatility of the asset the option's time to expiry the firm's own risk-management policies And note the link back to gamma: high gamma means delta moves rapidly, which requires more frequent adjustment. In practice five regimes are used. 1. End-of-day hedging. Many institutions rebalance once, at the end of each trading day.
