It is the cost-effective approach — it manages the risk without incurring excessive transaction costs. 2. Intra-day hedging. Hedging multiple times within a day. Used during periods of significant volatility — a market event, an announcement, the release of economic data — when the delta of the option can shift quickly. The cost is obvious: hedging repeatedly means paying transaction costs repeatedly, and in a volatile stock the option price is moving a lot while you do it. 3. Threshold-based hedging. Some institutions use a threshold or bands approach: they rebalance only when the delta exposure exceeds a certain threshold. This is the compromise between the two above — you tolerate a small amount of drift in exchange for far fewer trades. 4. Real-time hedging (automated). The HFT end of the spectrum: systems execute millions of transactions within a second. Appropriate where sensitivity to fluctuations in the stock price is high. 5. Less frequently — weekly or monthly. Suitable for a less volatile market and longer-dated options, where delta simply does not move fast enough to justify more. The through-line: rebalancing frequency is a trade against transaction cost. Hedge too rarely and you carry unwanted delta; hedge too often and the fees eat the protection.
documents.s: How often is delta hedging actually performed?

documents.t: Delta hedging makes a portfolio delta neutral, so the underlying's moves stop affecting it. A share has delta 1 (+1 long, −1 short) — that is the lever you use. 100 calls at delta 0.5 gives a portfolio delta of 50, neutralised by shorting 50 shares; a $1 move then nets to exactly zero. Calls are hedged by selling stock; puts by buying it. The costs are real: continuous rebalancing, transaction costs, weakness in volatile markets, and above all gamma risk — delta neutrality is instantaneous, not permanent.
Delta hedging ended on a problem: it removes directional risk but introduces gamma risk, because a delta-neutral portfolio is only neutral at the current price. Gamma hedging attacks that.

Gamma hedging is a risk-management strategy that aims to neutralize or reduce gamma risk in an option position. Gamma risk is the sensitivity of an option's delta with respect to a change in the underlying asset price: Γ=change in deltachange in the underlying asset\Gamma = \frac{\text{change in delta}}{\text{change in the underlying asset}}Γ=change in the underlying assetchange in delta​ The goal, stated plainly: even though my asset price changes, it should not affect my gamma — that is, my delta should stay put.

An option's own gamma is positive, but the position's gamma takes the sign of the side you are on: Position gamma Positions Positive Long call, long put Negative Short call, short put That is the lever: to cancel positive gamma you need to sell options.
You own 10 call option contracts with: Delta = 0.5 Gamma = 0.02
Total delta=10×0.5=5Total gamma=10×0.02=0.2\text{Total delta} = 10 \times 0.5 = \mathbf{5} \qquad\qquad \text{Total gamma} = 10 \times 0.02 = \mathbf{0.2}Total delta=10×0.5=5Total gamma=10×0.02=0.2
Delta is 5, so sell 5 shares (delta −5): Δp=5−5=0\Delta_p = 5 - 5 = \mathbf{0}Δp​=5−5=0 Portfolio so far: long 10 calls + short 5 stock.

The portfolio gamma is +0.2, so we need −0.2, which means going short an option. Suppose we short put option contracts with gamma = −0.04 each: 5×(−0.04)=−0.25 \times (-0.04) = \mathbf{-0.2}5×(−0.04)=−0.2 So short 5 put option contracts. The full portfolio is now: P=10 calls⏟Γ=+0.2 + short 5 stock⏟Γ=0 + short 5 puts⏟Γ=−0.2P = \underbrace{10 \text{ calls}}_{\Gamma = +0.2} \;+\; \underbrace{\text{short 5 stock}}_{\Gamma = 0} \;+\; \underbrace{\text{short 5 puts}}_{\Gamma = -0.2}P=Γ=+0.210 calls​​+Γ=0short 5 stock​​+Γ=−0.2short 5 puts​​Γp=0.2+0+(−0.2)=0\Gamma_p = 0.2 + 0 + (-0.2) = \mathbf{0}Γp​=0.2+0+(−0.2)=0 The portfolio is gamma neutral. Note the shape of the solution: the stock leg fixed delta and contributed nothing to gamma; the option leg fixed gamma. Which raises the obvious question.

Stocks do not have gamma — but they do have delta. And this is provable in one line. Gamma is the rate of change of delta with respect to the underlying: Γ=∂(Δ)∂S\Gamma = \frac{\partial (\Delta)}{\partial S}Γ=∂S∂(Δ)​ For a share, the delta is always ±1 — +1 if you buy it, −1 if you sell it. It never changes, no matter what the price does. So the delta is a constant, and the derivative of a constant is zero: Γstock=∂(±1)∂S=0\Gamma_{\text{stock}} = \frac{\partial (\pm 1)}{\partial S} = \mathbf{0}Γstock​=∂S∂(±1)​=0 The practical consequence: Buying or selling stock has no impact on the portfolio's gamma. But it does affect the portfolio's delta, by ±1 per share. Compare with an option, whose delta of (say) 0.5 does move as the stock moves — that changing delta is exactly what gamma measures. So gamma can only be hedged with another option, never with the underlying.

They are not the same objective, and conflating them is the common mistake: Delta hedging Gamma hedging Aim Make the delta of the portfolio zero (Δ=0\Delta = 0Δ=0) Stabilise the delta (Γ=0\Gamma = 0Γ=0) — the delta may stay at 0.4, it just stops moving Directional bias Eliminates directional risk Reduces the sensitivity of delta to changes in the asset Instrument Stock Another option The primary goal of gamma hedging is to neutralise gamma — to neutralise the change in delta with respect to a change in the underlying — rather than to make delta zero. Which means gamma hedging on its own leaves you still carrying directional bias: you can have Γ=0\Gamma = 0Γ=0 while Δ≠0\Delta \neq 0Δ=0. A stable delta is not the same as no delta.

While delta hedging neutralises the exposure to small price movements in the underlying asset, it does not account for gamma risk — delta itself can change significantly as the underlying asset moves. That is the whole case, and it splits into three benefits. a) Stabilise delta. A gamma hedge reduces the fluctuation in delta, making the portfolio less sensitive to large price changes in the underlying asset. The division of labour between the two hedges is a question of size: Move in the asset price Handled by Small fluctuation Delta hedging Large fluctuation Gamma hedging — delta hedging fails here Delta hedging is a local approximation. It is correct for the next penny and increasingly wrong after that; the bigger the move, the more of the error is gamma. b) Protects against larger price movements. By addressing gamma risk directly, the hedge protects the portfolio from large fluctuations rather than only from small ones. c) Reduces rebalancing cost. This is the one that pays for itself. Gamma hedging makes delta more stable, which means traders do not need to rebalance delta as frequently → lower transaction costs. Recall delta hedging's second challenge: continuous rebalancing is expensive precisely because delta keeps moving. Gamma hedging attacks the cause instead of paying the symptom.

a) Most effective in volatile markets. Gamma hedging is generally more effective during volatile market conditions, or when you see large price fluctuations. In calm markets it may not be necessary at all — if the asset is barely moving, delta is barely moving, and there is little gamma risk to pay for removing. b) Cost. Gamma hedging means buying or selling options, and that comes with a cost. It can be costly, since it requires both the frequent adjustment and the cost of purchasing additional options. Options carry spread and premium in a way that shares do not — hedging gamma is structurally more expensive than hedging delta. So the decision is a trade: pay the option premium to stop paying the rebalancing bill, and only when the market is moving enough for that to be worth it. Hedging both delta and gamma at once is the subject of the next note.

Gamma hedging neutralises gamma risk — the risk that your delta itself moves as the underlying moves. Position gamma is positive when long options, negative when short, so positive gamma is cancelled by selling options. Worked: 10 calls at Δ\DeltaΔ 0.5 / Γ\GammaΓ 0.02 → portfolio Δ=5\Delta = 5Δ=5, Γ=0.2\Gamma = 0.2Γ=0.2; short 5 stock zeroes delta; short 5 puts at Γ=−0.04\Gamma = -0.04Γ=−0.04 zeroes gamma. Stock has zero gamma because its delta is the constant ±1 and the derivative of a constant is zero — so gamma must be hedged with options. Delta hedging makes delta zero; gamma hedging makes delta stable. They are different goals, and Γ=0\Gamma = 0Γ=0 does not imply Δ=0\Delta = 0Δ=0. It matters because it stabilises delta, protects against large moves, and cuts rebalancing costs — delta hedging alone only covers small moves. It is most effective in volatile markets and often unnecessary in calm ones, and it costs more than delta hedging because the instrument is an option, not a share.

The Greeks are risk measures used in options to assess the sensitivity of the option price to various factors. An option's price does not depend on one thing. It moves with the underlying asset, with time, with interest rates, and with volatility. Each Greek isolates one of those and asks: if this input moves, how much does the option price move? There are five: Greek Sensitivity of the option price with respect to… Delta (Δ\DeltaΔ) the underlying asset Gamma (Γ\GammaΓ) (the sensitivity of delta to the underlying asset) Theta (Θ\ThetaΘ) time Rho (ρ\rhoρ) the risk-free rate Vega implied volatility Gamma is the odd one out: it is a sensitivity of another Greek, not of the price directly.

Delta tells the sensitivity of the option price with respect to the underlying asset — or equivalently, the rate of change of the option price relative to the change in the underlying asset. Δ=∂V∂S\Delta = \frac{\partial V}{\partial S}Δ=∂S∂V​ where VVV is the price of the option and SSS is the price of the underlying asset. So ∂V\partial V∂V is the change in the option price and ∂S\partial S∂S the change in the underlying asset price.

Because the option price is a function of several variables at once — the asset price, volatility, the rate, time. A function of one variable gives an ordinary derivative (an ODE, dV/dSdV/dSdV/dS); a function of many gives a partial derivative (a PDE, ∂V/∂S\partial V / \partial S∂V/∂S), which holds everything else fixed and varies only SSS. Option pricing is the second case.

Delta can be positive or negative, and which one depends on the type of option and the position you hold. Positive delta — a positive relationship with the underlying: the option value rises when the stock price rises the option value falls when the stock price falls Negative delta — a negative relationship: the option price falls when the underlying rises the option price rises when the underlying falls A put has negative delta for exactly this reason: you hold the right to sell, so a rising stock makes that right less valuable.

Call option: 0 to 1Put option: 0 to −1\text{Call option: } 0 \text{ to } 1 \qquad\qquad \text{Put option: } 0 \text{ to } -1Call option: 0 to 1Put option: 0 to −1 Taking the position into account as well: Position Delta range Long call 0 to +1 Short call 0 to −1 Long put 0 to −1 Short put 0 to +1 Laid on a number line, −1 is where long put and short call live; +1 is where long call and short put live.
documents.s: Range, by option and by position

documents.t: Suppose the delta of a call is 0.5. Then Δ=∂V∂S=∂V1=0.5 ⟹ ∂V=$0.5\Delta = \frac{\partial V}{\partial S} = \frac{\partial V}{1} = 0.5 \;\Longrightarrow\; \partial V = \$0.5Δ=∂S∂V​=1∂V​=0.5⟹∂V=$0.5 For every $1 increase in the underlying asset, the option price increases by $0.50. And for a put with delta −0.5: a $1 rise in the asset makes the put price fall by $0.50. These values come out of the option pricing models — Black-Scholes, the binomial tree, or Monte Carlo. Delta is not assumed; it is computed.

For a call: Moneyness Delta ITM 0.5 to 1 ATM ≈ 0.5 OTM 0 to 0.5 For a put, mirrored into the negatives: Moneyness Delta ITM −0.5 to −1 ATM ≈ −0.5 OTM 0 to −0.5 This is standard practice among traders and risk managers for defining moneyness — rather than comparing SSS and KKK directly, they read it off the delta.

This is the interpretation worth carrying around: Delta is the probability of the option contract being in the money at expiry. Δ=0.2\Delta = 0.2Δ=0.2 → roughly a 20% chance of finishing in the money — clearly OTM territory. Δ=0.5\Delta = 0.5Δ=0.5 → a coin flip — at the money. Δ\DeltaΔ between 0.5 and 1 → a 50% to 100% chance — in the money. Δ=1\Delta = 1Δ=1 → effectively certain. And recall what each outcome means at expiry: ITM you receive money, ATM no profit and no loss, OTM you have paid the money (the premium) for nothing.

Take an OTM call. With a long time to maturity, the stock has more time to move up to the strike, so there is a higher chance of expiring ITM — and therefore a higher delta. Two days from expiry, the stock has almost no room to travel, the probability collapses, and delta with it. Long-term maturity⇒higher deltaShort-term maturity⇒lower delta\text{Long-term maturity} \Rightarrow \text{higher delta} \qquad \text{Short-term maturity} \Rightarrow \text{lower delta}Long-term maturity⇒higher deltaShort-term maturity⇒lower delta

The same logic through a different lever. High volatility — the stock moves around more, so an OTM option has a higher probability of expiring ITM → higher delta. Low volatility — fluctuation is small, the probability of reaching the strike is low → lower delta. Both effects are really one effect: anything that raises the chance of finishing in the money raises delta, because delta is that chance.

The Greeks are risk measures: the sensitivity of the option price to each input. Five of them — delta, gamma, theta, rho, vega. Δ=∂V/∂S\Delta = \partial V/\partial SΔ=∂V/∂S — a partial derivative, because the option price depends on several variables at once. Call delta runs 0 to +1, put delta 0 to −1; the short of each flips the sign. A delta of 0.5 means a $1 move in the underlying moves the option $0.50. Delta is the probability of finishing in the money — which is why traders use it to define moneyness (ITM 0.5–1, ATM ≈0.5, OTM 0–0.5 for a call). More time → higher delta. More volatility → higher delta. Both raise the chance of expiring ITM.
Delta answers "how much does the option move when the stock moves?" But delta itself is not constant — it changes as the stock moves. Gamma measures that.

Gamma tells how sensitive your delta is with respect to the change in the underlying asset. Γ=∂Δ∂S=∂2V∂S2\Gamma = \frac{\partial \Delta}{\partial S} = \frac{\partial^2 V}{\partial S^2}Γ=∂S∂Δ​=∂S2∂2V​ Since delta is already the first derivative of the option price, gamma is the second derivative — the curvature of the option's price curve. Consequence Gamma is higher Delta is more sensitive to the underlying — when the stock fluctuates, delta changes rapidly Gamma is lower Delta is less sensitive — delta adjusts slowly, even if the stock price moves a lot Read geometrically, ∂Δ/∂S\partial \Delta / \partial S∂Δ/∂S is the slope of the delta curve. Where the delta curve is steep, gamma is high; where it is flat, gamma is near zero.

This is the shape to remember. Delta traces an S-curve against the stock price; its slope — gamma — is therefore a bell, peaking exactly where the delta curve is steepest: Delta (call)SATMGammaSATMhighestOTMITM Gamma is highest at ATM. Gamma is lowest at ITM and OTM — at both extremes the delta curve flattens out (delta is pinned near 0 or near ±1), so it has almost no slope left to give. And note: the gamma curve is the same for a call and a put. The delta curves are different (0 to 1 versus 0 to −1) but they have the same slope at every stock price, and gamma is that slope.

Gamma is always positive — for both call options and put options. This trips people up, because delta's sign depends on call versus put. Gamma's does not: buying either a call or a put buys curvature. What does differ is who benefits.

Long call. As the underlying price rises, the delta rises (say 0.5 → 0.7), so the option becomes more sensitive to price changes in the direction you want. A $1 rise now earns $0.70 instead of $0.50. Positive gamma benefits the long position. Short call. Gamma is still positive, but your exposure is negative. As the underlying rises, the delta of the short call moves further negative (−0.5 → −0.7) — so each additional $1 rise costs you $0.70 instead of $0.50. The position loses money at an accelerating rate. Long position⇒gamma favours youShort position⇒gamma works against you\text{Long position} \Rightarrow \text{gamma favours you} \qquad \text{Short position} \Rightarrow \text{gamma works against you}Long position⇒gamma favours youShort position⇒gamma works against you That asymmetry is the reason short option positions are dangerous in a fast market: the loss rate itself increases as the move continues.

Here is the part that surprises people, because it runs opposite to delta: Maturity Gamma Effect on delta Short-term Higher gamma Delta changes pretty fast Long-term Lower gamma Delta changes slowly over time Intuitively: near expiry, an at-the-money option is on a knife edge — a small move in the stock flips it from "probably worthless" to "probably exercised", so its delta swings violently from near 0 to near 1. That violent swing is high gamma. A long-dated option has time to absorb the same move, so its delta barely reacts. Compare with Part A: more time raises delta but lowers gamma.

Γ=change in deltachange in the asset=∂2V∂S2\Gamma = \dfrac{\text{change in delta}}{\text{change in the asset}} = \dfrac{\partial^2 V}{\partial S^2}Γ=change in the assetchange in delta​=∂S2∂2V​ — the second derivative, the curvature. Gamma is always positive, for calls and puts alike, and the gamma curve is the same for both. Highest at ATM; lowest at ITM and OTM — a bell, because it is the slope of delta's S-curve. Gamma favours the long position and works against the short, because the short's losses accelerate. Short-dated options have high gamma; long-dated have low gamma — the reverse of delta's relationship with time.
Delta and gamma are about the stock moving. Theta is about nothing happening at all — the option losing value simply because a day went by.

Theta measures the sensitivity of the option price with respect to time. It represents how much the price of an option falls as time passes (each day). Θ=∂V∂t=change in option pricechange in time\Theta = \frac{\partial V}{\partial t} = \frac{\text{change in option price}}{\text{change in time}}Θ=∂t∂V​=change in timechange in option price​ Theta is also called time decay, because an option loses its value as we approach maturity. An option contract bought at t=0t=0t=0 and expiring at t=3t=3t=3 months is, all else equal, worth a little less every single day of that journey. Formally: it tells how much the price of the option will decrease as each day passes, holding all other factors constant.

You own a call option: Current stock price $100 Strike price $100 Time to expiry 30 days Theta −$0.10 per day As every day passes, the value of your option decreases by $0.10. If theta is negative, the option price declines by that much. If theta is positive, the option price increases by that much.

This is the part that matters in practice. Theta is negative for a LONG position — long call and long put. When you are the buyer, theta works against you. Think of an ice cube. As time passes, does the ice cube melt? Yes. Time is working against the ice cube — and against you. Theta is positive for a SHORT position — short call and short put. As time passes, the short position benefits from time decay. Think of renting out a house. You collect rent from the person staying there. The more days they stay, the more rent they pay. Time is working in support of you. Long⇒Θ<0 (against you)Short⇒Θ>0 (in your favour)\text{Long} \Rightarrow \Theta < 0 \text{ (against you)} \qquad \text{Short} \Rightarrow \Theta > 0 \text{ (in your favour)}Long⇒Θ<0 (against you)Short⇒Θ>0 (in your favour) This is the mirror image of gamma, which favours the long. The option seller collects decay but carries accelerating directional risk; the buyer pays decay for that convexity. That trade-off is the heart of option trading.
Time decay is not linear. It is slow while the option is young and accelerates sharply into the final days: OptionvalueDays to expiration9060200decay is slow while there is time……then collapses

Theta only makes sense once the option price is split in two. Intrinsic value — the real value of the option if exercised right now: Call: ST−KPut: K−ST\text{Call: } S_T - K \qquad\qquad \text{Put: } K - S_TCall: ST​−KPut: K−ST​ If that is negative the option would not be exercised, so OTM intrinsic value is 0. (With K=100K=100K=100 and the stock at 110, a call's intrinsic value is 10.) Extrinsic value — also called time value: The additional value beyond the intrinsic value, which accounts for factors such as time to expiration and volatility. Putting them together: Option price=Intrinsic value+Extrinsic value\text{Option price} = \text{Intrinsic value} + \text{Extrinsic value}Option price=Intrinsic value+Extrinsic value Theta eats the extrinsic value only. Intrinsic value is untouched by the calendar — it is arithmetic on today's prices. So an option's exposure to time decay is exactly its exposure to extrinsic value.
Everything follows from that last sentence.

ITM options have a significant amount of intrinsic value, so the price is less dependent on time decay. As expiration approaches, the intrinsic value dominates and the extrinsic value becomes smaller and smaller — so theta is smaller.

Here ST=KS_T = KST​=K, so the intrinsic value is exactly zero and the option price is extrinsic value only. It is pure time value — and there is more of it here than anywhere else. Theta is highest for ATM options. They have the greatest potential to lose value as time passes.

Intrinsic value is zero as well, but the extrinsic value is small. Worked through — an OTM call with K=110K = 110K=110 while the stock sits at S=100S = 100S=100: Case 1 — 30 days to expiry There is still a real chance the stock climbs to 110, so the option still has some time value. Decay is relatively slow. Case 2 — 5 days to expiry In a normal market it is highly unlikely the stock travels from 100 to 110. Intrinsic value is zero and the remaining extrinsic value evaporates → theta is high, and decay accelerates in the final days. So the conclusion is two-sided, and both halves matter: Theta decay is relatively slower for an OTM option at longer maturity… …but as expiration approaches, the chance of becoming ITM diminishes and theta accelerates — the option loses its value much faster.

Θ=∂V/∂t\Theta = \partial V / \partial tΘ=∂V/∂t — the option's daily bleed, all else equal. A theta of −$0.10 costs you ten cents a day. Long → theta negative, time against you (the melting ice cube). Short → theta positive, time for you (collecting rent). Option price = intrinsic + extrinsic, and theta only consumes the extrinsic part. Theta is highest ATM (pure time value), lower ITM and OTM. Decay is convex — slow early, accelerating hard into the last days.
Delta and gamma track the stock. Theta tracks the calendar. Vega tracks uncertainty itself.

Vega measures the sensitivity of the option price with respect to implied volatility — how much the price of the option will change for a 1% change in the implied volatility of the asset. V=∂V∂σ\mathcal{V} = \frac{\partial V}{\partial \sigma}V=∂σ∂V​ where VVV is the option price and σ\sigmaσ the volatility, so ∂σ\partial \sigma∂σ is the change in volatility.

The distinction is simply which direction in time you are looking: Historical volatility Volatility of the past — what the asset actually did Implied volatility Volatility of the future — what the market currently expects Vega is about the implied one. Historical volatility is measured; implied volatility is a market expectation baked into today's option prices, and it can sit above or below the historical figure. Volatility itself gets modelled two broad ways: Family Models Time-series models ARCH, GARCH, EWMA (and the wider AR, MA, ARIMA, ARIMAX, SARIMA, VAR family) Stochastic-volatility models Heston, SABR, the 3/2 model

A call option: Stock price $100 Strike $100 Time to expiry 30 days Vega 0.15 For every 1% increase in implied volatility, the option price will increase by $0.15. Meaning High vega The option price is very sensitive to volatility — a small increase in volatility raises the option price significantly Low vega Changes in volatility have only a small impact on the price

Vega is always non-negative. Rising volatility always raises an option's value — call or put, in or out of the money. The reason is the payoff's asymmetry, and it is worth doing properly because it explains the entire Greek.

A long call pays max⁡(ST−K, 0)\max(S_T - K,\, 0)max(ST​−K,0), with K=100K = 100K=100. Suppose higher volatility means the stock could land at 120 or 80 instead of staying near 100: Outcome Payoff ST=120S_T = 120ST​=120 max⁡(120−100, 0)=20\max(120 - 100,\, 0) = \mathbf{20}max(120−100,0)=20 ST=80S_T = 80ST​=80 max⁡(80−100, 0)=0\max(80 - 100,\, 0) = \mathbf{0}max(80−100,0)=0 Up, you exercise and profit. Down, you simply do not exercise — no profit, no loss beyond the premium already paid. The upside is open-ended; the downside is floored at zero. More volatility therefore adds only upside.
documents.s: Why volatility helps the long — a call

documents.t: A long put pays max⁡(K−ST, 0)\max(K - S_T,\, 0)max(K−ST​,0), same K=100K = 100K=100: Outcome Payoff ST=120S_T = 120ST​=120 max⁡(100−120, 0)=0\max(100 - 120,\, 0) = \mathbf{0}max(100−120,0)=0 ST=80S_T = 80ST​=80 max⁡(100−80, 0)=20\max(100 - 80,\, 0) = \mathbf{20}max(100−80,0)=20 Identical logic, mirrored. Which gives the rule: Long position (call or put)⇒vega is your friend\text{Long position (call or put)} \Rightarrow \text{vega is your friend}Long position (call or put)⇒vega is your friendShort position⇒vega works against you\text{Short position} \Rightarrow \text{vega works against you}Short position⇒vega works against you The short side wrote that floored payoff, so every increase in volatility hands value to the buyer at the seller's expense.

Moneyness Vega ATM Highest ITM Low OTM Low Why ATM. At the money, ST=KS_T = KST​=K — the option sits exactly on the knife edge. Even a small change in volatility can tip it either way: to 101 and it is ITM, to 99 and it is OTM. That balance is where extra uncertainty is worth the most. Why not ITM. A deep in-the-money option is already going to be exercised; its value is mostly intrinsic. More volatility barely moves that, so the impact on the option price is small. Why not OTM. Far out of the money, the option is unlikely to be exercised regardless, so extra volatility changes little. Note this is the same bell shape as gamma — both peak at the money, for the same underlying reason: that is where the option's fate is least decided.

Maturity Vega Long-term (e.g. 3 months) High Short-term (e.g. 5 days) Low Short duration means the stock has less room to travel, so the option price is less impacted by a change in volatility. Think of bouncing a ball. Dropped from high up it bounces high — that is high vega. Held near the floor and released, it barely bounces — low vega. Volatility needs room, and room is time.

Worth holding the four together, because their behaviour with time diverges: More time to expiry Peak at Delta Higher — (monotonic S-curve) Gamma Lower ATM Theta Lower per day (until it accelerates near expiry) ATM Vega Higher ATM Gamma and vega share the ATM peak but move in opposite directions with time: a short-dated ATM option is a gamma instrument, a long-dated ATM option is a vega instrument.
documents.s: How vega compares with the others

documents.t: V=∂V/∂σ\mathcal{V} = \partial V / \partial \sigmaV=∂V/∂σ — the price change per 1% move in implied volatility. Vega 0.15 means +$0.15 per point of IV. Implied volatility is the market's view of the future; historical is the measured past. Vega is always non-negative, because the option payoff is floored at zero: volatility adds upside without adding downside. Long is long vega (calls and puts alike); short is short vega. Vega is highest ATM — the knife edge — and low both ITM and OTM. Long-dated options carry high vega; short-dated carry little — the bouncing ball needs height.
The last of the five, and the one traders think about least — until rates start moving.

Rho measures the sensitivity of the option price with respect to the risk-free interest rate — the change in price for a 1% change in that rate. ρ=∂V∂r\rho = \frac{\partial V}{\partial r}ρ=∂r∂V​ where rrr is the risk-free rate.

The theoretical return on an investment with no risk. In practice it is the US Treasury rate (or SOFR). The mechanism is simple: the US government issues bonds to acquire money, people lend to it because it is considered as close to riskless as exists, and the return on that lending is the risk-free interest rate.

Option Rho Meaning Call +0.05 For every 1% increase in the interest rate, the option price increases by $0.05 Put −0.04 For every 1% increase in the risk-free rate, the put price decreases by $0.04 So immediately: Call⇒ρ>0Put⇒ρ<0\text{Call} \Rightarrow \rho > 0 \qquad\qquad \text{Put} \Rightarrow \rho < 0Call⇒ρ>0Put⇒ρ<0

This is the one Greek whose sign is best understood through present value. When the interest rate rises, the present value of the strike price falls. Discounting means the interest rate and the discounted amount are inversely related — a $110 strike payable in three months might be worth only $100 in today's money once rates rise. Now split by option type, asking who pays the strike: Call — you PAY the strike. A call holder will hand over KKK to buy the stock. If the present value of that obligation falls, you are effectively paying less. Rising rates worked in your favour → rho is positive. Put — you RECEIVE the strike. A put holder sells the stock and collects KKK. If the present value of what you will receive falls, you are collecting a lesser price in today's terms. Rising rates work against you → rho is negative.

Maturity Rho Why Short-term (5 days) Low The interest rate has little chance to fluctuate in five days, so the option price will not fluctuate either Long-term (60 days+) High Rates can move a lot over that horizon, so the impact on the option price is significant Rho therefore grows with maturity — the same direction as vega and delta, the opposite of gamma.

Here rho breaks the pattern of the other Greeks. Gamma, vega and theta all peak at the money. Rho does not — it is monotonic, and highest in the money: Call option Put option ITM Highest +ve rho Highest −ve rho ATM Moderate +ve rho Moderate −ve rho OTM Lowest +ve rho Lowest −ve rho Why ITM is highest. An in-the-money option is dominated by its intrinsic value (ST−KS_T - KST​−K), with the extrinsic part small. That intrinsic value contains KKK — and KKK is exactly the term discounting acts on. So the option is impacted a lot by the interest rate → higher rho. Why OTM is lowest. An out-of-the-money option has no intrinsic value at all; it is pure extrinsic value. There is no strike payment in the money to discount, so the rate barely touches it → lower rho.

Rho becomes extremely important when interest rates are expected to rise or fall. Conversely, in a stable interest-rate environment rho becomes less significant, and delta, gamma, theta and vega dominate the risk picture. That is why rho is the Greek most often ignored — and why ignoring it stops being safe the moment a central bank starts moving.

With rho done, the full set: Greek Measures sensitivity to Sign Peaks at With more time Delta Δ\DeltaΔ Underlying price Call +, put − — (S-curve) Higher Gamma Γ\GammaΓ Delta (2nd derivative) Always + ATM Lower Theta Θ\ThetaΘ Time Long −, short + ATM Lower per day Vega V\mathcal{V}V Implied volatility Always ≥ 0 ATM Higher Rho ρ\rhoρ Risk-free rate Call +, put − ITM Higher Two patterns worth carrying away: Gamma, theta and vega all peak at the money — that is where an option's fate is least decided, so that is where uncertainty is worth most. Rho is the exception, peaking in the money, because it acts on the strike rather than on uncertainty. Long positions are long gamma and long vega but short theta. You pay decay every day in exchange for convexity and volatility exposure. The short side takes the opposite trade. That single sentence is most of option trading.
documents.s: All five Greeks, side by side

documents.t: ρ=∂V/∂r\rho = \partial V / \partial rρ=∂V/∂r — the price change per 1% move in the risk-free rate (US Treasury / SOFR). Calls have positive rho, puts negative — because rising rates cut the present value of the strike, which helps the buyer who pays it and hurts the buyer who receives it. Longer-dated options have more rho; short-dated have almost none. Rho is highest ITM, not ATM — it tracks the strike, and the strike matters most where intrinsic value dominates. It matters when rates are expected to move, and is largely ignorable when they are not.
The last hedge, for the Greek traders think about least — and the one that becomes urgent the moment a central bank starts moving.

Rho hedging is a risk-management strategy which is used to manage an option's exposure to changes in the interest rate. Rho itself measures the sensitivity of the option price with respect to a 1% change in the risk-free rate. The mechanism is direct: when the interest rate changes, the option price also changes — because the rate is what discounts the strike.

The goal is to neutralise the portfolio's rho exposure to prevent fluctuations coming from changes in the interest rate. ρp=0\rho_p = 0ρp​=0 So that even if the interest rate changes, there is no change in the option price.

Rho's sign table is the one that does not split cleanly along long/short. Gamma, vega and theta all key off which side of the trade you are on. Rho keys off the option type as well: Rho Positions Positive Long call, short put Negative Short call, long put The reason is in the rho note: a call holder pays the strike, so a falling present value of that strike helps them; a put holder receives it, so the same fall hurts. Take either side short and the sign flips again. Two flips, two dimensions — hence the crossed table.

Suppose you are a trader and you hold a portfolio with a long call option: ρp=200\rho_p = 200ρp​=200 Reading it in both directions: Change in the risk-free rate Effect on the portfolio Rises by 1% The portfolio value will rise by $200 Falls by 1% The portfolio value will decrease by $200 Now suppose you are anticipating a drop in the interest rate. That would reduce your portfolio value — $200 for every point of cut, with nothing you can do about the decision itself.

Rho is +200, so you need −200. From the sign table, negative rho comes from a short call or a long put. Enter a long put contract, whose rho is negative: 1 put⇒ρ=−2⟹100 puts⇒100×(−2)=−2001 \text{ put} \Rightarrow \rho = -2 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad 100 \text{ puts} \Rightarrow 100 \times (-2) = \mathbf{-200}1 put⇒ρ=−2⟹100 puts⇒100×(−2)=−200

ρp=200−200=0\rho_p = 200 - 200 = \mathbf{0}ρp​=200−200=0 After adding the 100 put option contracts, the portfolio is rho neutral — even if you see fluctuations in the interest rate, it will have no effect on your portfolio. Note what makes this hedge different from the others: the offsetting leg is a long position, not a short one. Because rho's sign depends on option type, you can buy your way to neutrality rather than having to sell.

a) Interest-rate volatility. If interest rates are about to fluctuate significantly, rho hedging is useful — it means no effect of those fluctuations on your portfolio. This is the rate-regime analogue of vega hedging around earnings. b) High rho exposure. A portfolio which has a high rho measure will be impacted a lot by a rate move. The difference between a 0.5% and a 1% move is small in the abstract and large on a book carrying size, so rho hedging can be useful here even in a calm rate environment. c) Long-term options. Long-dated option contracts are more sensitive to the interest rate than short-dated ones — compare 1 week against 6 months. Over a week the rate barely has time to move; over six months it can move a great deal, and the discounting acts on the strike for the whole period. So rho hedging is useful on the long end of the curve.

That completes the set. What the module has been building toward: Hedge Neutralises Instrument Matters when Delta Directional risk, Δp=0\Delta_p = 0Δp​=0 Stock Always — but only for small moves Gamma Delta's own movement, Γp=0\Gamma_p = 0Γp​=0 Another option Volatile markets, large moves Delta-gamma Both at once Option, then stock Small and large moves Vega Implied-volatility risk Short option Earnings, market events Theta Time decay Opposite side Very long or very short dated Rho Interest-rate risk Long put / short call Rates moving, long-dated books Two patterns run through all six: Only stock has a Greek it cannot touch. Stock moves delta and nothing else, which is why every other hedge needs an option — and why the option leg is always sized first. Every hedge is a trade against cost. None of them is free, and each is worth doing only when the risk it removes is actually live. That is why every one of these notes ends with a "when it matters" section rather than a rule to always apply it.
documents.s: The six hedges, side by side

documents.t: Rho hedging neutralises interest-rate exposure: ρp=0\rho_p = 0ρp​=0 means a rate change has no effect on the portfolio. Rho is positive for a long call or a short put, negative for a short call or a long put — the only Greek whose sign depends on option type as well as side. Worked: a long call portfolio at ρ=200\rho = 200ρ=200 (±$200 per point of rate), neutralised by buying 100 puts at ρ=−2\rho = -2ρ=−2 → 200−200=0200 - 200 = 0200−200=0. Do it when rates are about to move, when the book carries high rho, or when the options are long-dated — long maturities give the rate room to work on the strike.
Every hedge so far has defended against something that might or might not happen. Time decay is the one risk that is certain. The clock runs whether the market moves or not.

Theta hedging is a risk-management strategy which is used to manage an option portfolio's exposure to time decay. Recall what theta is: it measures the sensitivity of the option price with respect to time.

As every day passes, the option price loses its value. An option worth $2.50 today does not sit there: Day Option price D0D_0D0​ $2.50 D1D_1D1​ $2.40 D2D_2D2​ $2.25 … falling Nothing needs to happen in the market for this. The option is simply worth less because there is less time left for it to come good.
The goal of theta hedging is to offset or reduce the impact of time decay on the portfolio value — to eliminate the impact of time decay on our option price. Θp=0\Theta_p = 0Θp​=0

Theta's signs are the reverse of gamma's and vega's, and that reversal is the whole reason the hedge works: Theta Positions Positive Short call, short put Negative Long call, long put The buyer of an option pays for time and watches it drain away; the seller collected that premium up front and keeps a little more of it each day. Decay is a cost to the long and income to the short.
You are long 100 call option contracts, with: Θ=−50\Theta = -50Θ=−50 Theta is negative, which means every day the option price will lose its value — $50 a day, in this case, purely from the calendar.
Theta hedging: select those option contracts whose theta is positive — a short call or a short put. Suppose you enter a short position with: Θ=+5\Theta = +5Θ=+5
Short 10 of them: 10×5=5010 \times 5 = \mathbf{50}10×5=50
Θp=−50+50=0\Theta_p = -50 + 50 = \mathbf{0}Θp​=−50+50=0 Theta neutral. Every day that passes by, the option price will not change with time.

The structure is long call + short put, and the two legs are doing opposite things to the clock: decline⏟long call + gain⏟short put = 0\underbrace{\text{decline}}_{\text{long call}} \;+\; \underbrace{\text{gain}}_{\text{short put}} \;=\; \mathbf{0}long calldecline​​+short putgain​​=0 By adding a short position, your portfolio's net theta is zero. The decay you pay on the long leg is exactly the decay you collect on the short one.
documents.s: What the two legs are doing

documents.t: Because the hedge is always the opposite side of the position you hold: If the portfolio's theta is… Hedge with Positive a long position (call or put) — long options carry negative theta Negative a short position (call or put) — short options carry positive theta Either way you end at Θp=0\Theta_p = 0Θp​=0.

It is needed at both ends of the maturity spectrum, for opposite reasons. a) Long-term option contracts. If you plan to hold an option position for a longer period, theta hedging helps minimise the losses from time decay. Decay per day is small on a long-dated option, but you are exposed to it for a long time, and it accumulates. b) Short-term option contracts. When you have a shorter term, theta decay accelerates quickly. A contract with one week left bleeds far faster per day than one with a month left — the decay curve steepens into expiry. Here theta hedging becomes very important, because the loss arrives fast. The middle of the curve is where you can most afford to ignore it. The two ends are where it costs you.

Theta hedging eliminates the effect of time on the portfolio value — Θp=0\Theta_p = 0Θp​=0 means the option price stops changing simply because a day passed. Theta is positive for short positions (short call, short put) and negative for long positions (long call, long put) — decay is a cost to the buyer and income to the seller. Worked: long 100 calls at Θ=−50\Theta = -50Θ=−50, neutralised by shorting 10 contracts at Θ=+5\Theta = +5Θ=+5 → −50+50=0-50 + 50 = 0−50+50=0. The hedge is always the opposite side: positive portfolio theta is hedged long, negative portfolio theta is hedged short. It matters for long-dated positions (decay accumulates) and for short-dated ones (decay accelerates into expiry).
Delta, gamma and delta-gamma hedging all defend against the price of the underlying. Vega hedging defends against something else entirely: the market's expectation of how much that price will move.

Vega hedging is a risk-management strategy which is used to manage the sensitivity of options to a change in the implied volatility of the underlying asset. Hedging vega means the trader is trying to eliminate the impact of volatility fluctuations on the option price / portfolio. The transmission chain is worth stating, because it is why vega exists at all: volatility ⟶ stock price ⟶ option price\text{volatility} \;\longrightarrow\; \text{stock price} \;\longrightarrow\; \text{option price}volatility⟶stock price⟶option price Volatility moves the stock around, and the stock's movement is what the option is priced on. Vega hedging cuts the link at the first arrow. The goal is to neutralise the vega — meaning the portfolio value should not be impacted by the change in implied volatility. Vp=0\mathcal{V}_p = 0Vp​=0

Same structure as gamma, and for the same reason — it is the side you are on that sets the sign: Vega Positions Positive Long call, long put Negative Short call, short put The payoff algebra makes it obvious. A long call pays max⁡(ST−K, 0)\max(S_T - K,\, 0)max(ST​−K,0) and the short call is simply the negative of it: −max⁡(ST−K, 0)-\max(S_T - K,\, 0)−max(ST​−K,0) The buyer's floored, open-ended payoff is exactly what makes vega non-negative for the long — so the seller, holding the mirror image, has the sign flipped.

When you sell an option (call or put), you lose money if volatility rises. That is the entire meaning of negative vega, and it is also what makes the hedge possible: to cancel a positive vega you need somebody's negative vega, and the only way to get it is to sell an option.
A portfolio holds 200 option contracts with a vega of 5 each.

Vp=200×5=1000\mathcal{V}_p = 200 \times 5 = \mathbf{1000}Vp​=200×5=1000 Which reads, in both directions: Change in implied volatility Effect on the portfolio Increases by 1% The option price would increase by $1,000 Decreases by 1% The option price would decrease by $1,000 Note that this is a risk, not a bonus. A position that gains $1,000 on a one-point rise in IV loses $1,000 on a one-point fall — and IV is not something you control.

The portfolio vega is +1000, so we need −1000. From the sign table, a negative-vega exposure means a short call or a short put. Suppose we go short a put option with vega = −2, and short 500 of them: 500×(−2)=−1000500 \times (-2) = \mathbf{-1000}500×(−2)=−1000
Vtotal=+1000−1000=0\mathcal{V}_{\text{total}} = +1000 - 1000 = \mathbf{0}Vtotal​=+1000−1000=0 The portfolio is vega neutral. A change in implied volatility now has no effect on its value.

The same conditional logic as gamma hedging, driven this time by the volatility regime rather than the size of price moves. In a low-volatility market, option prices are small, so the gains and losses are small too. There is not much vega exposure to remove, and paying to remove it is hard to justify. In a higher-volatility environment — an earnings announcement, or some other market event — vega neutrality earns its keep by protecting the portfolio from sudden volatility changes. These are precisely the moments when implied volatility gaps rather than drifts. Market stability. When markets are stable (a low-volatility environment), vega hedging may not be necessary. It is high uncertainty that calls for it. Which is a familiar shape by now: every Greek hedge is worth its cost only when the thing it protects against is actually moving.

Vega hedging neutralises exposure to implied volatility: Vp=0\mathcal{V}_p = 0Vp​=0 means the portfolio value will not change even if implied volatility does. Vega is positive when long (long call, long put) and negative when short (short call, short put) — selling an option means losing money if volatility rises. Worked: 200 contracts at vega 5 → Vp=1000\mathcal{V}_p = 1000Vp​=1000 (±$1,000 per point of IV), neutralised by shorting 500 puts at vega −2. The hedge instrument must be an option — and specifically a short one, since that is the only source of negative vega. It matters around earnings and market events, and is largely unnecessary in a stable, low-volatility market.
The CIR theory note adds one term to Vasicek. This note builds it on the same data, and the interesting part is how little of the workbook changes — and where that turns out to be a problem.

The CIR Parameter Est (MLE) sheet is laid out identically to the Vasicek one: 252 observations of the 3-month Treasury rate, with the same seven-column pipeline. Col Label Formula D Actual =C2/100 F r(t)−r(t−1) =D2-D3 G dr (CIR) =$O$2*($O$3-D3)*$O$7 H residual =F2-G2 I pdf =NORMDIST(H2,0,$O$4,FALSE) J ln(pdf) =LN(I2) L2 Sum =SUM(J2:J252) Column G is a(b−rt−1) dta(b - r_{t-1})\,dta(b−rt−1​)dt — the same as Vasicek, which is right, because CIR and Vasicek share a drift. The square root lives only in the diffusion.

Parameter Vasicek CIR aaa — mean reversion speed 0.10232 11.07860 bbb — long-term mean 0.05741 0.05490 σ\sigmaσ — volatility 0.00018280 0.00018093 Log-likelihood 1804.10 1806.81 Two things stand out. The two σ\sigmaσ values are almost identical — 0.00018093 against 0.00018280, a 1% difference. For models whose diffusion terms differ by a factor of rt≈0.235\sqrt{r_t} \approx 0.235rt​​≈0.235, that is suspicious. It is the first sign of the problem below. The two aaa values are not remotely similar. Vasicek fits 0.102, CIR fits 11.08 — a factor of over 100, on the same data. In half-life terms: Half-life ln⁡2/a\ln 2 / aln2/a Vasicek 6.8 years CIR 16 trading days One model says the rate reverts over years, the other over three weeks. Both "fit" the data about equally well (log-likelihoods 1804 and 1807). That is weak identification — as noted in the Vasicek note, one year of data contains very little information about mean reversion, so the optimiser is free to land almost anywhere without the likelihood objecting.

The theory note flagged that CIR's non-negativity guarantee requires the Feller condition: 2ab≥σ22ab \ge \sigma^22ab≥σ2 With the fitted parameters: 2ab=2×11.0786×0.054897=1.2164σ2=3.27×10−82ab = 2 \times 11.0786 \times 0.054897 = 1.2164 \qquad\qquad \sigma^2 = 3.27 \times 10^{-8}2ab=2×11.0786×0.054897=1.2164σ2=3.27×10−8 Comfortably satisfied — by seven orders of magnitude. The simulated rate cannot reach zero, so CIR's headline property holds here.

Look again at column I, in both workbooks: Vasicek: =NORMDIST(H2, 0, $O$4, FALSE) CIR: =NORMDIST(H2, 0, $O$4, FALSE) They are the same formula. But under CIR the residual is not σ dWt\sigma\,dW_tσdWt​ — it is σrt dWt\sigma\sqrt{r_t}\,dW_tσrt​​dWt​, so its standard deviation varies with the rate level and the density should be NORMDIST(H, 0, σrt−1Δt, FALSE)\text{NORMDIST}\left(H,\; 0,\; \sigma\sqrt{r_{t-1}}\sqrt{\Delta t},\; \text{FALSE}\right)NORMDIST(H,0,σrt−1​​Δt​,FALSE) Because the rt\sqrt{r_t}rt​​ is missing, the sheet is fitting a Vasicek likelihood and labelling the answer σCIR\sigma_{CIR}σCIR​. That is why the two volatilities came out nearly equal — they are estimates of the same thing. The consequence appears when the simulation does apply the square root: Value σ\sigmaσ consistent with the data, given r0\sqrt{r_0}r0​​ 0.00077863 σ\sigmaσ actually fitted 0.00018093 Understated by 4.3×
documents.s: The likelihood forgot the square root

documents.t: The CIR Simulation (MLE) sheet is the Vasicek simulation with one insertion — 10 paths across E:N, 252 days down the rows, all starting at r0=0.0552r_0 = 0.0552r0​=0.0552: E3 = $B$1*($B$2-E2)*$B$6 + $B$3*SQRT(E2)*SQRT($B$6)*NORM.S.INV(RAND()) + E2 Set against the Vasicek version, the difference is exactly SQRT(E2): rt+Δt=a(b−rt)Δt+σrt⏟CIR onlyΔt Z+rtr_{t+\Delta t} = a(b - r_t)\Delta t + \sigma\underbrace{\sqrt{r_t}}_{\text{CIR only}}\sqrt{\Delta t}\,Z + r_trt+Δt​=a(b−rt​)Δt+σCIR onlyrt​​​​Δt​Z+rt​ E2 is the previous row's rate, so SQRT(E2) is rt\sqrt{r_t}rt​​ — the theory implemented literally, and correctly. The two defects compound — CIR paths come out 68× too smooth This sheet inherits the units mismatch documented in the Vasicek note (a per-day σ\sigmaσ multiplied by Δt\sqrt{\Delta t}Δt​ a second time), and adds the missing-r\sqrt{r}r​ calibration error above. Together: Daily shock std Actual 3-month rate 0.00018294 Vasicek simulation 0.00001152 — 15.9× too smooth CIR simulation 0.00000268 — 68× too smooth The 68 is the 15.9 from the units mismatch multiplied by the 4.3 from the missing rt\sqrt{r_t}rt​​ in the likelihood. To fix it properly, both ends have to agree: put rt−1Δt\sqrt{r_{t-1}}\sqrt{\Delta t}rt−1​​Δt​ into the calibration's NORMDIST so the fitted σ\sigmaσ is a true annualised CIR volatility, and leave the simulation formula as it stands. The structure of both sheets is right — the columns, the mean reversion, the square root in the simulation, the Feller-safe parameters. It is the scaling that does not survive the trip from one sheet to the other.

Vasicek CIR Equation drt=a(b−rt)dt+σ dWtdr_t = a(b-r_t)dt + \sigma\,dW_tdrt​=a(b−rt​)dt+σdWt​ drt=a(b−rt)dt+σrt dWtdr_t = a(b-r_t)dt + \sigma\sqrt{r_t}\,dW_tdrt​=a(b−rt​)dt+σrt​​dWt​ Rates produced Positive and negative Positive only Fits which economy Germany, Japan US, India, China Calibrated aaa 0.1023 (6.8-year half-life) 11.08 (16-day half-life) Calibrated bbb 0.0574 0.0549 Log-likelihood 1804.10 1806.81 The module's real lesson is in that last row. Two models with materially different dynamics fit the same year of Treasury data almost equally well, and their mean-reversion speeds differ by a factor of 100. Choosing between them cannot be done on goodness-of-fit alone — it has to be done on the structural question the theory note posed: can the rate you are modelling go negative or not? That is the honest state of short-rate modelling. The maths is exact; the calibration is not.

The CIR calibration sheet is structurally identical to the Vasicek one — same seven columns, same drift in column G, since CIR and Vasicek share a drift. Calibrated: aaa = 11.0786, bbb = 0.054897, σ\sigmaσ = 0.00018093, log-likelihood 1806.81. The Feller condition holds easily (2ab=1.222ab = 1.222ab=1.22 vs σ2=3.3×10−8\sigma^2 = 3.3\times10^{-8}σ2=3.3×10−8), so the simulated rate stays positive. The likelihood omits rt\sqrt{r_t}rt​​ — it is a Vasicek likelihood, which is why the two fitted volatilities are nearly equal, and it understates σCIR\sigma_{CIR}σCIR​ by 4.3×. Combined with the inherited units mismatch, CIR's simulated paths are 68× less volatile than the data. The simulation's SQRT(E2) is the theory implemented correctly — the scaling, not the structure, is what breaks. aaa differs by 100× between the two models on identical data while the log-likelihoods barely move: mean reversion is weakly identified in one year of observations.
The Vasicek model ended on a specific flaw: it can produce negative interest rates. CIR is the answer to that, and the fix is one square root.

The CIR model — Cox-Ingersoll-Ross — is a mathematical model which is used to model interest rate movement. It was developed in 1985 by John C. Cox, Jonathan E. Ingersoll and Stephen A. Ross. The CIR interest rate model is also called a "one factor model", because it describes interest rate movement as driven by a sole source of market risk. Both models share that property: CIR→f(market risk)Vasicek→f(market risk)\text{CIR} \rightarrow f(\text{market risk}) \qquad\qquad \text{Vasicek} \rightarrow f(\text{market risk})CIR→f(market risk)Vasicek→f(market risk) One component, one factor. Which is a simplification, because in reality the interest rate responds to monetary policy, market sentiment, inflation and economic policy — four forces compressed into one term.

drt=a(b−rt) dt+σrt dWt \boxed{\;dr_t = a(b - r_t)\,dt + \sigma\sqrt{r_t}\,dW_t\;}drt​=a(b−rt​)dt+σrt​​dWt​​ Symbol Meaning drtdr_tdrt​ Change in rtr_trt​ (the interest rate) aaa Speed of mean reversion bbb Mean of the interest rate dtdtdt Change in time σ\sigmaσ Volatility of the interest rate rtr_trt​ Interest rate dWtdW_tdWt​ Wiener process / Brownian motion — the random fluctuation that happens in the interest rate Set it beside Vasicek and the difference is a single factor: Vasicek:drt=a(b−rt) dt+σ dWt\text{Vasicek:}\quad dr_t = a(b - r_t)\,dt + \sigma\,dW_tVasicek:drt​=a(b−rt​)dt+σdWt​CIR:drt=a(b−rt) dt+σ rt⏟the addition dWt\text{CIR:}\quad dr_t = a(b - r_t)\,dt + \sigma\,\underbrace{\sqrt{r_t}}_{\text{the addition}}\,dW_tCIR:drt​=a(b−rt​)dt+σthe additionrt​​​​dWt​ rt\sqrt{r_t}rt​​ is the additional component that is added to the Vasicek equation to give CIR. The drift is untouched. Mean reversion works exactly as before — the two cases are identical to Vasicek's: Direction b>rtb > r_tb>rt​ b−rt>0⇒drt>0b - r_t > 0 \Rightarrow dr_t > 0b−rt​>0⇒drt​>0 Adjust the interest rate upwards b<rtb < r_tb<rt​ b−rt<0⇒drt<0b - r_t < 0 \Rightarrow dr_t < 0b−rt​<0⇒drt​<0 Adjust the interest rate downward with aaa, dtdtdt and rt\sqrt{r_t}rt​​ all positive, so the sign of (b−rt)(b - r_t)(b−rt​) decides everything.

The square root of any number is always positive. That is the whole argument, and it works through the size of the shock rather than its sign: σσ√rVasicek — constantCIR — shrinks with r0interest rate rshock sizeno shock at r = 0 In Vasicek, the shock is σ dWt\sigma\,dW_tσdWt​ — the same size at every rate level. So when rtr_trt​ is already near zero, a normal draw of the usual magnitude can push it straight through into negative territory. In CIR, the shock is σrt dWt\sigma\sqrt{r_t}\,dW_tσrt​​dWt​. As rtr_trt​ falls toward zero, rt\sqrt{r_t}rt​​ falls toward zero too, so the randomness switches itself off exactly where it would do damage. At rt=0r_t = 0rt​=0 the diffusion term vanishes entirely and only the drift ab dtab\,dtabdt remains — which is positive, pushing the rate back up. CIR →rt→\rightarrow \sqrt{r_t} \rightarrow→rt​​→ positive value →\rightarrow→ interest rates can't go negative. The guarantee has a condition The notes state non-negativity as absolute. Strictly, CIR keeps the rate strictly positive only when the Feller condition holds: 2ab≥σ22ab \ge \sigma^22ab≥σ2 If volatility is large relative to the mean-reversion pull, the rate can still touch zero (though it cannot pass through it). Worth knowing, and it is checked against the calibrated parameters in the CIR Excel note.
documents.s: Why the square root fixes negative rates

documents.t: 1) It assumes mean reversion. This means the interest rate tends to move towards the long-term equilibrium level over time — rising when it sits below bbb, falling when above. 2) It assumes aaa, bbb and σ\sigmaσ are constant. aaa speed of mean reversion bbb long-term mean σ\sigmaσ volatility / standard deviation The notes flag this immediately with a question: for a stock ABC, will volatility always remain constant? Obviously not — and the note beside it is blunt about what that means: Assumption → limitation. The long-term mean bbb in particular has to be obtained by calibrating the model to market data, and it is economy-specific — the US economy has one level, India and China another.

Vasicek CIR Equation drt=a(b−rt)dt+σ dWtdr_t = a(b - r_t)dt + \sigma\,dW_tdrt​=a(b−rt​)dt+σdWt​ drt=a(b−rt)dt+σrt dWtdr_t = a(b - r_t)dt + \sigma\sqrt{r_t}\,dW_tdrt​=a(b−rt​)dt+σrt​​dWt​ Rates it can produce Positive and negative Positive only Diffusion Constant Proportional to rt\sqrt{r_t}rt​​ Which model to use is therefore an empirical question about the economy you are modelling, not a matter of taste: Economy Rates observed Use USA, India, China Positive CIR Germany, Japan Have gone to 0 or negative Vasicek The notes are direct about the mismatch: for economies whose rates are firmly positive, a model that generates negative rates "makes no sense". And conversely — if you need to represent a genuinely negative rate, CIR structurally cannot do it. So the fix is not free. CIR trades away the ability to model negative rates in exchange for never producing spurious ones.

a) It assumes constant aaa, bbb and σ\sigmaσ. In reality these parameters might change due to changes in market and economic conditions. The assumption that made the model tractable is the same one that makes it wrong over long horizons. b) It is not suitable for modelling negative interest rates. The rt\sqrt{r_t}rt​​ term makes the interest rate non-negative — which is a feature in the US and a defect in Germany. c) It is a single-factor model. drt=a(b−rt) dt⏟+σrt dWt⏟random fluctuationdr_t = \underbrace{a(b - r_t)\,dt}_{} + \sigma\sqrt{r_t}\,\underbrace{dW_t}_{\text{random fluctuation}}drt​=a(b−rt​)dt​​+σrt​​random fluctuationdWt​​​ with rtr_trt​ as the sole market risk factor. But interest rates can rely on multiple factors — market sentiment and economic policies among them — and a one-factor model cannot separate them. d) No jumps or discontinuities. The CIR model assumes a continuous path for the interest rate. This may not reflect real-world market behaviour, which can include jumps or sudden changes due to unexpected events. A central bank announcement moves rates in a step, not a wiggle. Brownian motion has continuous paths by construction, so no amount of parameter tuning will reproduce that.

The two in this module are the start of a family: Model 1 Vasicek 2 CIR 3 Hull-White (John C. Hull) 4 Black-Karasinski 5 Libor Market Model 6 Heath-Jarrow-Morton Each relaxes one of the assumptions above — time-varying parameters, log-normal rates, or modelling the whole forward curve rather than a single short rate.

CIR (Cox, Ingersoll and Ross, 1985) is a one-factor stochastic interest rate model: drt=a(b−rt) dt+σrt dWtdr_t = a(b - r_t)\,dt + \sigma\sqrt{r_t}\,dW_tdrt​=a(b−rt​)dt+σrt​​dWt​. It is Vasicek plus rt\sqrt{r_t}rt​​ in the diffusion term. The drift, and therefore the mean-reversion behaviour, is unchanged. That square root is what prevents negative rates: as rtr_trt​ approaches zero the shock shrinks to nothing, leaving only the upward drift. (Strictly, under the Feller condition 2ab≥σ22ab \ge \sigma^22ab≥σ2.) Use CIR where rates are positive (US, India, China); use Vasicek where they can go negative (Germany, Japan). Neither dominates. Limitations: constant parameters, cannot model negative rates, only one risk factor, and no jumps — real rates move in steps that a continuous path cannot reproduce. The wider family includes Hull-White, Black-Karasinski, the Libor Market Model and Heath-Jarrow-Morton.

The theory note gives the model. It does not give the numbers. The three parameters — aaa, bbb and σ\sigmaσ — have to come from observed data, and the method for extracting them is maximum likelihood estimation.

MLE is a method which is used to find the best-fitting parameters for a mathematical model, based on observed data. Applied here, that means finding aaa, bbb and σ\sigmaσ in drt=a(b−rt) dt+σ dWtdr_t = a(b - r_t)\,dt + \sigma\,dW_tdrt​=a(b−rt​)dt+σdWt​ The principle in the notes' own words: Adjust the parameters in such a way that the values generated from the Vasicek model closely align with the actual data. So there are two columns of numbers — what the rate actually did, and what the model says it should have done — and calibration is the search for the parameters that make the gap between them as small (as likely) as possible.

1. Calculate drtdr_tdrt​ — for both the actual data and the Vasicek model. Actual rate Vasicek Δr\Delta rΔr actual Δr\Delta rΔr Vasicek TTT 5.0% 4.5% T−1T-1T−1 5.1% 4.75% 5.0% − 5.1% 4.5% − 4.75% T−2T-2T−2 5.05% 4.6% 5.1% − 5.05% 4.75% − 4.6% T−3T-3T−3 5.15% ⋮ ⋮ ⋮ 2. Calculate the residual — the error term: Residual=ΔrActual−ΔrVasicek\text{Residual} = \Delta r_{\text{Actual}} - \Delta r_{\text{Vasicek}}Residual=ΔrActual​−ΔrVasicek​ 3. Take a normal distribution of the residual, with Mean=0Std deviation=σ\text{Mean} = 0 \qquad\qquad \text{Std deviation} = \sigmaMean=0Std deviation=σ The residual is assumed normally distributed around a mean of 0. This is not an arbitrary assumption — it falls straight out of the model. The deterministic part is what the model predicted; whatever is left over is the realisation of σ dWt\sigma\,dW_tσdWt​, and dWtdW_tdWt​ is normal with mean zero by construction. So the residuals should look like normal draws, and σ\sigmaσ is exactly the parameter that says how wide they should be. 4. Take the log likelihood. Each residual gets a probability density from that normal distribution; take the log of each. 5. Sum all the logs, and maximise the sum — by changing aaa, bbb and σ\sigmaσ. We are trying to maximise the likelihood of the function by changing the parameters aaa, bbb, σ\sigmaσ.

Since we are working with multiple time steps, the total likelihood of the entire dataset is the product of the likelihood of each individual time step. L=A×B×C×⋯L = A \times B \times C \times \cdotsL=A×B×C×⋯ And a product of many probability densities is awkward — multiply 251 small numbers together and you underflow to zero. The logarithm turns it into something tractable: log⁡(A×B×C×⋯ )=log⁡(A)+log⁡(B)+log⁡(C)+⋯\log(A \times B \times C \times \cdots) = \log(A) + \log(B) + \log(C) + \cdotslog(A×B×C×⋯)=log(A)+log(B)+log(C)+⋯ A product becomes a sum. Since the logarithm is monotonically increasing, whatever maximises the log-likelihood also maximises the likelihood — so nothing is lost by optimising the easier quantity.

The data is the US Treasury yield curve — the workbook carries full 2024 and 2023 sheets with the 1 Mo through 10 Yr columns. The calibration uses the 3-month rate, 252 observations. The Vasicek Parameter Est (MLE) sheet is the five steps as seven columns: Col Label Formula Step C 3 Mo the raw quote, e.g. 5.52 D Actual =C2/100 → 0.0552 convert percent to decimal E Return =(D2/D3-1) F r(t)−r(t−1) =D2-D3 1 — actual drdrdr G dr (V) =$O$2*($O$3-D3)*$O$7 1 — model drdrdr H residual =F2-G2 2 — the error I pdf =NORMDIST(H2,0,$O$4,FALSE) 3 — normal density J ln(pdf) =LN(I2) 4 — log L2 Sum =SUM(J2:J252) 5 — the objective Two details worth noticing. Column G has no random term. It is only a(b−rt−1) dta(b - r_{t-1})\,dta(b−rt−1​)dt — the deterministic part. That is correct and it is the point: the model's prediction is the drift, and the residual in column H is what the stochastic term must have supplied. Calibration then asks which σ\sigmaσ makes those residuals most plausible. NORMDIST(..., FALSE) returns the density, not the cumulative probability. The FALSE is what selects the PDF — exactly what a likelihood needs.

Cell Parameter Initial guess Calibrated O2 mean reverting speed aaa — 0.10232419 O3 long-term mean bbb 0.05 0.05740609 O4 volatility σ\sigmaσ =STDEV.S(E2:E252) 0.00018280 O5 initial rate r0r_0r0​ =D2 → 0.0552 O6 n_days 252 O7 dtdtdt =1/O6 → 0.00396825 Maximised log-likelihood: 1804.0966. Excel's Solver does the maximising, changing O2:O4 to push L2 as high as it will go.

Worth checking rather than assuming, and there is a clean test. If MLE is doing its job, the fitted σ\sigmaσ should come out close to the actual standard deviation of the daily rate changes — because that is what the residuals are. Value Std deviation of daily changes in the 3-month rate 0.00018294 Calibrated σ\sigmaσ 0.00018280 They agree to four significant figures. The calibration recovered the volatility correctly — a small but real confirmation that the likelihood was set up right. Where the data is thinner than it looks Two things about the input are worth knowing. The 3-month rate is quoted to two decimal places, so 86 of the 251 daily changes (34%) are exactly zero — the rate simply printed the same number two days running. That rounding does not break the fit above, but it means the "daily volatility" being measured is partly a quantisation artifact. aaa and bbb are weakly identified over one year. The fitted a=0.1023a = 0.1023a=0.1023 implies a mean-reversion half-life of ln⁡2a=0.6930.1023≈6.8 years\frac{\ln 2}{a} = \frac{0.693}{0.1023} \approx 6.8 \text{ years}aln2​=0.10230.693​≈6.8 years Over a single year of data, a process reverting on a 6.8-year timescale barely reverts at all — so the data contains very little information about where bbb actually is. That is why the fitted bbb (5.74%) sits noticeably above the sample average rate (5.49%) without the fit objecting. σ\sigmaσ is pinned down by 251 observations; aaa and bbb are not. This is a general feature of short-rate calibration, not a mistake in the sheet — mean reversion is a slow phenomenon and short samples struggle to see it.

The Vasicek Simulation (MLE) sheet takes the three fitted parameters and runs the model forward — 10 simulations across columns E:N, 252 days down the rows. Cell Holds B1, B2, B3 the calibrated aaa, bbb, σ\sigmaσ B4 r0=0.0552r_0 = 0.0552r0​=0.0552 B5 / B6 n_days = 252, dtdtdt = =1/B5 E2:N2 =$B$4 — every path starts at r0r_0r0​ and the step itself: E3 = $B$1*($B$2-E2)*$B$6 + $B$3*SQRT($B$6)*NORM.S.INV(RAND()) + E2 which reads directly as the Euler discretisation of the SDE: rt+Δt=a(b−rt) Δt⏟drift+σΔt Z⏟shock+rt⏟where we werer_{t+\Delta t} = \underbrace{a(b - r_t)\,\Delta t}_{\text{drift}} + \underbrace{\sigma\sqrt{\Delta t}\,Z}_{\text{shock}} + \underbrace{r_t}_{\text{where we were}}rt+Δt​=drifta(b−rt​)Δt​​+shockσΔt​Z​​+where we werert​​​ The shape of that step is right — drift scaled by Δt\Delta tΔt, shock by Δt\sqrt{\Delta t}Δt​ — unlike the Monte Carlo workbooks in Module 4, which scaled the drift by Δt\sqrt{\Delta t}Δt​ too. But the units of σ\sigmaσ do not line up between the two sheets. The simulation is 15.9× too smooth — a units mismatch The calibration sheet fits σ\sigmaσ with =NORMDIST(H2, 0, $O$4, FALSE) where H2 is a one-day residual. So the fitted σ\sigmaσ is already a per-day standard deviation — and indeed it came out at 0.00018280 against a measured daily-change standard deviation of 0.00018294. The simulation sheet then multiplies it by Δt\sqrt{\Delta t}Δt​ again: $B$3*SQRT($B$6)*NORM.S.INV(RAND()) which treats that same number as an annualised volatility. The result: Daily shock std Actual 3-month rate 0.00018294 Simulated by the sheet 0.00001152 Ratio 0.0629 — that is 1/2521/\sqrt{252}1/252​ The simulated paths are 15.9× less volatile than the data they were calibrated on. You can see it in the saved values: the first path moves 0.0552 → 0.05518 → 0.05520 in steps of about 2×10⁻⁵, where the real rate moves in steps of about 1.8×10⁻⁴. Either fix works, not both: calibrate against the scaled quantity — NORMDIST(H2, 0, $O$4*SQRT($O$7), FALSE) — so σ\sigmaσ is annualised, or drop the Δt\sqrt{\Delta t}Δt​ from the simulation — $B$3*NORM.S.INV(RAND()) — keeping σ\sigmaσ per-day. Because the rate is added back rather than compounded, the process is arithmetic — which is precisely why it can cross zero into negative territory, the limitation the CIR model sets out to fix.

MLE finds the best-fitting parameters for a model given observed data — here aaa, bbb and σ\sigmaσ for Vasicek. The five steps: compute drdrdr for actual and model → take the residual → assume it is normal with mean 0 and std σ\sigmaσ → take logs → sum and maximise by changing the parameters. The log turns a product of 251 densities into a sum, which is both numerically stable and easier to maximise; being monotonic, it does not change where the maximum is. The model column carries only the drift; the residual is what σ dWt\sigma\,dW_tσdWt​ must have contributed. Calibrated on the 3-month Treasury: aaa = 0.1023, bbb = 0.0574, σ\sigmaσ = 0.00018280, log-likelihood 1804.10. The fit checks out — σ\sigmaσ matches the sample standard deviation of daily changes (0.00018294) to four significant figures. But aaa and bbb are weakly identified, because a 6.8-year half-life barely shows up in one year of data. The simulation sheet has the right Euler shape but a units mismatch: the calibration returns a per-day σ\sigmaσ and the simulation multiplies it by Δt\sqrt{\Delta t}Δt​ again, making the paths 15.9× too smooth. Fix it at one end or the other, not both.
Every model so far has been about a stock. This module changes the underlying: the thing being modelled is the interest rate.

Look at daily data for, say, the US 3-year Treasury rate and you see the same thing you see in a stock chart — a jagged, unpredictable line. The pattern that we see in the interest rate is random in nature. So it needs the same treatment: for modelling the randomness of interest rates, we use a stochastic interest rate model. This module covers two of them — Vasicek and CIR — in theory, and then in Excel, where there are two separate jobs: calibrate the model (with MLE) and then implement it.
documents.s: Why a stochastic model at all

documents.t: The Vasicek model was introduced by Oldrich Vasicek in 1977. It is a stochastic interest rate model used to model how interest rates will move in the future. drt=a(b−rt) dt+σ dWt \boxed{\;dr_t = a(b - r_t)\,dt + \sigma\,dW_t\;}drt​=a(b−rt​)dt+σdWt​​ Term by term: Symbol Meaning rtr_trt​ The interest rate at time ttt drtdr_tdrt​ The change in the interest rate aaa Speed of mean reversion — how fast the rate returns to the mean bbb Long-term average rate dtdtdt Small change in time — 1/252 σ\sigmaσ Volatility of the interest rate dWtdW_tdWt​ Wiener process / Brownian motion Where bbb comes from: take the historical data — the notes use 3-year Treasury data — and average it. That average is bbb. Why 1/252: a year has 365 days, minus Saturdays, Sundays and holidays, leaving 252 trading days. dt=1252dt = \frac{1}{252}dt=2521​ What dWtdW_tdWt​ is doing: it represents the random, unpredictable fluctuation that you see in the interest rate over time, and in practice it is generated exactly as in the previous module: dWt=Zt×ΔtdW_t = Z_t \times \sqrt{\Delta t}dWt​=Zt​×Δt​ where ZtZ_tZt​ is a random number generated from a standard normal distribution.

The notes list the real-world causes that dWtdW_tdWt​ is standing in for: economic news policy change market sentiment None of them are predictable, which is why they are modelled as Brownian motion rather than forecast.
documents.s: Why rates fluctuate in the first place

documents.t: The equation splits cleanly, and this split is the whole model: Term Name Job a(b−rt) dta(b - r_t)\,dta(b−rt​)dt Deterministic part / mean reversion Drives the interest rate toward the long-term bbb σ dWt\sigma\,dW_tσdWt​ Stochastic part Captures the random and unpredictable deviation from the deterministic trajectory The first term knows where the rate should go. The second term is everything that stops it getting there in a straight line.
documents.s: Two parts, doing two different jobs

documents.t: The mean-reverting component is a(b−rt) dta(b - r_t)\,dta(b−rt​)dt, and its sign is what matters. Note that aaa and dtdtdt are both always positive — dt=1/252dt = 1/252dt=1/252, and aaa is a speed. So the sign of the whole term is decided by (b−rt)(b - r_t)(b−rt​) alone. brₜ > brₜ < bdrₜ < 0drₜ > 0pulled down toward bpushed up toward b Case 1 — the rate is above the mean (rt>br_t > brt​>b). rt>b ⟹ (b−rt)<0 ⟹ drt<0r_t > b \;\Longrightarrow\; (b - r_t) < 0 \;\Longrightarrow\; dr_t < 0rt​>b⟹(b−rt​)<0⟹drt​<0 The change is negative, so the model adjusts the short rate downward. Case 2 — the rate is below the mean (rt<br_t < brt​<b). rt<b ⟹ (b−rt)>0 ⟹ drt>0r_t < b \;\Longrightarrow\; (b - r_t) > 0 \;\Longrightarrow\; dr_t > 0rt​<b⟹(b−rt​)>0⟹drt​>0 The change is positive, so the model adjusts the short rate upward. The direction of the short rate depends on the values of bbb and rtr_trt​. Direction rt>br_t > brt​>b drt<0dr_t < 0drt​<0 Downwards rt<br_t < brt​<b drt>0dr_t > 0drt​>0 Upwards That is mean reversion in one line: the further the rate is from bbb, and the larger aaa is, the harder it is pulled back.

a) It is intuitive. The concept of mean reversion aligns with how many people think about interest rates — returning to a normal level after a period of being high or low. The model's central assumption is one most practitioners already hold. b) It has an analytical solution. It is possible to derive a closed-form solution for certain use cases — notably bond pricing and risk management. The notes make "closed form" concrete with the simplest possible example: x+2=5x + 2 = 5x+2=5 solves directly to x=3x = 3x=3. No iteration, no simulation. Vasicek admits that kind of solution, which is why it survived — you can price a bond with a formula rather than a Monte Carlo run.

a) It can produce negative interest rates. It can produce a negative interest rate, which can be unrealistic in the case where interest rates are high. The culprit is identifiable: the stochastic part σ dWt\sigma\,dW_tσdWt​ is responsible for negative interest rates. Since dWtdW_tdWt​ is normally distributed, it is unbounded below — a large enough negative draw can push rtr_trt​ through zero, and nothing in the equation stops it. Whether that is a flaw depends on where you are: Rates USA, India, Pakistan, Sri Lanka, China Positive Germany, Japan Have seen negative rates So negative rates are not impossible in reality — but a model that produces them in a high-rate economy is producing nonsense. This is exactly what the CIR model fixes, and it is why the next note exists. b) It is a single-factor model. The model is driven by market risk, which is the only factor affecting the change in the interest rate. One source of randomness, one dWtdW_tdWt​. Everything that moves rates in reality — policy, inflation, credit, liquidity — is compressed into that single term.

Interest rates are random in nature, so they are modelled with a stochastic interest rate model. Vasicek (Oldrich Vasicek, 1977): drt=a(b−rt) dt+σ dWtdr_t = a(b - r_t)\,dt + \sigma\,dW_tdrt​=a(b−rt​)dt+σdWt​. aaa is the speed of mean reversion, bbb the long-term average rate (the historical average), σ\sigmaσ the volatility, dt=1/252dt = 1/252dt=1/252, and dWt=ZtΔtdW_t = Z_t\sqrt{\Delta t}dWt​=Zt​Δt​ the Brownian shock. The equation is deterministic mean reversion + a stochastic deviation: one term pulls toward bbb, the other knocks it off course. Above the mean the drift is negative, below it positive — the rate is always being pulled back toward bbb. Strengths: intuitive, and it has a closed-form solution usable for bond pricing and risk management. Limitations: it can generate negative rates (the σ dWt\sigma\,dW_tσdWt​ term is unbounded below), and it is a single-factor model.
The interest rate swap exchanged one kind of interest for another in the same currency. A currency swap crosses the currency boundary, and that one change alters the mechanics considerably.

A currency swap is a financial derivative that commits 2 counterparties to exchange streams of interest payments and principal payments in different currencies. Currency swaps are typically used by institutions to manage exposure to foreign exchange.

An Indian company owes $100,000 three months from now. Today the bank quotes 1 USD = ₹85, so the obligation is ₹8,500,000. But the rate moves every day — 82, 84, 85, 86 — and in three months it could be anything. The amount should not be reduced. The company does not want its rupee cost floating around with the exchange rate. A currency swap fixes the terms of the exchange in advance, converting an uncertain FX exposure into a known schedule.

Unlike an IRS, a currency swap exchanges principal as well as interest — and it does so twice. 1) Initial exchange of principal. At the inception of the swap, the principal amounts in 2 different currencies are exchanged between the counterparties at a spot rate. 2) Exchange of interest payments. Interest payments between the 2 counterparties are exchanged — on each payment date through the life of the swap. 3) Re-exchange of principal. At the maturity of the swap, the original principal amounts are swapped back at the same exchange rate as at the inception, regardless of the prevailing market exchange rate. t=0⏟principal exchanged → t=1,2,3,4⏟interest exchanged → t=5⏟principal + final interest\underbrace{t=0}_{\text{principal exchanged}} \;\rightarrow\; \underbrace{t=1,2,3,4}_{\text{interest exchanged}} \;\rightarrow\; \underbrace{t=5}_{\text{principal + final interest}}principal exchangedt=0​​→interest exchangedt=1,2,3,4​​→principal + final interestt=5​​ This is why the principal is real here In an interest rate swap both legs are in the same currency, so exchanging identical principals would be pointless — they would cancel. Hence "notional". In a currency swap the two principals are in different currencies, so they do not cancel. Exchanging them is the entire point: it is how each party gets the currency it actually needs. And because the re-exchange happens at the inception rate regardless of the prevailing market rate, the FX risk over the swap's life is removed — which is precisely what the Indian importer above was trying to achieve.

Type Structure 1 Fixed for Fixed Both parties exchange fixed interest payments 2 Fixed for Floating One party pays a fixed rate, the other pays a floating rate 3 Floating for Floating Both parties exchange floating interest payments — in different currencies
